The *Śrī-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*,
composed by the venerable *Īśānaśivagurudevamiśra*.

(I take refuge in) that Lord of Speech, Giriśa; that Speech, Gaurī; and Gaṇeśa, the elephant-faced one; and Durgā, the remover of the distress of those in difficulty; and Viriñca, Lakṣmī, and also Lakṣmī’s Lord. (1.1)
With a concentrated mind, I bow to my gurus, who are exceedingly venerable, more weighty than the heavy, equal to all yet most exalted;
who, like the risen sun through their great majesty, dispel the darkness of great delusion.
Having considered as far as my capacity allows, I shall compose a manual for the tantras, based on various extensive and distinguished tantras. (1–3)

It possesses a coherent collection of its own meanings that does not depend on other systems, like another Veda upon the sacrificial altar, made known through perfected ritual procedures and the significance of mantras. (1.4)
Clear, not overly crooked, neither too concise nor too prolix,
variegated and possessing many virtues— like the serpent Bhogavatī, it was the bed of Viṣṇu.
It is composed in various meters, adorned with diverse poetic figures and descriptions;
it is to be cultivated by those who desire pleasure, as beloved as a graceful young woman. (1.6)

She was like the life-restoring science (*sañjīvinī-vidyā*), which shows the means for pacifying poisons, planetary afflictions, diseases, and the like, through mantras, images, medicinal herbs, and meditations.
By means of subduing enemies, expulsion, inciting hatred, paralyzing, bewildering, ruining,
and killing, it was like another form of the science of statecraft (daṇḍanīti).
She was as skillful as the form of the Enemy of Mura (Kṛṣṇa) when he subdued Pūtanā, Naraka, Ariṣṭa, and others, closely embraced by Satyabhāmā.
It was joined with many Manus and likewise with the gods;
it consisted of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages, like an autumn of Brahmā.
Accessible only by those who know the path of their own secret conventions through various means,
she is like another inaccessible terrain from which all calamities have been driven away.
The Dvāpara age has departed through the son of Dharma’s attainment of heaven;
here, the course of time is as bitter as the onset of the Kali age.
It was endowed with four feet that produced meanings not excessively divergent,
and it was dependent upon the sequence of the four ages, like a creation of Brahmā.

Even a single form, such as that of Vināyaka, which possesses the distinct characteristics of both the upper half of an elephant and the lower half of a human, [is perceived as a single entity]. (1.14)
Just as one knows the power of a great magician’s net— which produces a proliferation of cognitions,
which is known only through the conviction of those who know it, and which bestows liberation— so too is the sovereign power of the Lord.
Like the three Vedas, she brings about liberation and is to be known through their respective successive stages.

For human beings are indeed accompanied by their preparatory practices, along with their limbs, deities, and rites; they possess Vedic meters, sages, and directional bindings; they are endowed with meditations and purposes. 1-17.
And those mantras, along with their ritual prescriptions, are observed; they are of four kinds:
seed-syllables (*bīja*), seed-mantras (*bījamantra*), mantras, and those known as garland-mantras (*mālāmantra*). (1–18)
From the combination of various syllables, there may arise a single seed-syllable (*bīja*). Seed-mantras consist of fewer than ten syllables, while other mantras consist of fewer than twenty. (1.19)
Those which consist of more than twenty syllables are *mālāmantras*; generally, their seed-syllables (*bījas*) bestow abundant accomplishment (*siddhi*) even in childhood. (1.20)
Seed-mantras (bījamantra) belong to the stage of youth and grant success in youth;
however, garland-mantras (mālāmantra) always bring success even in old age.

Through the constant practice of faith and devotion, all things are always accomplished; for the nature of the deity resides in the mantra, which possesses the quality of protecting through contemplation. (1.22)
Where that which is known as "mantra" exists, it does not reside in the seed-syllables (*bīja*).
Here, in this Triple Gem (*ratnatraya*),
[it is so called] because it protects all beings from the ocean of saṃsāra through its power of reflection (*manana*).
"For that power, whose nature is that of mantra, has the characteristic of protecting through reflection. Thus [it is said].
Having realized the identity of the signified and the signifier, even with respect to the Guru.
Therefore, for the sake of self-realization, one should cultivate devotion toward that deity which is equal to [the chosen mantra];
for the Mātṛkā is indeed the source of all mantras and of all sounds. (1.24)
She, however, is considered to have arisen from Śakti and to consist of the essence of the seed of Śakti;
she is Brahman, whose nature is free from conceptual construction and whose form is eternal bliss. (1-25)
That is auspicious, immovable, the inherent nature of the universe, the supreme illuminator;
it is exceedingly subtle, eternal, solid, all-pervasive, omnipresent, and subtler than the subtlest atom.

Even from that which is great, there arises a greater purity consisting of the emergence of will, knowledge, and action, due to the maintenance of knowledge, desire to act, and effort at the beginning of the primary creation. (1.27)
Just as a lamp brings about the manifestation of its own light, so too do these—sattva, rajas, and tamas—manifest their own powers, possessing respectively white, red, and black radiance. (1.28)
Power (śakti) is indeed unborn, one, and the ordainer of the manifestation of the universe;
that power attains the state of the bindu, and that bindu also becomes threefold. (1.29)
Bindu, nāda, and rava—this rava is considered unmanifest (avyakta).
From the unmanifest arises the principle named Mahat, which is threefold.
And from the Mahat, the ego (ahaṃkāra) arises; it is said to be threefold:
the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the other, the Bhūtādi. (1.31)
From that *śākta* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the voiced letter *ha* arose. Regarding this, the venerable *Kālottara* states: "That supreme seed called *nāda*, which resides within all beings..."
It bestows liberation, is supremely divine, and grants all spiritual accomplishments.
"Peaceful, all-pervading, and empty, it abides through twelve measures;
the short vowels are declared to be Brahmā, while the long vowels, O Six-faced One, are indeed the limbs. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the Three Jewels as well: "That sound, which arises from the agitation of the *bindu* for the sake of accomplishing the infinite goal, is fourfold through the divisions of *vāk*, *vaikharī*, and so forth."
Power (śakti), resonance (nāda), the great illusion (mahāmāyā), and the void (vyoman)—thus it is fourfold.
Furthermore, from this very *bindu*, four modes of operation (*vṛtti*) are traditionally taught:
Vaikharī, Madhyamā, Paśyantī, and Sūkṣmā.
These [powers] arise in reverse order from Kuṇḍalinī onwards;
Sūkṣmā is in the middle of Kuṇḍalinī, consisting of pure light and extremely subtle.
Therefore, she who is beyond the range of hearing arises upward;
self-luminous, she becomes the Paśyantī [speech], resting upon the Suṣumṇā.
That very [power], having reached the heart-lotus, becomes the central channel (madhyamā) in the form of sound;
it consists merely of internal discourse and moves upward without being differentiated.
That very [speech] resides in the chest, throat, and palate; it reaches the head, nose, and teeth;
it issues from the root of the tongue and the lips; thus it assumes the form of articulated phonemes.
Vaikharī, which is perceivable by the ear and gives rise to the proliferation of sounds, is the letter *ha* along with its modifications; then it was joined with the letter *ra*. (1.38)
Therefore, it assumed the vowel *ī*, adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*;
for through union with that, it became the seed-syllable of Śakti, the cause of the emergence of the phenomenal world. (1.39)
When the two forms, masculine and prakṛti, are joined and uttered with a pun (*śliṣṭa*), that verbal form is declared to be the seed (*bīja*) [of the double entendre]. (1.40)
The letter *ha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while the letter *ra* is declared to be fire;
the letter *ī* is Māyā, and the nasal dot (*bindu*) is called Īśvara. (1.41)
Nāda should be known as Sadāśiva, while the end of nāda (nādānta) is Śiva himself;
it is the letter *ha* that has attained manifestation, intended as the resonance within the heart.
Having attained the state of being "A," its differentiation is indeed the conjunction with syllables;
for its six syllables, beginning with A and ending with U, are as follows: || 1.43 ||

There would be a specific modification of the letter *ra* into *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*; however, due to the distinction of the vowel *ī*, there are six letters beginning with *e* that are proximate to it. (1.44)
Thus, the sixteen [vowels] produced from the seed-syllable of Śakti are called *svara* (vowels);
because they are limbs of Śakti, they are the *kalās* (aspects), consisting of the digits of the Moon. || 1.45 ||
The short vowels joined with the nasal drop (bindu) are masculine and have the nature of fire and the sun;
the long vowels ending in the visarga are feminine and have the nature of the moon.
The group of four—ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ—is lunar, fiery, and neuter;
it is written here first, at the beginning of the emergence of the vowels.
Thus concludes the section on vowels.

The letter *ha*, possessing the quality of sound (*śabda*), first produced the letter *a*. From space (*vyoman*) arose air (*vāyu*) with the quality of touch (*sparśa*); from that touch, the consonants beginning with *ka* came into being. (1.48)
Those five groups of five syllables each are devoid of the letter *a*.
However, the tetrad of letters beginning with *ya* is the body of air, fire, earth, and water.

Touch, form, smell, and that which is called taste are their qualities respectively; the remaining elements, beginning with space (śa), are all-pervasive, accompanied by fire and moon, and possess vowels and consonants as their touch.
Thus, fifty phonemes have arisen through the differentiation of Śakti:
the twenty-five letters beginning with *ka*, as well as those beginning with *ya* and *śa*. (1.51)
Indeed, [the consonants] arise from the vowel *a* through differences in place and effort; they also arise from the mutual conjunction of consonants with vowels such as *a* and others. (1.52)
The entire proliferation of sound clearly arises as manifold; this is the domain of the *hal* consonants. That very power becomes twofold: namely, the *Tāra* and the *Vāgbhava*. (1.53)
The syllable 'A', the syllable 'U', and the syllable 'M', together with the Bindu and Nāda—this is indeed the Praṇava known as Tārā, considered to be the very essence of Śabdabrahman. (1.54)
The seed-syllable of Vāgbhava is said to be enriched with the vowel *a*, the nasal drop (*bindu*), and the resonance (*nāda*);
it bestows the power of speech upon the universe and constitutes the very body of Vāgīśvarī. (1.55)
The Praṇava is Śiva himself, while Vāgbhava is the sovereign Śakti;
likewise, the Śakti-bīja is the Tāra, and after that follows Vāgbhava. (1.56)
The fifty letters beginning with 'a' in their proper sequence, and the various distinct speeches arising from their permutations that belong to different regions; || 1.57 ||
The Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, the Purāṇas, and various Śāstras;
the elements beginning with space, the subtle elements, and the sense organs. || 1.58 ||

The mind, the intellect, the ego, attachment, time, and likewise the creative powers (kalās)—what is the use of much talk? Whatever consists of the nature of sound and meaning is entirely [He]. (1.59)
This phenomenal world (prapañca) indeed arises from Śakti; therefore, Śakti is Mātṛkā.
For within this one called Mātṛkā, the nature of "writing" (lipitva) is inscribed.
It is "akṣara" (the imperishable) because of the absence of decay; it is "varṇa" (color/letter) because it comprises all colors (or letters);
it is "arṇa" (water) because its nature is nectar, since water is said to be "arṇas. || 1.61 ||
Air, fire, water, earth, and ether— these five, consisting of the letters *ha*, *ra*, *va*, *la*, and *a*, are indeed the material causes of the Mātṛkā who is the soul of the universe.
The *a*-group together with its vowels constitutes her face; the *ka*- and *ca*-groups are her two arms;
likewise, the *ṭa*- and *ta*-groups are her two feet; and the *pa* and *pha* sounds are considered her two sides.
The letter *ba* is the back, the letter *bha* is the navel, and from the letter *ma* comes the heart;
the letters beginning with *ya* correspond to skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
The seven elements are the colors; the letter *ha* is held to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The letter *kṣa* is the manifestation, together with wrath, whose body consists of the entire world. (1.65)
The seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, as well as the seven nether regions (pātālas),
from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, are all established within Mātṛkā.
The seven planets, beginning with the Sun, have emerged separately from the [seven] groups of consonants:
the Sun has emerged from the *a*-group, and Mars also from the *ka*-group.

From the *ca*-group arose Bhārgava (Venus), from the *ṭa*-group Jña (Mercury), from the *ta*-group Guru (Jupiter), from the *pa*-group Śani (Saturn), and from the *ya*-group the Lord Candra (the Moon) came into being. (1.68)
The lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī, as well as the zodiac signs beginning with Aries, will indeed be described hereafter through their conjunction with the letters of the Mātṛkā. (1.69)
From the fifty syllables, however, the fifty forms of Rudra have emerged,
as well as the powers (śaktis) of Rudra in that same number.
There are as many specific forms of Viṣṇu as there are powers of Viṣṇu;
likewise, there are fifty medicinal herbs and thirty-eight kalās.
From the fivefold division of Tārā, the fifty kalās came into being.
Thus has the origin of Mātṛkā, as taught in the Āgamas, been demonstrated. (1.72)
The seed-syllables (bījas) and the seed-mantras (bījamantras), together with their respective mantras, are extracted here in summary according to the *Prapañcasāra*. (1.73)
In the case of *mālāmantras*, there may be arrangements such as extraction (*uddhāra*) or transposition (*vyatyaya*);
beyond that, they should be clearly understood by the skilled exactly according to their recited form. (1.74)
Huṃ phaṭ vaṣaṭ namo vauṣaṭ—the limbs and the retinue are written here in their proper order, conjoined with the word "Bhagavat. (1.75)
The syllables are joined clearly with the utterance *svāhā* and the two *ṭha*s;
the half-stroke and crescent moon form the *bindu*, and emission (*sarga*) is held to be between the two *bindu*s. (1.76)

The mantras are known as the human [letters]; the letter *va* is designated as Brahman; the letter *ma* represents poison and time; and the letters beginning with *ya* are considered to be the elements (*dhātu*). (1.77)
These very [elements] become air, fire, water, and earth;
the letter *ha*, known as the Lord of the World of Space and Vital Breath, is designated as Śiva. (1.78)
The *ka*-group and the *ṭa*-group are likewise mutually inverted; so too are *pa*, *pha*, and *ba*, as well as *bha*, *ma*, and *kṣa*—these three triads are each inverted from one another. (1.79)

In the same way, the two groups of consonants (yaśa and varga) should be understood as being mutually interchangeable when their syllables are transposed; however, such transposition is not desired among the vowels, nor likewise among the conjunct consonants.
Indeed, those Rudras beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, or the locations for the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the letters, serve as conventions for the comprehension of their respective syllables. (1.81)
One should know that the gods, the elements, and the worlds are enumerated according to their respective numbers: seven vowels and ten directions. (1.82)
The arrows are indeed five, seven, and likewise the oceans;
the sages are four, as are the Vedas; the Rāmas are three, and the fires are three. (1.83)
The Nandas are nine, the Yugas are four, and the Vedas are six; these are known as the Rasas.
Furthermore, [the meters] are said to be Uktā, Atyuktā, Madhyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Supratiṣṭhitā.
The Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and likewise Jagatī; after that, Atijagatī is considered [the next]. (1.85)
The Śakvarī and the Atiśakvarī, the Aṣṭi and the Atyaṣṭi, the Dhṛti and the Atidhṛti, as well as the Kṛti, the Prakṛti, and the Ākṛti. || 1.86 ||
Vikṛti, Saṃkṛti, Abhikṛti, and Utkṛti have been declared;
the enumeration of these meters is prescribed here in certain instances. (1.87)
Wherever the enumeration of principles (tattvas) occurs, the objects of perception are indeed thirty-six;
likewise, in the Śaiva system, the principles are thirty-six in number.

Alternatively, the number here may be determined by the nine syllables consisting of the four *kaṭapāya* groups, the negative particle (*nañ*), the conjuncts (*sandhi*), and the vowels (*svara*), which are [respectively] nine, five, eight, and nine. (1.89)
The Chapter on Conventions:
Thus, this presentation of the subject matter is known in this treatise; for indeed, the easy comprehension of the meanings leads to the accomplishment of one’s desired goal. (1.90)
The Brahman of Sound is that single, imperishable, unborn, and pure consciousness from which the eternal forms arise for the purpose of the creation, destruction, and preservation of the universe;
and from whom the divine Mother Mātṛkā herself was born, whose very body is composed of the imperishable syllables.
The wise know that entire seed-syllable called Praṇava to be the seed of the Nyagrodha tree, which possesses that power.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Indication of Subjects and the Establishment of the Mothers," in the *Tantrasārapaddhati* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Īśānaśivagurudeva Miśra.
Now begins the second chapter:
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, Amareśvara, Aśvīśa, Bhārabhūti, Tithīśa, Sthāṇuka, and Hara. (2.1)
Jhaṇṭīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, Anugraheśvara, Akrūra, and Mahāsena—these sixteen are the Lords of the Vowels (Svareśvaras). || 2-2 ||
Then there were Krodheśa, Caṇḍeśa, Pañcāntaka, Śivottama, Ekarudra, Kūrma, Ekanetra, and Caturānana. (2–3)
Ajeśa, Śarma, Someśa, Āstra, Lāṅgalin, Dāruka, Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Aṣaḍi, and Ḍiṇḍina. (2.4)
Atri, Mīna, Meṣa, Lohita,
Śikhin, Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mahākāla, and Pālin.
Bhujaṅga, Pinākī, Khaḍgīśa, and Baka;
then Śveta, Bhṛgu, and likewise Lakulīśvara. (2–6)
The last is known as Saṃvartaka; fifty Rudras are proclaimed. This concludes the section on the Rudras.
Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and the third shall be Śālmalī. (2.7)
Then there is Lolā, Vartulākṣī, and Dīrghaghoṇā;
then Sudīrghamukhī, Gomukhī, and Dīrghajihvā. || 2-8 ||
Kuṇḍodarī, Ūrdhvakeśī, and likewise Vikṛtānanā;
then Jvālāmukhī, Ulkāmukhī, and Śrīmukhī shall follow. (2.9)
And Vidyāmukhī is declared; these are the sixteen powers of the vowels, along with Mahākālī, Sarasvatī, Sarvasiddhā, and Gaurī. (2.10)
Then there shall be Trailokyavidyā, consisting of the power of the mantra and the power of the self;
thereafter Bhūtamātā shall arise, and after that she is known as Lambodarī.
Drāviṇī, Nagara, Khecarī, Mañjarī, Rūpiṇī, Vīriṇī, Koṭarī, and likewise Pūtanā. || 2-12 ||
Bhadrakālī, Gominī, Śaṅkhinī, and Garjinī; then Kālarātrī and Kapardinī, and thereafter Karṣaṇī is considered [the last]. (2.13)
Mahājñānā, Jayā, Sumukhā, and Revatī; then Mādhavī, Vāruṇī, and Vāyavī should follow in succession. (2-14)
Another, Rakṣovadhāriṇī, arises from that as Sahajā;
Lakṣmī and Māyā—these fifty are indeed the powers (śaktis) of Rudra.
The powers of Rudra:
Keśava is the first form, followed by the one called Nārāyaṇa;
then Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana. (2.16)
Trivikrama, Vāmana, the one named Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Dāmodara, and thereafter Vāsudeva. (2-17)
And Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are the lords of their respective realms;
thereafter [he appears] as the wielder of the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the sword, the conch, and likewise the plow.
Musalī, Śūlin, Pāśī, and likewise Aṅkuśī; then Mukunda, Nandaja, Nandī, Nara, Narakajit, and Hari. (2.19)
Kṛṣṇa, Sattva, Sāttvata, Śauri, Sūra, Janārdana, Bhūdhara, Viśvamūrti, Vaikuṇṭha, and Puruṣottama. (2.20)
Bali, Bālānuja, Bāla, Vṛṣaghna, and likewise Vṛṣa;
Haṃsa, Varāha, and Nṛsiṃha—these are to be known as the Viṣṇus. (2–21)
The presiding deities of the forms of Viṣṇu are Kīrti, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, Śānti, Kriyā (and Dayā), Medhā, Harṣiṇī, Śraddhā, Lajjā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī. (2.22)
Prīti and Ratī are the powers (śaktis) of the vowels in their respective order;
they are Jayā, Durgā, Prabhā, Satyā, Caṇḍā, Vāṇī, and Vilāsinī. (2.23)
Vijayā, Virajā, Viśvā, Vimadā, Nandanā, Smṛti, Ṛddhi, Samṛddhi, Siddhi, Buddhi, Bhakti, Mati, and Kṣamā. (2.24)
Rama, Kledini, Klinna, Vasuda, Vasudha, Para;
Parā, Parāyaṇā, Sūkṣmā, Sandhyā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Niśā. (2.25)
And Amoghā—thus the fifty powers of Viṣṇu have been described according to their syllables.
This concludes the section on the Powers of Viṣṇu.
Now, regarding medicinal herbs: the two types of sandalwood, laghū, karpūra, and uśīra—
Gdhrībera together with the species of Takola, Māṃsī, Uru, Coraka, Granthi,
Bhāskaravartinī, Aśvattha, Bilva, Guhā, Rakta, as well as Lavaṅga, Kumbhī, Vandinī, and Udumbara are thus described. (2-26)

Kārṣmarya, ambuda, śaṅkhapuṣpī, śikhinī, plakṣa, agnimantha, as well as siṃhī, darbha, kuśa, and aparājitā; rohiṇa, ḍuṇḍuka, the well-known bṛhatī, pāṭala, taraṃ, caitra, and atulasyā— these are the [herbs].
The paths are Śakralatā, Madhuvrata, Harikrāntā, and Musalya as well. || 2-27 ||
There may be Bhītā, Haritālikā, Harivadhū, likewise Sahā, Śrīlatā, and Bhadrā; these are said to be the medicinal herbs of Lipi in their respective order.
With these, through pills, decoctions, ashes, ointments, and baths—
It brings prosperity, the power of speech, victory over untimely death, protection, and purification. (2-28)
The section on medicinal herbs:
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti. (2.29)
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅganā, Pūrṇā, and Pūrṇāmṛtā—these are the digits (kalās) that arise from the vowels. (2-30)
Tapanī, Tāpanī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhanī, Dhāraṇī, and Kṣamā. (2–31)
The kalās of the twelve letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*, respectively, are:
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Viṣphuliṅginī. (2.32)
Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and likewise Havyakavyavahā—these ten digits (kalās), joined with the initial vowels, have been described in their proper order. (2.33)
The Section on the Thirty-eight Kalās:
The fifty kalās of the fivefold Tāra arose:
Sṛṣṭi, Ṛddhi, Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, and Sthirā. (2.34)

Stability and accomplishment arise from the letter *A*; these ten digits (*kalā*) are proclaimed as having the purpose of the creation of Brahmā according to the Ṛgveda, as it has been described in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). (2–35)
Old Age, Protectress, Peace, Sovereign, Delight, Lust,
Bestower of Boons, Gladdener, Affection, and Long— these are the digits (kalās) born from the syllable Oṃ.
Joined with the Yajus and Viṣṇu, they are the causes of the world's maintenance:
Tīkṣṇā, Raudrā, Bhayā, Nidrā, Tandrī, Kṣut, Krodhanī, and Kriyā.
Utkārikā and Mṛtyu are the digits (kalās) originating from the letter 'ma';
together with Rudra and the Sāmaveda, these are known as the digits for the purpose of withdrawal.

Yellow, white, reddish, and fair-complexioned are the four [energies] of the Bindu, whose deity is the Sun; they are associated with the Atharvaveda, together with their Lord, and grant all desires. (2-39)
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti; then Indhikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, and Mocikā. (2.40)
Sūkṣmā, Asūkṣmā, Amṛtā, Jñānā, and then Amṛtāpyāyanī;
Vyāpinī, Vyomarūpā, Anantā, and Nādajā—these are the [energies] born of Nāda. (2.41)
The sixteen digits (kalās) are enumerated as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
these, being of the nature of Sadāśiva, are established in a general sense. (2.42)
Thus ends the section on the Kalās of the Praṇava.

One should place the vowels at the hairline, the circumference of the face, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the two cheeks, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, the head, and the mouth. (2.43)
One should place the *ka*-group on the right hand, the *ca*-group on the other arm,
the *ṭa*- and *ta*-groups on the two feet, and the *pa* and *pha* letters on the two sides of the body.
One should place those designated as *ba*, *bha*, and *ma* on the back, the navel, and the heart;
[and the letters] *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, and *bha* in the lotuses of the skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and breath.
With the [mantra] residing in the heart, one should place the eight syllables beginning with *ya* and ending with *da*, which are located on its petals, within oneself;
however, one should place the letter *kṣa* in the pericarp, recollecting it in its entirety.
The Chapter on the Locus for the Deposition of the Script.
Now, having sequentially described the loci for the phonemes beginning with 'a', the specific modes of deposition for the script, together with their limbs and deities, are here written down. (2.47)
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the pure alphabet is said to be performed with the very letters of the script, including the nasal dots (*bindu*).

[The mantra is: "O Sañjīvanī! O you whose hair stands erect! O you whose crest is a blazing flame! O you who embody the three worlds! O you who revolve a thousand times! *oṃ hrīṃ sauṃ*—*vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes! Then, the six limbs of the script are joined at the beginning with the six groups of consonants starting with *ka*, combined with the winds and waters. (2–48)
Generally, for all mantras of the limbs, the heart-mantra should end with *namaḥ*;
the head-mantra is indicated as ending with *svāhā*, and the tuft-mantra (*śikhā*) should end with *vaṣaṭ*.
At the beginning [of the mantra] there should be *huṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*); the weapon (*astra*) is desired to end with *phaṭ*.
Likewise, the eye (*netra*) ends with *vauṣaṭ*, and it is thus declared that the eye ends with [the syllable *vaṃ*]. (2.50)
In some cases, the procedure for the limbs ends with the weapon-mantra; in that instance, one should place the weapon-mantra at the end.
The arrangement of the eyes for the six-limbed mantra is now described. (2.51)
For that five-limbed mantra, no eye-mantra exists;
having first uttered the limb-mantra, one should then [utter] the limb with the fourth case-ending. (2.52)
Afterwards, one should append "namaḥ," "svāhā," and so forth, together with the limb-mudrā (aṅgamudrā).
One should place the palm of the hand with fingers extended upon the heart. (2.53)
Then, with the fingers curled at the tips and the thumb released, that [mudrā] is placed on the head;
furthermore, with the tip of the thumb released from the clenched fist, one touches the topknot.
Raising both hands above his body without touching his own form, with the palms turned upward and the fingers of the right and left hands slightly curved. (2.55)
One should bring protection to both sides up to the navel; that indeed is the armor (*kavaca*).
Raising those same two hands up to the neck with the fingers contracted, [that is the gesture of the sword]. (2.56)

The weapon mudrā (*astra-mudrā*) arises from snapping the tips of the index fingers while they are held over the tips of the thumbs; the eye mudrā (*netra-mudrā*), however, results from binding the right hand into a fist.
If, by suddenly touching the three eyes with the ring, middle, and index fingers extended forward, there should be only two eyes; || 2.58 ||
There, by joining the index and middle fingers, one should touch the two eyes;
[the eyes] are white, yellow, blazing light, the color of lightning, and like fire. (2.59)
The six limbs are red, both collectively and individually, in due order. This is the section on the numerical designations. She holds a seal, a crystal rosary, a water-pot, and a book.

With her three eyes, wearing white garlands and unguents, with a body as radiant as jasmine and the moon, and a serene countenance, she who is the goddess of the alphabet sits upon a lotus; bearing a digit of the moon upon her head, she is adorned with ornaments of pearls and holds [the manuscript] with her hands, the right one foremost. (2.60)
Having thus meditated upon that very form consisting of fifty phonemes within one's own body, [one should proceed]. (2.61)
Having sequentially assigned [the letters] to the previously mentioned locations,
one should daily recite the syllables fifty times until the total of one hundred thousand is completed.
Having offered oblations with sesame seeds soaked in the three sweets according to one's capacity, he shall attain purity of speech, and poetic talent shall arise within him. (2.63)

The learned scholar who knows the reality of the scriptures, wise and possessing a healthy body, having thus accomplished the Goddess of Writing, shall become one for whom all mantras are effective. (2.64)

The *śuddhalipi* (pure script): Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the phonemes along with Rudra in the sequence as before, this placement, preceded by Śrīkaṇṭha, bestows peace from minor diseases and other ailments. (2.65)
Maṃ maṃ aṃ aṃ āṃ āṃ ka va ca iṃ ra kṣa; preceded by Hṛllekhā and Vyoma, these are the six limbs in sequence.
[The deities] beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha.
The written syllables, together with the bindu, are taken from the division of Rudra and Śakti.
One should install these [deities] joined with their Śaktis, beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha;
one should likewise conceive of his limbs as being identical to those previously mentioned.
The meter for these two nyāsas is called Virāj;
Śrī Brahmā is designated as the sage (ṛṣi), and Vāgdevī shall be the deity (daivata). (2.68)
Some maintain that for the second [deity] there is the Ardhanārīśa Nyāsa;

she has a pair of upper arms holding a rosary and a water-pot, while her lower right hand displays the *samudra* (conch) and *abhaya* (protection) gestures, and in her other hand is a book along with the *varada* (boon-granting) gesture.
One should meditate upon that goddess, white in complexion, with three eyes, her matted locks adorned with crescents of the moon,
presided over by Śrīkaṇṭha and other deities, and adorned with white ornaments.

For the sake of one's own perfection, one should meditate upon the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, who is preceded by [the syllable] *Śrī*, whose complexion is like that of vermilion and gold on both sides, who is half-female (Ardhanārīśvara), who holds a goad and a noose in his hands, who possesses a garland, and whose hand bestows one's desired objects.
The placement (nyāsa) of Śrīkaṇṭha along with his Śakti; the Ajapā mantra consisting of the syllables of the alphabet together with the Tāra and the Śakti, and "So 'ham" (I am He). (2.71)
This is the ritual placement (nyāsa) for the sacrifice of conceptual proliferation (prapañca-yāga); it bestows one's desires through its placement, recitation, and so forth.
The mantra of Ajapā consists of the syllable *la*, followed by *ku* with the nasal drop (*bindu*), the creative emission (*sargī*), and the syllable *bhṛgu*. (2.72)
The seer is Brahmā, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Supreme Self, the supreme light, who is to be meditated upon within the lotus of one's own heart. (2.73)
The heart consists of the two syllables *sa* and *śakti*; *so 'ham* is said here to be the head.
The *ajapā* is to be known as the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the armor (*varma*) is remembered as the breastplate (*kavaca*). (2.74)
The *tāra* (om) itself is the eyes; the letter *ha* is the weapon here; the ear is the seed-syllable of Hari (hr); and they know the odd-numbered syllable to be the letter *ī*. (2.75)
The goddess to be meditated upon is one who holds the gesture of fearlessness and a rosary, and who bears a book;
she possesses the pure luster of a cluster of white lotuses, the moon, and jasmine;
her limbs are lovely, she wears jeweled earrings, has three eyes, and is radiant with a mass of matted hair.
Brāhmī, the Mistress of the Manifest World, is accompanied by the half-moon and adorned with white garlands, perfumes, and garments. (2.76)
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the sacrifice of proliferation (*prapañca-yāga*):

[it is performed] with the letters of the alphabet beginning with *Śakti*, or with the letters of the alphabet preceded by *Śrī*, or with those beginning with *Śrī-manmatha*, or with those beginning with *Moma-aṅga*, and so forth. (2.77)
These Nyāsas bring about prosperity for the sake of growth; their sage is Prajāpati, their metre is Daivī Gāyatrī, and the Moon is their presiding deity. (2.78)

Indeed, the six limbs arise from the seed-syllables of the [six] faces according to their respective characteristics; having recollected the deities beginning with Umā, Sarasvatī is to be meditated upon during the ritual placement (nyāsa). (2.79)
She whose crown of matted hair is adorned with a wreath of *mandāra* flowers and the moon,
whose three eyes possess a body beautiful with the luster of vermilion,
who wears garments as white as jasmine, and who holds the goad, the noose, and the sciences—
May Bhāratī, whose hands are like lotuses in full bloom, protect you. || 2-80 ||

The Samṛddhi-nyāsa consists of Lakulī seated on the Kalāsana, possessing the left eye and the half-moon; when placed as residing in both the letters and the phonemes (lipyarṇa), it is declared to be the Kṣobhaṇī-nyāsa. (2.81)
But the one mounted on Kāma is of the Laṅkula lineage; joined with the long vowels as before, the six limbs are assigned according to their respective signs, and the meter is indeed Gāyatrī. (2.82)
The sage is Vāmadeva, the deity is Kāma, and the presiding power is Akṣareśvarī.
Her limbs are beautiful with the lovely luster of vermilion-red; she is clad in red garments and anointed with red paste;
her tresses are adorned with Mandāra flowers; her face is graced with a smile, and her cheeks shine with radiant earrings.

For the sake of prosperity, one should meditate upon the Blessed Lady Saṃkṣobhaṇī, who has lips like the bimba fruit, is adorned with jewels, and holds in her hands a lotus, a noose, a goad, and a book.
The deposition of Kṣobhaṇī: Pāśa, Śrī, Śakti, Madana, Lipyarṇa, Madana, and Ramā. (2.84)
The Mālinī-nyāsa is joined with Lakṣmī, Aṅkuśa, Kalā, and Hṛd;
Ananta with the Bindu is the Pāśa, and the mantra itself ends with Śrī and the Bindu. (2.85)
Brahmā is the left eye together with the flesh [the letter *u*] and the staff [the letter *ra*]; the seed-syllable of Manmatha is [the letter *ka*].
The power (*śakti*) is known as *kha*, which is [the letter *ha*] with fire [the letter *ra*], a tooth [the bindu], and likewise the goad [the letter *ū*]. (2.86)
The fifty kalās, born of the syllables and arising from the Praṇava, are to be grasped;
likewise, the six [syllables] consisting of the repeated seed-syllables, the creative (sargī), and the destructive (saṃvartaka).
These are the limbs of Mālinī; its meter is Uṣṇih, its seer is Guha, and its deity is the Goddess Tripurabhairavī, the Mother of the World. (2.88)
By means of this [mantra], ritual placement (nyāsa) and fire sacrifice (homa) with sweet substances grant all accomplishments;
through recitation, meditation, and so forth, one may even instantly attract all beings.
Her body is as crimson as the bandhūka flower, she has three eyes, and she is adorned with red garments and unguents;
she wears shimmering golden earrings, bestows boons, and holds a noose and a goad;
her lovely breasts are slightly reddened by frost-white necklaces and the essence of saffron.
One should meditate upon her, who has a moon-segment in her matted hair, who displays the gestures of granting fearlessness with her left hand, and who wears a garland.

The Mālinī-nyāsa: Karṣaṇī is formed by the letters of the alphabet enclosed between the noose (pāśa) and the goad (aṅkuśa). The nyāsa, however, is performed with the six groups of consonants beginning with *ka*, enclosed as before by the noose and the goad. (2.91)
It has six limbs; its meter is Anuṣṭubh, its seer is Prajāpati, and its deity is Vāgvādinī, who bestows all perfections through the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites. (2.92)

She should be meditated upon as having a body like molten gold from a lake of *rocanā*, holding a lute and a book, endowed with a noose and a goad, her limbs adorned with ornaments radiant with clusters of jewels;
she wears a crescent moon upon her crown bound with a diadem, and is clothed in red garments, perfumes, and the like.
She is the speaker of her own unity, possessing three eyes, with a face graced by the play of her eyebrows and a smile.
The Nyāsa of Vāgvādinī: The letters of the alphabet together with the bindu, the Viṣṇus beginning with Keśava, and their Śaktis should be installed in sequence, ending with "namaḥ. (2.94)
In the Viṣṇu-mantras, the nyāsa performed with Keśava and the others bestows success;
one should remember Viṣṇu, whose body consists of the eight syllables, as the presiding deity.
One should assign the Gāyatrī meter; Nārada shall be its sage (ṛṣi).

The Goddess, fair as the jasmine and the moon, beautiful with a necklace that steals the splendor of shimmering digits of nectar, should be meditated upon as bearing a garland, a pleasant body, a pen, and a rosary.

She who bears the moon upon her matted locks, who holds a palace, a water-pot, and a lotus—the treasure-house of knowledge—who is clothed in silken garments, who is adored by the three worlds, who possesses six arms and three eyes; || 2-96 ||
The Keśavādi-nyāsa:
Thus have been described these types of nyāsa for the letters, which bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). (2.97)
The practitioner should indeed resort to one of these placements;
having placed the letters of the alphabet upon his body, he should perform recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth. (2.98)
One should perform this for the sake of protecting oneself through mantra and likewise for the accomplishment of that rite;
then, having meditated upon the inscribed syllables, one should worship them in the lotus of the Mātṛkā.

A white lotus with eight petals corresponding to the directions, having at its center a pair of the final letters of the seven groups; its pericarp contains the letter *ma* conjoined with fire (*ra*) and the final letter (*ha*), while its filaments consist of the vowels.
Surrounded by the seven oceans and encircled by the orb of the earth, it is known as the lotus of the letters of the Mātṛkā, which removes poison, death, and old age. (2.101)
One should contemplate that [mantra] upon one's own head; it removes the afflictions of death and poison.
Having meditated upon a divine crystal pavilion situated in the midst of the ocean of milk— (2.102)
In this lotus-seat, at the tips of the eight petals, reside these powers:
Medhā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Vidyā, Dhī, Dhṛti, Smṛti, and Buddhi. (2.103)
And Vidyeśvarī is situated in the center; she is white, wearing white garments and so forth, with both hands joined in the añjali gesture, and likewise with her two upper hands.

Holding a book and a water-pot, peaceful and of beautiful form; the ancillaries (aṅgas) are in the intermediate directions, the weapon (astra) in the cardinal directions, and the eye (nayana) on the petals in front.
Then the vowels [are worshipped] with that same number of digits (kalās), beginning with Amṛtā:
Amṛtā, Mānasī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Prīti, Rati, and Śrī. (2.106)
Śānti, Sudhā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Haimavatī, Chāyā, Pūraṇī, and Vāmā—these are the digits of the moon (indukalā). (2.107)
One should visualize [the petals] as falling in pairs, raining down showers of nectar;
from that, the letters of the classes [of consonants] arise, and from those, the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍī, and Mahālakṣmī, according to the sequence of the directions. (2.109)
Then there are the ten lords of the directions: Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Dhanada, Īśāna, and Kāla. (2.110)
These eight [deities] shall be in the directions starting from the east; then Brahmā, situated between Indra and Īśāna, is the lord of the upper world, while Ananta is between Varuṇa and Rakṣas.

The Lord of the Lower World (Adholokeśvara) should worship these six who reside in the enclosures; in the center, he should worship the syllable situated in the pericarp of the lotus as the essence of consciousness.
One should meditate on the form described in the *Svanyāsa* with the ritual offerings as previously stated:
the seat (*āsana*), invocation (*āvāhana*), the water of honor (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*).
Likewise, the bath along with its primary and secondary components, as well as garments, ornaments, scents, flowers, incense, lamps, and the offering of sacrificial oblations (caru). || 2.114 ||

The fire-ritual, prostration, and the offering of royal honors—these constitute the sixteen modes of service (ṣoḍaśopacāra). Having thus worshipped the deity residing on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should worship it mentally as well. || 2-115 ||
One should also worship the sages and so forth, as well as Vighneśa and the Guru, in the north.
Then one should perform the "eightfold flower offering" (aṣṭapuṣpikā), which consists of non-violence, forbearance, and compassion.
Likewise, restraint of the senses, knowledge, purity of disposition, and freedom from anger—these eight are the flowers of disposition in their proper order. (2.117)
The seat, its form, the deity, and the five limbs—thus one should worship these eight with mantras; this is the "eight-flower offering" (aṣṭapuṣpikā).
For the sake of the accomplishment of the foremost practitioners and for the propitiation of the deities, these [mudrās] should be employed, especially for the manifestation of the mantras. (2.119)
Then, saying "Forgive me" to the Goddess along with those attendants, one should effect her dissolution up to the head with this mantra: "O Nirañjanā, go to dissolution. (2.120)
One should unite the conscious self with the moon situated within the lotus at the *dvādaśānta*.
This is the procedure for the worship of the syllables (*lipipūjā*).
One should draw the wheel, as prescribed in the sequence of worship, upon birch bark, gold, or other suitable materials. (2-121)
By retaining this [mantra], all goals are accomplished for him without effort.
A wise person, having recited this three times in the morning, should drink water. (2.122)
Within a year, wisdom shall arise and poetic inspiration will be born for him;
by reciting that [mantra] one thousand and eight times, he should drink the juice of the *brāhmī* plant.
Alternatively, during an eclipse or for a continuous day and night,
one should take one *pala* of white *vacā* powder and one *karṣa* of *turagagandhinī*.
Having finely powdered one niṣka each of black turmeric, turmeric, rock salt, emblic myrobalan, ginger, and costus, one should add them to one prastha of ghee. (2.125)
One who knows how to cook with a gentle fire should boil four *prastha*s of *brāhmī* juice;
this is *brāhmī-ghṛta*, which the wise man should consecrate ten thousand times with the mantra. (2.126)
One should drink it during a solar eclipse and thereby attain omniscience;
or one should constantly lick it at the beginning of the day, having consecrated it fifty times with mantras.
Within a year, he shall become wise, a seer, and esteemed among the learned.
In the center of the lotus of the Mātṛkās, it is filled with the waters of medicinal herbs and the [letters of the] scripts. (2.128)
Then, one should daily recite [the mantra] over the water-pot (kalaśa) one thousand times according to the prescribed rule;
consecrated by that for a month, one becomes endowed with speech, longevity, beauty, and fame. (2.129)
The healthy man is joined with fortune; the barren woman gives birth to an auspicious son.
[One perceives] the radiance arising from the Bindu of the Supportive Power (ādhāraśakti), which travels along the path of Suṣumṇā. (2.130)
Having meditated on the moon situated at the *dvādaśānta*, one should write the letters beginning with *kṣa* within it;
by causing [the letter] to fall, [the practitioner], being thoroughly protected by fire and moon, shall be liberated from disease. (2.131)
One should install that script, whose meaning has been understood, which follows a single path,
and which has been obtained from the mouth of the Guru; one should also recite it a hundred thousand times,
having offered oblations with white flowers, sesame seeds, and clarified butter in one-tenth of that number.
Having attained mastery over speech, he brings the world under his control and achieves whatever is desired.

By means of this placement (*nyāsa*), one destroys planetary afflictions, enemies, poisons, diseases, and other calamities— whether occurring in one's own body or that of another— up to a number equal to the syllables of the mantra itself.
Indeed, all mantras in the world will surely become perfected.
For writing, even when mastered, cannot fulfill all desires.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Śrīkaṇṭhādipaṭala, in the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the third chapter:
Next, [the description of] Mātṛkā, the birthplace of all mantras.

The specific presiding deities of the vowels are written here separately according to their sequence, following the method of groups and sub-groups; they are obtained by dividing the vowels by the letters [of the alphabet] and taking the quotient as the nature of the respective signs. (3-1)

How could one who desires fruit engage here in the recitation and other rites of that [mantra] without knowing the nature of its syllables, their phonetic modifications, and their ritual applications—
just as one who does not know the classifications of medicinal plants cannot apply them to specific ailments?
Like a quack physician greedy for his practice, he is a fool. (3.2)
One who has not learned the training of elephants, who lacks a goad,
and who is ignorant of the principles of mantras, might mount a lordly elephant from which thick streams of ichor are flowing, without regard for its purity.
That foolish teacher or practitioner indeed falls. 3-3.
Thus, for the purpose of explaining the arrangement of the letters, the teachers should understand that many mantras are manifested herein;
the seven groups known as *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *ya*, along with the *śākhya* group—
But here, the vowel-group (avarga), whose nature is that of the vowels, would have the color of the sun and the moon. || 3-4 ||
The vowels, distinguished as male and female, fierce and gentle, short and long, do not arise separately; rather,
when the solar-colored (short) vowel arises on the right side, [the others follow in sequence].
And indeed, when the moon is long, the nostril is short. || 3-5 ||
In this pair of rice-packets, fire is above, wind is horizontal, water is below, and the earth is in the middle of the cavity;
for whatever is the internal space here, it consists of these five elements.
And those vowels arise in both the sun and the moon. || 3-6 ||
One should know both [the breaths] where the wind of exhalation flows through the body equally, in one whose body and senses are healthy;
and when questioned, let him declare the success of an undertaking or its failure.
Having observed one's own or another's voice as it becomes joyful, by means of proper application. || 3-7 ||
The cities of Kapila, Vakuśa, and Rāma; those inclined toward desire; the knower of night;
the animals, the rules, and the cows; what [are] the forests and the channels of the Saṃkhya; the syllables of the ages recited in order; and the twelve zodiac signs—[these are the components].
The division of day and night is made by them into six and six [parts] respectively. || 3-8 ||
The signs known as Aries, Taurus, and Gemini; Cancer, Leo, and Virgo;
Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius; Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces—these are the movable, fixed, and dual signs respectively, occurring in groups of three.
Indeed, along with the letters of the script, there arise [the experiences] beginning with the sensation of a dog's breath.
When the wind known as the Sun is in the right nostril, the movable sign rises;
when the wind known as the Moon is in the left, the fixed sign rises;
and when [the breath] is released through both passages, the dual sign rises.
The movement of the breath is the indicator of the time of the entire world. || 3-10 ||
If both wind and life-force (jīva) are present, or if the moon, fire, and earth are in the gentle wind or in water, they indicate the element of air.
If both earth and sun are present, or if the root is in water and the moon, [they indicate the element of earth].
And the accomplishment of the fruit would not occur in milk, nor in the sun, the earth, or water. || 3-11 ||
If Mars is in both the seventh and the third houses, death occurs; if the Sun is in the third house, there will be death or a very short life.
If the Sun is in the tenth house, the wealth will be lost or one's life will be brief.
One should declare long life from the presence of Venus and the Moon, as well as from the water [element].
There is happiness even on the lunar plane, but there is little accomplishment in its own [element].
In the case of both earths, one should accomplish the desired goal over a long period;
in the case of both winds, it will be accomplished after a short time of ripening.
In the case of both skies and fires, there is neither accomplishment nor loss.
Situated in both the fire and wind [houses], it quickly grants small desires. || 3-13 ||
When the moon is situated in the earth element, one should perform rites for pacification (śāntika) or nourishment (pauṣṭika);

when it is in the moon, wind, or water elements, one should perform subjugation (vaśya) and attraction (ākarṣaṇa). One should perform immobilization (stambhana) when the sun is in the earth element, or when it is in the sun or water elements.
By means of *rujā*, *māraṇa*, *maruta*, *sve*, *bhrāmaṇa*, and *uccāṭana*. || 3-14 ||
In the sky of the sun, it is enchanting; in the fire of the sun, it swiftly slays and destroys the host of enemies.
Thus, one should indeed practice the vidyās of recitation and oblation according to the prescribed rule.
However, one should quickly begin for the sake of accomplishment by relying on a voice that is joyful. || 3-15 ||

The Chapter on the Arising of the Breath (Svarodaya). The five groups of consonants known as ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and pa are to be understood there as being associated with Earth, Wind, Fire, Ether, and Water respectively.

In this [system], air, fire, earth, and water are to be understood as having the colors of the three qualities (guṇas) and the sky; the letters beginning with śa have these colors, while the final letter (kṣa) is passion (rāga). || 3-16 ||
Golden-hued, wearing garlands of lotuses and garments, and possessing the scent [of sandalwood], he has eight arms,
holds the trident and the excellent mace, rides upon a tortoise, and has eight eyes;
with four faces like the moon, he wears matted hair upon a circular seat.
Indeed, the letter *a* has the fragrance of a blue water-lily and the luster of Mount Mandara. || 3-17 ||
Seated upon a white, radiant lotus, possessing two arms, mounted upon a noble elephant, holding a goad and a noose in her hands,
adorned with necklaces as pure as snow, and sixty digits in height— Please perform the translation.
The extent of the thirty-three [gods] is called the consort of the yojanas.

One should remember the one who holds a vajra, who is intensely yellow, who rides upon a tortoise, who has a deformed body, who is two-armed, and whose scent is foul; he is two yojanas in height and half that in width, possessing various magical powers and great expansion.
It destroys poison, impurities, and disease; it is a paralyzer known as "subtle. || 3-19 ||
A woman with hands like golden fruit-baskets, surrounded by five *gavyūtis*, moist with white, beautiful nectar, and charming with captivating necklaces;
she moves on a swan across the surface of the earth, which is twice as wide as a *yojana*.
The threefold form, with its ten perfected aspects, shall be the bestower of nourishment.
Two hundred yojanas in length and one hundred yojanas in width, possessing an exceedingly foul odor, the Kākavāha wind is two cubits high;
it resides in the abode of fire, is copper-colored, and is accompanied by pain.
The *sagada* [measure] is for all protective rites; however, the *ṣaṇḍa* is odd-numbered.
Two-armed and red in color, stationed within a circle of fire, mounted upon a camel,
extending for a thousand [yojanas], twice as long as that [camel], with three pairs [of limbs],
adorned by snakes and groups of serpents, and possessing a foul odor—
For the destruction of poison, one should remember the six-limbed [mantra] consisting of the spear and the noose.
One should meditate on [the deity] holding a vajra, exalted, mounted upon a swan, bearing a noose, with two faces, extremely yellow, seated upon a fragrant earthly lotus,
possessing two hundred and ten fingers and toes, thirty finger-breadths in height, and having six testicles.
One should remember Svarṇacūḍa, the destroyer of hosts of enemies and the master of paralyzing spells.
He whose face has the wheels of a chariot as its pupils, who possesses four arms shimmering with conchs and lotuses, who is blue like the throat of a peacock,
who has a beautiful countenance, wears pure necklaces, bears the fragrance of a lotus, and has matted hair.
May he remember Jhaṇḍin, who brings all under his control, like a cakravāka bird.

For the sake of successful childbirth, one should remember the elemental goddess (Bhautikī), who is white in color, fragrant, adorned with two arms and a garland of pure pearls, borne upon Garuḍa, and holding a three-pronged vajra in her hand within a circle of fire.
That woman was likewise tall, with her [hair] spread out to a hundred crores [of yojanas].
Pervading the midst of the entire universe, yellow in color, possessing two sets of a thousand arms, radiant and three-eyed,
with his limbs adorned while seated upon a bull against the orb of a doubled sun;
Meditate immediately upon the body of the youthful man, which bestows liberation.
Fragrant with white flowers, clad in white garments, possessing a golden luster yet appearing like a flower, and bearing a vajra and a noose;
[he stands] upon a lotus disc upon the earth measuring a thousand yojanas.
In rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), the Lord of Grace (Anugraheśa) with that body should be meditated upon here.
His limbs are adorned with many ornaments as radiant as saffron; he removes the dullness of every pair [of opposites], grants his devotees' desires, and holds a lotus in his hand.
Seated upon a lotus, he bestows prosperity and possesses a most beautiful complexion.
He who is to be meditated upon for liberation from all evils—may He protect us. || 3-28 ||
Having gone to the city of Dahana, one should visualize that three-eyed deity with two hands joined, holding in his grasp black garments and perfumes,
bearing a trident and a thunderbolt in his hands, and skilled in the incantation for the destruction of enemies.
And one should contemplate the final vowel, which has a measure of one thousand times ten (ten thousand).
The section on the forms of the vowels:

He who holds a vajra and a mace in his hands, whose fragrance is that of a lotus, who possesses the luster of gold, who resides in the orb of the earth, and whose presiding deities are Brahmā and Śakra.
May he who appears in the form of a two-armed man, the performer of subjugation, the one with matted hair surrounded by a thousand [rays], protect us—may he be recited twice. 3-30.
May he protect you— he who has the sapphire of Indra’s crest-jewel, who wears a serpent as a sacred thread, whose white face is fierce, whose feet are tawny, who is the purifier,
the pillar, and his own self, seated upon a goat amidst a blazing lotus.
He is ten hundred in stature, armed with a *tomara* and holding a *śakti* in his hand. || 3-31 ||
Seated upon a red-colored serpent and a blooming lotus, possessing a hundred-fold expansion, gracious, bestowing nourishment,
and lofty; the lord of Gaṇapati and Dhanada, borne by a swan, and fragrant—
May the syllable GA, holding a noose in its hand and accompanied by a goad, protect you. || 3-32 ||
That lofty cluster of celestial palaces, surrounded by a thousand [attendants] and endowed with the excellent vajra and mace, should be meditated upon as mounted upon a camel;
it has two arms and is employed for the rites of black magic, subjugation, hatred, and expulsion.
And let him remember that supreme [state] which resides within the mortar of his mouth.
One should remember the six-armed Lord who has a crow for his vehicle, who is exceedingly black, whose hands hold a trident, a mace, a chisel, a spear, a staff, and a serpent,
who is mounted upon a snake, and whose body is half a *koṭi* [ten million] leagues in height.
One who has swelling in the feet and limbs, and who is hostile toward those who seek refuge, is a single Rudra. (3-34)

May Guhyakeśa— the Lord of the Guhyakas, who possesses matted locks, is adorned with red fragrant garlands, and holds a conch, a lotus, a water-lily, and a citron, radiant as the moon— protect you for the sake of all prosperity in the world.
The Tortoise, measuring ten million [yojanas], rests upon the lotus of the earth. || 3-35 ||
May he who is mounted upon a crocodile and a lotus, who possesses the luster of the sun,
who bestows the waters of the ocean and the lotuses of the world, who is endowed with divine fragrance,
who wears white garments and garlands, and who is of immeasurable splendor, protect you.
Adorned with stainless jewels, the One-Eyed One is the bestower of subjugation.
May those two who possess the color of the moon rising from a white lotus, who hold a fruitful vajra and noose, and who bear white jars,
protect you— those two who are of a peaceful hue and measure one thousand [hands].
They destroy gray hair, death, and disease, and are primarily effective in pacifying the effects of poison.
One should recognize Asitamaśubhaṇḍa, Durmati, and Kākavāha—
the messengers of Yama— with their limbs adorned with many iron ornaments,
holding three-pointed axes in their hands during acts of hatred.
The color known as Śarman, however, has a measure of one thousand and ten.
With a roar like that of the ocean, wielding a mace, holding a thunderbolt in his hand,
encircled by serpents upon his arms, possessing a pair of mighty limbs, exceedingly fierce,
the destroyer of the pride of his foremost enemies, and having the Krauñca mountain as his vehicle— [he is Śiva].
May that noble Someśvara, radiant with the hue of Kapila, protect you all.
Resembling the stainless moon, white as a conch or cow’s milk,
adorned with nets of necklaces variegated by pure jewels,
holding a lotus in his trunk— the elephant [Airāvata] who stands upon the lotus of the earth and wind— may he protect us.
May Lāṅgalī, who destroys all poisons and is perceived as the goal, protect you.

Seated upon the horse Kuvalaya, possessing the luster of a ripe plantain tree, variegated with golden jewels, four-faced and eight-armed, measuring a thousand [hands] in extent, [bearing] a lotus, a noose, a goad, and a lotus— Please provide the remainder of the verse for a complete translation. As it stands, the provided text is incomplete. However, based on the fragments given, the translation would continue as follows: ...[holding] a lotus, a noose, a goad, and a lotus—may he protect you. (Note: The standard iconography of Gaṇeśa includes a broken tusk, a sweetmeat ball (modaka), a rosary, and a bell, among other attributes. The provided text describes a specific variant or artistic representation.)
May Dāruka protect [us], holding the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, as well as a trident.
May that god of fire protect you, who, while pursuing the city of Anala,
wields the thunderbolt, the excellent *bhuśuṇḍī*, the *bhindipāla*, arrows, the noose,
the axe, the discus, and the bow.
The tenfold transformation is the lofty ocean of Ardhanārīśvara.
[One should visualize him] with a three-pronged axe in his hand, riding a tiger, deep smoky-grey in color,
and having three faces; destroying the most terrible diseases upon the body of Kubera,
and enriched with an enemy-slaying vajra, a *bhusuṇḍī* weapon, a noose, a staff, and a banner.
One should also remember the one who is ten hundred times sublime and whose complexion is like that of Umā’s beloved.
Mounted upon his excellent elephant, bearing a conch, a goad, a lotus, and a noose,
possessing a fragrant scent that does not fade, measuring a thousand cubits, with his limbs adorned, may he who brings Indra, Varuṇa, and Īśa under his control grant you subjugation.
May he, who is as pale-red as the *āṣāḍhī* flower due to his bracelets, crown, and neck-ornaments, protect you.
Seated upon a bull, white in color, four-faced, and eight-armed, the Lord of Wind and Fire, possessing ten million forms and wielding a trident,
a mace, an axe, a spear, a javelin, and a slingshot— may he protect you!
And may this Diṇḍin, wielding both the staff and the spear, protect you.
May he who holds the trident, axe, sword, staff, thunderbolt, and ploughshare— Asita, Yama, Īśa, with six arms, three faces, and adorned with bracelets and necklaces of serpents— protect you.
In the skull situated upon the buffalo, he is known as Atri, possessing ten million-fold pride. || 3-46 ||
May that fierce Lord of Nirṛti, mounted upon a preeminent deer, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, holding a sword, a noose,
and a *bhuśuṇḍī*, and bearing a mallet— deep tawny in hue— protect you as he sits upon a lotus seat.
He who splits the enemy of fear and measures four hundred thousand [leagues]. || 3-47 ||
May he who has two arms, a dark complexion, and wears a tiger-skin upper garment;
who bears a hand-drum and a trident, and whose eyes are blood-red; and who is adorned with saffron-colored robes and other ornaments—may he protect you for a long time.
The one called Daśaśatatati, Kākavāha, and Ṣaṇḍa. || 3-48 ||
May he who has mounted Garuḍa upon his lotus-throne, who wears a serpent as a sacred thread,
whose body is white like that of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who possesses twenty arms and is variegated with jewels, protect us— he who is of immeasurable extent.
This Brāhmaṇa, Lohitārṇa, is the remover of various poisons. || 3-49 ||
May the twice-born one— richly adorned with the footprints of Paraśurāma, seated upon a lion-throne marked by lotuses, possessing ten extended arms,
and wearing a sacred thread of pearls— remove your misfortunes.
The fire, tawny like lightning and iron, which is desired for protection. || 3-50 ||
Seated upon a blue lotus, borne by swans, possessing six faces,
and holding both a lotus and a conch, may the Lord of the Lord of Wealth—
clad in white garments, fragrant, and as red as the bandhujīva flower— grant you prosperity.
May the syllable *baka*, which has ten extended rays and bestows glory, protect [us]. || 3-51 ||
May the trident-bearing Śaṇḍaka protect you— he who has three faces and three eyes, is fierce, has tawny hair,
is smoke-colored, possesses three hands, and stands upon the orb of a fire atop a jackal.
He is enriched with a discus and a mace.
That which is known as Dviraṇḍeśa consists of ten lakhs expanded out.
Possessing the luster of the rising sun, radiant as the fire of cosmic destruction, bearing the moon upon his matted locks and a garland of skulls,
and holding the trident, axe, serpent, and fire— may he grant you prosperity.
On the lotus, there should be one with a body of uneven form and the color of Mahākāla. || 3.53 ||
May that deity of the wind-element, dark brown like the gait of a deer,
who holds a pestle, a mace, and fire within his aerial form,
protect you— he who subdues all the worlds and performs minor rites.
The letter Ya, adorned with the sun, the moon, garments, and perfumes, belongs to you. || 3-54 ||
Resembling a blazing fire, seated upon a lotus within the orb of the sun,
the pride of all the worlds, borne by a ram, and gracious,
he holds the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, as well as the *śakti* and the *svastika*.
May the serpent, fragrant with white garments, protect you. || 3-55 ||
May she who rests upon a lordly elephant standing on a lotus, whose color is like that of a woman, who holds a stalk of rice, a golden creeper, and a vajra-noose,
and who is adorned with all yellow ornaments, grant her blessings upon the surface of the earth.
May Dhāriṇī, who is spread across the earth, protect and support you. || 3-56 ||
White as a ray of nectar, bearing a white lotus and a noose within the orb of the water,
may she who destroys the pain of various poisons and diseases grant you prosperity.
May the expanse of the worlds become the very form of milk and nectar.
Holding a white lotus in her hand, seated upon a white lotus,
adorned with pure garments and perfumes, golden-hued,
possessing a thousandfold [splendor], and bearing a mass of hair tied with turmeric.
May he whose form has the color of a crane's beak bestow prosperity upon you.

May the one who has the sapphire of Indra as his crest-jewel, who rides upon a tortoise, who is two-armed, who wears saffron-colored garments and is fragrant, and who bears the thunderbolt and the noose—
may he, whose measure is a thousand times ten, be the agitator for your prosperity.
With a smiling moon-like face, he is known as Śveta and is intoxicated. || 3-59 ||
White as the luster of the moon, holding a vajra, lotus, water-lily,
noose, a treasure jar, a casket, and also a wheel; adorned with ten million ornaments upon a swan standing on a lotus.
May Bhṛgu, the lord of the givers of wealth, grant you your desired object.

Clad in white garments, adorned with perfumes and garlands, with matted hair and the moon upon his crest, Lakulīśa— tawny as Hara, three-eyed, and bearing a deer, an axe, and a trident— is the very measure of the universe.
May the son of Śivagiri protect you with his very life-breath as his own self.

May the lordly deity Kṣetrapāla, mounted upon an elephant, protect [us]— he who holds in his hands the conch, vajra, discus, noose, goad, mace, *bhuśuṇḍī*, sword, bell, and skull-cup within the lotus of the abode of the Lord of the Gods.
The final [syllable] is "dvidaṃṣṭraḥ," which has the yellow eye of the Goddess spread over the worlds.
Those Brāhmaṇas are of a most brilliant white complexion; here, the Kṣatriyas are red, those who are Vaiśyas are yellow, and those born of the Śūdra lineage are black—
each indeed possessing their own specific characteristics.
Those [beings] are males, females, and eunuchs, to be known according to each verse. || 3.63 ||

In this section on the forms of each syllable, the long vowels joined with the bindu and visarga are indeed the gurus; furthermore, that syllable upon which another consonant is placed is also [heavy].
And that [long vowel] should be known as a *guru* (heavy); what remains after it would be a *laghu* (light).
A *laghu* consists of only one short syllable (*mātrā*), while a *guru* consists of two *mātrās*. || 3-64 ||
The eight metrical feet (gaṇas) here are indeed known as ma, ya, ra, sa, ta, ja, bha, and na; they consist of three *hal* [syllables] each, and by three [syllables] they are formed.
That foot which consists entirely of long syllables (*guru*) is known as *masa*, and it is called *avani*.
The group [of syllables] beginning with *la*, *ya*, and *sa* is known as the first; it is Water-bodied. || 3-65 ||
One should know that the *ragaṇa* has *la* in the middle and Agni as its deity;
the *sagaṇa* likewise has Vāyu as its deity and is enriched by a long syllable at the end.
They call the *tagaṇa* "space" (*kha*), and it should have a short syllable at its end.
Furthermore, if there is a *jjagaṇa* in the middle, it has the Sun as its presiding deity. (3-66)
The first group (gaṇa) is named *gurubha* (heavy-bha), and the one consisting entirely of light syllables is called *somadeva*; the eighth is to be designated as *dyaus*.
Thus, the universe is pervaded by these eight groups, distinguished by heavy and light syllables.
The production of words occurs through groups [of phonemes] consisting of the letters recited in the sequence of the script. || 3-67 ||
Those groups whose colors are fire (red), water (white), and earth (yellow) are enemies;
those whose colors are air (black), fire (red), and space (blue) are mutual friends;
and those known as water (white) and earth (yellow) are also friends with one another.
The groups known as water (salila), wind (pavana), and earth (khā) are the intermediate ones here.
Men, women, and eunuchs who are affectionate, those situated among eunuchs, men who are enemies of men, and women who are enemies of women— these are mutually hostile.
One should [deal with] a friend, a debtor, a group, or a neutral party as a friend.
But that mantra, which is the designator of the deity, should be joined [with the name]. || 3-69 ||
Even Manu became a god endowed with the powers of the hosts of Siddhas by means of a single mantra accomplished according to rule;
how much more so for one who knows or accomplishes many kinds of mantras?
He becomes equal to Śiva, a treasury of those fruits.
The beloved one with a charming hip is Śrī; the other beloved is Night; the one known as the ocean containing the wombs of the women of the mountain-ranges of the flocks of birds;
and those whose letters and syllables have been declared in the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī.
In the asterism of Puṣya, a pair of vowel-transformations should be applied.
And the letter *la* [indicates] the Kurus, Vṛṣas, Dadhis, and numbers; the stars will be auspicious.
There will be fear, death, disease, and suffering from cattle and pairs; with innumerable fears, there will be [calamity].
Whatever name may indeed have been given here by the parents at birth, let that also be favorable to both of them. (3.72)

The syllables *pha*, *la*, *gu*, *ru*, *ru*, *śā*, *ṇā*, *śarma*, *śarva*, *stva*, *ja*, *ādyā*, and the letters of the alphabet (*lipi-varṇa*) are the signs (*rāśayaḥ*); those beginning with *śa* are feminine.
From the name consisting of the syllables *jana-na-bha-ni-ja*, the application of the initial letter—
That which is desired should be purified by means of the first syllable of the mantra. || 3-73 ||
Having smeared a pure ground with water mixed with cow dung,

one should draw there a sixteen-square grid (cakra) surrounded by a single row; the zodiac signs, the deities of obstacles, the field-deity, Vāstu, and the house-construction rules are situated within the squares, with [the central deity] residing in the middle.
Having worshipped those [syllables], one should bring about the arrangement of the mass of letters and phonemes into the essence of the mantra and the name.
The first, or alternatively the fifth, the ninth, and the tenth and second houses from one's own sign are the houses of kinsmen; the sixth house becomes that of servants.
If, according to the number of Rudras (eleven), fires (three), and Svaras (six), this is considered so in the Tantras, it is the nourisher.
It may be that the twelfth [syllable], which is the eighth according to the sacred tradition, is remembered as the mantra that causes destruction. (3.75)
He who is a kinsman (Bandhu) is Manu;
he protects this [world] and expands all its purposes. He who is called a servant (Sevaka) bestows nourishment, fortune, power, and fame; he whose nature is that of a nourisher (Poṣaka).
And he who is called the "slayer" destroys even those things that are essential for life. (3.76)

In the four sets of four-syllable letters beginning with Īśa (the eight directions), those syllables that are indeed Siddha in the first word are Sādhya when they occur in the second word, and Susiddha in the others.
Those syllables which are Ari (enemies) occurring in the fourth word bestow death and suffering.
But those who are disciplined succeed in them either quickly or after a long time, through recitation, muttered prayers, and burnt offerings.
First placing the name of the object to be accomplished (sādhya) and afterwards the name of the practitioner (sādhaka),
there [the result] will be a debt from the remainder of the eight;
[this is determined] by the letters of one's own name increased by the letters of the object to be accomplished.
Having subtracted eight from that, or conversely, it is a debt. (3.78)

Having performed a calculation of the letters called the practitioner's name together with the syllables of the mantra, starting from the *siddha* group and so forth, this portion of the mantra is to be known. (3.79)
From west to east, one should write [the letters] in the two rows on the right and left;
the syllables of the mantra and the name [should be written] separately, according to their respective consonants and vowels. (3.80)
When the syllables of either the name or the mantra are unequal,
then one should write out each of those syllables until they become equal.
Then, having subtracted by means of the Siddhas and so forth, one should determine the result and so on as before.

One should write in a row the groups (vargas) of the names of the practitioner (sādhaka) and the object of practice (sādhya), distinguished by vowels and consonants. Having divided by three, one should know them as hostile, friendly, or neutral; and if [the result] is hostile, one should abandon that [practice]. || 3.82 ||
One should discard the syllable obtained from the continuous recitation (saṃhitā) during the purifications.
Furthermore, having abandoned the nasalized *anusvāra*, the *jihvāmūlīya*, and the *visarga*, one should purify the mantras as it is stated in the *Tattvasāgara*: (3.84).
Just as one performs purification for the first syllable, so too should one perform the purification of all the limbs;
having done so, one should mark [the mantra] with the number of Siddhas and others contained within this mantra.
That mantra in which there are four *siddha* syllables bears the name *Siddha*;
one devoid of *siddha* syllables is called *Sādhya*; the *Susiddha* is that which is free from *ripu* (enemy) syllables. (3.86)
One who is well-accomplished (susiddha) but deficient [in other qualities] becomes an enemy; thus one should calculate in four ways.
A mantra that is well-accomplished at the end leads to success, for it is indeed a granter of desires.
That mantra which is without enemies, established from the beginning, and whose initial syllable is well-perfected, being devoid of enemy letters, indeed bestows all desires. (3.88)
That mantra whose goal (sādhya) occurs at both the beginning and the end is indeed difficult to accomplish;
one should not practice that mantra which has an enemy (ari) either at the beginning, at the end, or at both. (3.89)

Even if well-practiced, [an ordinary mantra] may destroy one even after hundreds of lifetimes; but for whom this mantra is perfectly mastered at its beginning and end, it is his wish-fulfilling gem. (3.90)
In this way, one should purify the mantras as it has been taught in the *Tattvasāgara*.
Indeed, the forms and other qualities of each individual letter in the Mātṛkā have been explained; through the recitation and other practices of those devoted to them,
the purposes are accomplished by means of the specific syllables that constitute the collection of mantras.
And whatever arises from those [elements] joined together, all that is to be inferred. (3.91½)
Having thus purified the first syllable in many ways, and having examined the remaining collection of letters of that mantra—
whether the mantra begins with a pure syllable or consists of letters other than those [already purified]—
The Guru should bestow [it] according to the specific method appropriate for that qualified recipient. || 3-92½ ||
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Forms of the Individual Letters of the Mātṛkā and the Svarodaya," in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānadeva.
Now begins the fourth chapter:
Mantras are of three kinds—feminine, masculine, and neuter; those ending with *svāhā* are feminine, while those ending with *namaḥ* are [masculine].
Those known as *ṣaṇḍas* are men whose mantras are incomplete; this has been stated by Gautama regarding the application of mantras. (4-1)
Men should perform rites for subjugation, attraction, and the neutralization of poisons;
women should perform those for delusion and the destruction of outcastes; and all remaining types of ritual action should be performed by eunuchs.
One should perform [the rites] quickly with mantras for the attainment of those respective fruits. || 4-2 ||
Those mantras whose colors are like the stars, the sky, the ocean, wind, or fire are indeed fiery (āgneya); those other than these are lunar (saumya).
Even a fiery mantra may be accompanied by the lunar quality when it ends with "namaḥ."
Even a mantra for Agni may be gentle, ending with "phaṭ. || 4-3 ||
Success in cruel deeds may occur through the Āgneya [planets];
one should perform gentle actions properly through the Saumya [planets];
while those with both Saumya and Āgneya characteristics possess the marks of both.
One should perform all actions, both cruel and gentle, with those [mantras]. || 4-4 ||
In the same way, one should know their periods of sleep and awakening according to the divisions of the *āsanas*;
for those that are gentle, the time of practice should be gentle.
The practice of the fire-related [mantras] has been stated to be from the Saura [tantra]. 4-5.

When the movement of the Sun is in a Saumya (northern) course, there is a Saumya sleep; however, for those belonging to the Āgneya (southern) category, sleep is said to occur during the Āgneya course, and awakening occurs during the Saumya.
When the movement is situated in both [courses] simultaneously, it is equal for both.
Even one who has merely awakened from sleep is not desired [as a fit recipient] when [the teaching] is practiced. || 4-6 ||
One should perform the recitation (jāpa) of the mantras at the prescribed times, or the recitations for those bound by vows, during the rites of recitation and fire-offerings (homa).
Having commenced these previously during the time of practice, falling asleep in the midst of ritual acts does not constitute a fault. (4–7)
The section on the characteristics of mantras:

A mantra that possesses six limbs is indeed "with eyes" (sanetra), whereas a mantra with five limbs is "eyeless" (anayana), provided that the mantras for both [the deity and the practitioner] have [these] respective limbs.
