They would be separate if not for the fact that, at the very root, one should perform the construction of the limbs using the nine and ten long vowels in pairs.
Just as the sun is invincible by its own rays, or as fire is capable through its preeminent brilliance,
so too is he whose form is the mantra, together with its ancillaries, and whose very self is that [mantra].
Endowed with those constituent factors, he shall be capable and invincible. || 4-9 ||
The heart is accessible through the intellect; the Self residing in the heart is endowed with consciousness, and by means of the heart, the mantra [is realized].
Salutations to that which is performed preceded by the intellect.
Therefore, the primary limb is to be known as the heart alone. 4-10.
The head, indeed, is the primary limb of the embodied Manu, for it is exalted by the qualities of all the senses;
therefore, since it naturally seizes objects [for itself], it is rightly said that the limb of the head is associated with the *svāhā* [exclamation]. (4-11)
For the *śikhā* (topknot) is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the ritual acts of the Mantras,
since it is that limb which brings about the manifestation of the *vaṣaṭ* call;
for by means of the *śikhā*, Agni possesses invincible splendor.
Therefore, "vaṣaṭ" is employed for the crest-lock (śikhā). || 4-12 ||
But because the root [of the mantra] seizes the object by grasping it by the hair, the armor (kavaca) of the mantras encompasses the body;
the syllable *huṃ* [repels] all the host of misfortunes (*ariṣṭa*).
One should ward it off with that which is joined to the armor. || 4-13 ||
In this world, the mantra *vauṣaṭ* clearly serves as the eye for the purpose of seeing; therefore,
it is the limb known as the Eye (*netra*).
For the sake of accomplishment, however, "vauṣaṭ" is said for the vision in the eyes.
Because it protects by bestowing life, it is called an *astra* (missile/weapon) from the root *as*, which signifies "throwing";
for the mantra protects by casting away what is undesirable.
From "traiṃ pālane astrāya phaṭ," [the mantra] "astram" [is derived]. || 4-15 ||
Previously, the preceptor who was the sage that had understood and accomplished the ritual procedure for this mantra—
[he taught] the discourse on the meaning primarily concerned with the will, according to the Yoga system.
The meter shall be correctly applied according to the phonemes. || 4-16 ||
That deity which, through the granting of the status of a divinity, bestows desired things here upon one from suffering,
is called a "deity" (devatā), being a thing denotable by the word *manu*.
That which has been described as having its own essential nature within the phenomenal world.
Furthermore, for the deity whose essence is mantra, every collection of phonemes (manu-varṇa-pūga) is indeed her form;
her power, however, is consciousness (citi), which brings that form to completion.
But that which is called the seed is indeed its very life-force.
When that sage recites the mantra devoid of its seed-syllable (bīja),
it indeed yields a fruitless result due to the power of the seed;
through ignorance, the mantra falls into a state of insentience along with its limbs.
The hosts of asuras carry away the recitation performed by others.
Viṣṇu is pure when touched by whichever vowel; Vahni (Ra) is the fire that brings about the dissolution of the oblation.
That same [Vahni], joined with the left eye (U), is the seed-syllable Khaḍgī; even the Lord of the Immortals (I) is [included] in the mantra. (4-20)

The letter *sa* with *ā* (sā), or with *aṇ* (sāṇ), or on the left side (vāma) such as the left arm (*bhuja*) and so forth, or enriched with the left eye (*akṣa*), or subtle like the womb (*meṣodhi*), these are the seeds common to all mantras where no specific seed has been mentioned. (4-21)
They say that for the single-syllable mantra there is no seed of the deity higher than this which was previously mentioned;
and if Śakti consists of the unmanifested *nāda* and *bindu*, then indeed the Unborn (*aja*) is superior to the seed, for Śakti is said to be even beyond that. (4.22)
In this matter, everything is favorable when the zodiac signs, as well as the names of the practitioner and the object of practice, and the two constellations are compatible.
A mantra that is accomplished according to the stated rules will succeed; otherwise, even another mantra may take a long time to succeed.

In these seven mantras—the Haṃsa, the eight-syllabled, the five-syllabled, the Vahni, the Tāra, the Sāvitrī, the Sañjīvana, and the Gopaka—favourable conditions such as [auspicious] names, asterisms, and zodiac signs are not to be considered. (4.24)
Through the distribution of the syllables of the script, twenty-seven lunar mansions are assigned;
there should also be deities and trees equal in number to that.
One should not cut down those [trees] which are one's own mantra-tree or constellation-tree. || 4-25 ||
To increase one's own lifespan, one should nurture that mantra-tree; one should protect it and worship it for the sake of accomplishment.
One should also worship the deity who is the lord of the constellation of the mantra.
And those planets arising from the groups [of letters] on their own day.

Dasma, Yama, Dahana, Prajeśa, Soma, Śiva, and the gods beginning with Āditya, the serpents (Bhujaṅgamas), as well as Pitṛ, Aryaman, Bhaga, Bhāskara, and Viśvakarman— Please note: The provided text fragment appears to be a list of names from the Vedic or Puranic pantheon, likely part of a larger enumeration of deities or guardians. The final word "viśvakarma-" indicates the list continues. I have translated the available portion into English.
The vital breaths are Mahendra, Dahana, and those known as Mitra. || 4-27 ||
Indra, as well as Nirṛti, Salila, the Viśvedevas,
Cakrāyudha, the Vasus, Varuṇa, Aja-aṅghri, the one known as Ahi-pūrva-pada-budhni, and Pūṣan— these are here [the lords of the directions].
These deities of the lunar mansion (bhagaṇa) are proclaimed in their respective order.
The Kāraskara, Āmalaka, Udumbara, Jambū, Khadira, Kṛṣṇa, Vaṃśa,
Aśvattha, Nāga, Taru, Rohiṇaka, and Palāśa trees.
Then you were the Plakṣa tree, known previously by the name Baṣṭha.
The bilva and arjuna trees, as well as those known as vikaṅkata and kesara, likewise the trees named śabara,
sarjaka, and vañjula, and finally the panasa, arka, śamī, and kadamba, have been mentioned in their proper order.
Of the lunar mansions, however, the names are Cūta, Taru, Nimba, and Madhūka. || 4-30 ||
Emerging from these lunar mansions together with their presiding deities are the lunar days (*tithis*), beginning with the first (*pratipad*), belonging to both the bright and dark fortnights.
Due to the increase and decrease of the moon, those lunar days (tithis) are of two kinds;
and for these lunar days, there exist deities who preside over them in successive order. (4.32)
Agni, the two Aśvins, Ambikā, Vighna, the Nāgas, Skanda, Sūrya, the Mātṛs, and Durgā;
Āśā, Śrīda, and then Vaikuṇṭha and Dharma.
Rudra, Candra, then Pitrya; Kuhū shall be [the fifth]. || 4-33 ||
From the asterisms, the signs of the zodiac, the letters of the alphabet, and the lunar days— manifested through the power [of Śiva]—
there arose the seven Karaṇas, beginning with Bava, throughout the two fortnights.
Bava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila, Gara, that which is called Vaṇija, and Viṣṭi as the seventh.
The seven animals, beginning with the lion, are the sources (yoni) of the [letters] starting with Ba;
they are the lion, the tiger, the boar, the elephant, the goat, and the dog. (4.36)
The seven deities—Śakra, Ajamitra, Aryaman, Dhara, Śrī, Yama, and Karaṇa—are to be worshipped during those respective Karaṇas. || 4-37 ||
Thus has the exposition of the letters of the Mātṛkā been proclaimed, as it was taught in the Gautamīya and in the grammatical treatises on mantras. (4.38)
And as it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra* by Udgārgya:
"It is clear that this entire universe is an expansion of the phonemes of the Mātṛkā. (4.39)

At the tip of the bow, there was a sound; from that sound arose the sixteen vowels at the beginning, followed by the five groups of consonants starting with 'ka', then those headed by 'ya', along with the elements, the five gross elements,
the subtle essences (tanmātras), the senses, primordial nature (prakṛti), and the qualities (guṇas)— thus is she whose form is the universe, known as 'Na'.
Indeed, this Śakti is Vāgīśvarī, for the entire world is that which is designated by the term "manifestation" (prapañca). 4-40.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Mantras and so forth," in the *Tantrasāra*, which is the manual (*paddhati*) of the venerable teacher Īśānadeva.
Now begins the fifth chapter.

Now, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall here explain in its entirety the methods of accomplishment and so forth for various rites—such as mantra-recitation, worship, and oblations—according to their proper application. (5.1)

Indeed, the ritual procedures such as *pallava*, *yoga*, and *rodhana* have been explained in the *Tattvasāgara* and other works, along with the green [mantras], together with the appropriate directions, times, and methods, using various substances, days, seats, and sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*). (5.2)

Furthermore, pallava, yoga, rodhana, grathana, sampuṭaka, and vidarbhaṇa—thus the application in ritual acts is sixfold, by means of the practitioner’s syllables together with the letters of the mantra. (5.3)
The yoga beginning with the *pallava* is said to be that in which the name of the practitioner is inserted within the *mantra*;
in both cases, however, when stringing together the two names of the *mantra*, they are separated by intervening syllables in their respective order.

If the mantra is inserted on both sides of the practitioner's name, they call that "encasement" (saṃpuṭa). If each syllable of the practitioner's name is placed between pairs of mantra-syllables in sequence, that would be "piercing" (vidarbhaṇa). || 5-5 ||

For the subduing of planets, spirits, and piśācas, and for the neutralizing, destroying, and killing of poisons; for the driving away of enemies, their suppression, and even for the rite of inciting enmity among them—the *pallava* [mantra] should be used. (5–6)
They say that for the rites of supreme delusion, the *rodha* [arrangement] is used; for those of paralyzing others, the *yoga* [arrangement];
for those of winning over people, the *saṃpuṭa*; and for subjugation, pacification, and nourishment, the *vidarbha*. (5.7)
The chapter on the [directions] beginning with the sprout:
For rites of pacification and nourishment for Taurus, the east is indeed prescribed; for subduing and fever, the southeast;
for killing and deluding, the south is said to be used; and for inciting hatred, the southwest.

The direction of the waters (the west) is for the quelling of the burning heat from rain-showers; the direction of the wind (the north) is for wandering and immobilization; the direction of Śiva’s speech (the northeast) is for worship and rites of subjugation; and the direction of the Giver of Wealth (the east) is declared for liberation. 5-9.

Temples of Śiva, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and Paścimāśāmukha; the abodes of Śarva, cow-pens, and auspicious rivers; the dwellings of the supreme deity, the sacrificial fire, and Brahmins; and forests and mountains—these indeed are the locations for rites of pacification (śāntika). (5-10)

The regions at the roots of the banyan, the holy fig, and the wood-apple trees, which were mentioned first, are auspicious and recommended for rites of prosperity; indeed, they are also highly recommended for the acts of plowing and subjugation, as well as for building one's own beautiful home.
Having thoroughly purified the ground so that it is free of thorns and devoid of defects such as clods of earth, charcoal, and husks;
having filled it with soil as fine as sand, making it mirror-like and sloping toward the north and the direction of Indra (the east); || 5.12 ||

Having worshipped the deities of the site and the subterranean spirits, and having smeared with cow-dung from the sky [the ground] of a cow that is free from calving and disease, one should also sprinkle it with water filtered through a cloth.

One should construct there a monastery, hall, or similar structure according to the requirements of the site, using purified bricks, wood, straw, and so forth, as well as sacrificial materials, with dimensions as desired and a height equal to the length of a staff.

An atom, a mote of dust, a nit, a louse-egg, and a barley-corn are successively eightfold in number; and the hollow space of a barley-corn across its width is indeed intended in the treatise as the *mānāṅgula* (measurement-finger). 5-15.
They declare that a *vitasti* consists of twelve *mānāṅgula*s;
two *vitastis* they call a *hasta* known as a *kiṣku*, and four *hastas* they call a *daṇḍa*. (5.16)
The bow is indeed their staff, for the string of those bows is said to be eight finger-breadths [in length].
O Lord of Creatures, one should know that the bow-house consists of the fist of the bow together with the string, measured by the digits of the essence of the gods.
In this context, the *mātrāṅgula* is intended as the middle joint of a straight middle finger; otherwise, it may be different.
For the construction of temples and such, the former [the *pūrvāṅgula*] should be used, whereas for ritual practices (*sādhana*), the *mātrāṅgula* alone is indeed to be employed.
The number of staffs (daṇḍas) representing the width and length of the house multiplied by three, when divided by eight, yields the remaining staffs;
these are, in order, the Banner, Smoke, Lion, Dog, and Bull, known as the Svara, Elephant, and Crow.

The halls, characterized by the lion, bull, elephant, and banner, should be situated in the directions of the Lord of the East (Indra), the Lord of Water (Varuṇa), the Lord of the North (Kubera), and the Lord of Wealth (Yama) respectively;
they may also be in the middle of the house. When the ground is level and circular, one should construct this with pillars of equal height for auspiciousness.
Moreover, when engaging in impure rites such as subduing or killing, one should indeed employ the punishment of the crow, the donkey, the dog, and smoke against the target. (5.21)
In that place, the halls are constructed from the wood of poisonous trees, corpses, funeral pyres, and thorny trees;
the ground is exceedingly fierce for all minor rites, being flooded by the fires of Yama and the winds from the northwest. (5.22)

Forests, a solitary self-manifested Śiva-liṅga, the abode of Karālikā, and the dwelling of Mahiṣāsuramardinī are recommended for malevolent rites, as are places that are devoid of any habitation. (5.23)

And those places which are immovable, secluded, and waterless, devoid of the sounds of pestles, women, and children; whether in inauspicious or auspicious locations, they should be free from outcastes, donkeys, horses, and winnowing baskets. (5.24)
Recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites performed in a place frequented by cocks and cats will not bear fruit;
moreover, widows, the deformed, sinners, and women in their courses destroy all such ritual action. (5.25)

O Brahmins, maidens, truthful women, and excellent ladies of auspicious marks, as well as the sounds of cows, horses, and elephants, together with conchs, musical instruments, and songs, shall yield fruit in auspicious rites. (5-26)

In the performance of malevolent rites (abhicāra), however, virgins and the like, widows and the like, and the sounds of cattle, horses, and the Vedas—these utterly destroy the efficacy of the ritual; therefore, auspicious things should be present in that location. (5.27)

In secluded places, especially those well-guarded and not too far from various groups of trusted guards, in forests and other locations with the previously mentioned characteristics, and where he is unseen by others, one should perform rites such as killing. (5.28)

Even the lakes, rivers, the Sahya and Vindhya mountains, and those distinguished rivers flowing from the ocean—if these were situated in the middle [of the battlefield], they would be sufficient to destroy the power of the [enemy's] application [of weapons]. (5.29)

Even for those actions that qualify the subject matter at hand, when he sows the seed in a worthy and well-examined place, it will surely grow toward its fruit in accordance with that location. (5.30)

The Section on Localities: One should perform rites of subjugation during the spring; rites for inciting enmity against others in the summer season; the practice of driving away enemies during the rains; and if one would perform the rite of killing, let it be done in the winter. (5.31)
Indeed, autumn is praised for rites of pacification (śāntika), while winter is for those of nourishment (pauṣṭika).
But surely others say that both pacificatory and nourishing rites may be performed in winter or even in the month of Madhu (Caitra).
In this context, the two watches following sunrise are said to be Hemanta and Vasanta respectively;
the two final watches until sunset are declared to be the months called Nidāgha. (5.33)
From sunset until twenty ghaṭikās have passed, this period is designated as the autumnal season;
beyond that, however, it is the winter season, according to the *Tattvasāgara*, which states that [the division] is prior to sunrise. (5.34)
The Section on Time: With white rice, cooked grain, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), sesame, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and white perfumes;
indeed, in the daily rite (nityavidhi), there are also varieties of grain such as palāśa, dūrvā grass, barley, śāli rice, and so forth. (5.35)

Now, for pacifying rites and especially for oblations and the like, one should perform the ritual with fuel-sticks as prescribed: with those of *śamī*, *vaṭa*, *āmra*, *nitya* (or *nyagrodha*), *khadira*, *udumbara*, *mārga*, *bodhi*, and *bilva*.

In rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), sacrificial porridges (caru) made with curd, honey, milk, milk-rice (pāyasa), and clarified butter; bilva fruits, sesame seeds, and various types of śāli rice; as well as fruits, sweetmeats, sugar, and prescribed flowers; and various kinds of fuel-sticks (samidh) are desired. (5.37)

Salt, sesame, and mustard seeds; fuel sticks as previously described; flowers, fruits, and effigies; sweet substances along with the wood of the *jantu* tree and gold; and sandalwood and yellow pigment—these are used for subjugation (*vaśya*). (5.38)
Madhu, indralatā, sahā, bhītā, haripatnī, harilaṅghitā, asubhadrā, musalī, girikarṇī, mohanī, suratālī, utpala, mādalā, abja, and dūrvā. (5.39)

The gift of an elephant, white mustard seeds, the root of the white sun-plant (*sitārkamūla*), gold, milk-yielding trees, and products of one's own body—these are proclaimed in the Tantras as being for the purpose of subjugation and attraction, along with lac, birch bark, and so forth. (5.40)
With husked sesame, mustard, crow, raven, *vairiccha*, *chada*, *daṇḍī*, poison, neem, and citron;
and with buffalo [blood] even in water, along with the essence of lac—these indeed are declared to be the substances for the rite of inciting enmity. 5.41.

They say that this poison, when ground together with *phaṇi*, *sūraṇa*, *citraloṇa*, *piṇḍa*, *kanaka*, *ambhogṛha*, *dhūmra*, and *koṣaṇa*, is desired for the rites of inciting hatred and killing one's enemies. (5.42)

A crow's nest situated on a *picumanda* tree, charcoal from clothing, earth obtained from a cremation ground, wood from a funeral pyre, *markaṭī*, *kadaṇḍī*, human hair, bone, and so forth—such items are used for the act of attraction (*cāṭana*). (5.43)
And for the purpose of causing wandering [of the spirit], one should prepare [the mixture] with *piśāca*, *vṛkṣa*, *nimba*, *avasīta*, *unmatta*, *kalāṅgalī*, and *śaṇa*;
likewise with *rujic*, *citraka*, *daṇḍi*, *śālmalī*, and others, as well as *viṣa*, *bhallāta*, and *vibhītaka*. (5.44)
Poisonous trees, poison, raw ghee, snakes, human skulls, bones, and the wood of a funeral monument;
black garments, mustard seeds, and the like, as well as the nails, hair, and dust from the feet of the person to be subdued (the *sādhya*). 5-45.

One should perform the rite of killing with flowers that are double-petaled, nine-petaled, black, red, or yellow, as well as with red blossoms and red fragrances, and even with images made of clay from a birthplace and the like, using pungent and hot substances. (5.46)
With *busa*, mustard seeds, yellow-scented flowers, and the products of *kaṭuka*, hot water, turmeric, and buffalo horn;
with rags from a cemetery, *kokilākṣa*, and *cakrī*—these are the means for accomplishing the rites of immobilization (*stambhana*). 5.47.
The Section on Substances:

For pacificatory rites (*śāntika*), the lunar days (*tithi*) of the Sun, Serpent, Mountain, Soul, and Ashvini; the degrees (*aṃśa*) and days of the auspicious planets; and the asterisms (*bhāni*) presided over by Śiva, the Aśvins, Hari, Indra, Sūrya, Pūṣan, and the Ādityas, are to be employed. (5.48)

The lunar days (tithis) of Mahiṣāri, Vighna, and Yāmya; the portions of the Moon and Jupiter; the rising of the day and so forth; and the asterism of Bhaga belonging to Jupiter, Viṣṇu, and the Moon—these have been correctly described as bestowing success in rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika). || 5-49 ||
The ninth lunar day, the asterisms Harṣaṇā, Mātṛ, Dik, and Guhā, the weekdays of Venus, Mars, and the Sun,
and the Siddha yoga joined with the Sun and the Tiṣya asterism— these are declared for the purposes of subjugation and attraction.

The ninth lunar day, those presided over by the Moon, the Mother, and Fire; the dates beginning with the days of Venus, Mars, and the Sun; and those presided over by Yama, Agni, Hara, and the Serpent—these indeed grant success in the rite of inciting enmity. (5.51)
On the dark lunar day, during the dark onset of night, on the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight,
and when the moon is in conjunction with the stars of Śiva, Agni, Yama, the Serpent, and Vāyu, all rites for eradication shall be successful.

The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the new moon (Kuhū), and the eighth day of the dark fortnight, occurring on Sundays or Tuesdays; or when the Kulika is present, or during the periods of Yamabhāga and Ambubhāga, or when Mars and Saturn are rising—these are the times for lethal rites.

When the planets are situated in the eighth house from an enemy, in the eighth house from the nativity, or in the houses numbered according to the path of destruction (the ninth), and when joined with the rising signs of Mars and Saturn and so forth, they grant success in rites of sorcery (abhicāra). (5-54)

Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, the Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn, and Jupiter—these are, respectively, the lords of the quarters beginning with Āśvayuja (Kārttika), and they are indeed the lords of the zodiac signs beginning with Aries. (5-55)

Mars, the Sun, Jupiter, Saturn, and Venus; Mercury, Venus, Saturn, Mercury, the Moon, and Mars; and Jupiter—these are the lords in the threefold divisions of the signs beginning with Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius respectively. (5-56)

Furthermore, when Jupiter is in its debilitated sign, or when the asterism and its sub-division belonging to Jupiter are devoid of strength, they declare that to be the state called "the Elder" (sthavira); it is praised for employment in destroying enemies, diseases, and the ocean.
Having divided the day into eight parts, one shall release the two portions of the day belonging to the planets—the last and the first.
The other six planets each occupy for half a watch (prahara) in successive order; among them, Gulika is that which belongs to Saturn.

Whichever eighth portion is said to be greater than ten degrees from the birth asterism, that is designated as the "destructive" (vināśaka) and is destructive; however, the seventh asterism from one's own [natal] sign is called the "house of death" (naidhana). (5-59)
The auspicious stars numbered one, nine, three, four, and seven are praised for virtuous deeds.
Let the Lord of Passion (Kāmadeva), together with his consort Rati, perform auspicious acts from his own zodiacal sign at the number eleven. (5–60)
Chapter on Time:

Nor does one who is traveling in a vehicle, nor one standing on a mount, nor one situated on a mechanical device, nor one who is impure, nor one whose mind is deeply attached to sense objects, obtain the fruit of recitation, burnt offerings, and so forth. (5–61)

In this world, a seat should not be excessively low nor too high, nor should it be made of skins or woolen blankets that are impure; furthermore, it should not be produced from inauspicious wood, nor be cracked, burnt, or stained with the impurities of human excrement or food leavings. (5-62)
Auspicious seats made of *kuśa* grass or *darbha*, large wooden planks from sacred trees, as well as skins of tanned deer or antelope, and those made of fine iron or ivory, are recommended. (5.63)

Seats that are wide and covered with white, pure, washed garments are indeed effective for the accomplishment of gentle rites; however, those made from poisonous trees and the like are used for ungentle activities. (5–64)
Having sat upon a seat, then pressing the big toes together within the space between the knees, with the body, neck, and gaze held straight, one becomes established in the Svastika posture. (5-65)

Having placed the tips of both feet above the root of the pair of thighs and sitting as before, that is called the *padma* posture; when it is performed in the reverse manner, however, it is the *bhadra*.
Having placed the right foot upon the thigh and the right thigh upon the left foot,
if one sits well-settled as before, they call that the desired *yogāsana*.

Having firmly grasped the left calf and foot at the ankle, with the buttocks and thighs mounted upon it, and the right knee placed above the thigh, that yogi indeed stands in the cow-faced posture (gomukhāsana). 5-68.

Having sat upon a plank or similar surface with the right leg bent and placed [across], and having set the left foot upon the ground with the shank raised, they indeed call that the "Half-Svastika" (ardhasvastika). (5-69)
Having sat upon the seat in that manner, with both feet placed on the ground and the shanks bound together,
and with hands resting upon the knees which are aligned with the arches of the gateways, he is as if bound by the yoga-band of the heroic posture (vīrāsana).

If he remains standing on both feet on the ground without a plank or similar support and sits down with his thighs and shanks positioned like a gateway arch, that is the *utpuṭika* and *kukkuṭa* postures. (5.71)

Likewise, in the victory over the vital breaths (*marut*) and the senses, in liberation from worldly existence, and in the firm maintenance of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the lotus-seat is desired here; indeed, it is declared to be auspicious and beneficial for daily nourishing rites (*pauṣṭika*) and other such practices. (5.72)
Indeed, it has been taught that in rites for pacification (*śāntika*), one should perform them entirely with the *svastika* [mudrā]; likewise in consecrations (*abhiṣeka*).
Furthermore, in the recitation, fire-oblation, and worship of pacification, the *svastika* is desired as being preceded by the half-[mudrā]. (5.73)
In the rite of sakalīkaraṇa, when one's own identity is merged with the deities to be consecrated through the yoga of the swan of meditative absorption (samādhi),
and during the exposition of the ultimate reality— if the Guru is present before one, the yogic posture (yogāsana) is indeed desired.

Indeed, for victory in battle, for their suppression, for paralyzing, subduing spirits, and so forth, as well as for enchantment or attraction, the *vīrāsana* posture is prescribed for swift accomplishment. (5.75)
Indeed, it has been stated that the *kukkuṭa* [mudrā] is used for causing aversion, subduing, and bewildering enemies;
furthermore, the *ardhakukkuṭa*, known as the "heel-sign," is understood to be employed for lethal purposes. (5.76)
In victory over the hosts of Maruts, for the pacification of one's own faults, and in the rite of paralyzing an army, one should employ Gomukha;
and in attracting women, the Abja [mudrā] is employed, as it is known to have been taught by the Guru. (5.77)

Just as the fruit of these seats is victory through one-pointedness and clarity of mind, so too the mind alone is the cause of everything; for if that [mind] is conquered and brought under one's own control, what indeed is not conquered? (5.78)
In this context, the circle in front is said to be watery; therein, an earthly one is recommended for rites such as pacification (śānti) and all daily nourishing (pauṣṭika) rituals.
Furthermore, a windy one is used for hatred and eradication, while a fiery one is used for subjugation and attraction.
Indeed, for the rites of paralyzing, one should use the Bhauma or Aindra [mantras], as well as for the rites of pacification and nourishment.

One should perform the rite of killing within a mandala marked by a vajra and encircled by wind, or else within a six-spoked [mandala] enclosed by fire; likewise, rites for pacification and subjugation may also be performed there. (5.80)
The Section on the Seat and Other Matters:

Having understood all of this in its entirety according to the rule from a guru distinguished by his learning, one who possesses a perfected mantra as his very self should perform each respective rite with constant discipline.

Whatever task there might be to be done for the sake of his own interest or the interest of others, the practitioner, having accomplished it, enjoyed the fruit thereof in this world, as confidence in him was born among the people. (5.81)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Chapter on Practice (*sādhanapaṭala*), in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Śiva of the Īśāna lineage.
Now begins the sixth chapter:
here [are described] the fire-pits (*agnikuṇḍa*) and the mandalas, each one individually for their respective [rites].
I shall explain, in brief and according to their primary importance, those [teachings] which are well-proclaimed in the tantras. (6-1)
For rites of pacification and nourishment, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be square; for subjugation, it should be circular like a womb;
for attraction, it should be like a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha); for paralyzing, it should be octagonal; and for driving away, it should be hexagonal.
In rites such as the killing or driving away of enemies, the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) should be marked with a vajra, a triangle, or have six or three corners;
for the installation of the liṅgas of deities, one should construct all types of fire-pits in every direction.
Whether in a temple, a pavilion, or a house— wherever that rite is performed—
it should be done on a thoroughly purified spot smeared with products of the cow (gavya).
Having placed and stretched here a long thread from Varuṇa to Indra in the middle, and having made a dot in its center,
one should then mark the western and eastern points equally according to that thread.
Furthermore, having divided that thread-segment equally, one should mark it as well; then,
using a thread measured by the marks for the east, west, and middle of the central point (bindu) and fixed therefrom,
one should draw a pair of fish (matsya-yugma) by rotating the thread from the central point toward the south and north, reaching the corresponding marks.
Having laid the cord between those two, it should extend from south to north.
In this manner, one should establish the thread called Brahma and the northern thread.
Then, situated at the central point (bindu) and measuring half the extent of the field, one should mark the numbers in the four directions according to the threads as desired.
From those pairs of numbers and the two threads, the "fish" figures of the corners (koṇamatsya) will indeed arise.
Those fish were caught on all sides in the various directions by means of threads cast down.
The field should be square, divided into four equal and auspicious compartments;
it is the general source for the production of all mandalas, fire-pits (kuṇḍas), and so forth.
The preparation of the square [fire-pit]:
A square pit is recommended at the outset, as are those shaped like an aśvattha leaf, a half-moon, likewise a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, a lotus, or an octagon. (6–11)
In a rite of one hundred oblations, it should be half a *ratni*;
for one thousand, it should be the measure of a *hasta*; and for ten thousand, it should be two *hastas* long.
For one hundred thousand oblations, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be four cubits; for one million, six cubits;
and for ten million oblations, it should be eight cubits, as stated in the Bhojendrapaddhati.
All the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be equal in length and width according to the prescribed measurements;
their depth, however, should be made equal to their width, and there should be three girdles (mekhalās) above them in succession.
The excavation should be level on all sides; above the excavation, leaving a space of one finger-breadth on each of the four directions, one should then construct three girdles.
The first girdle should indeed be one *stnī* in measure; the others should be made with two, one, or half a finger-breadth [less than the preceding].
Alternatively, in the case of a *ratni*, they should be made with three, two, or one *mātrā* of finger-breadths.

Regarding this, King Bhoja states: for a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*), the first [line] is two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the second is one finger-breadth, and the third is half a finger-breadth; for a pit measuring one forearm (*aratni*), they are three, two, and one finger-breadth respectively.
In a one-cubit (hastaka) vessel, the girdles should be four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively;
in a two-cubit vessel, one should likewise make them six, four, and three finger-breadths in sequence.
In a four-cubit pit, they [the lines] are formed by groups of eight, six, and four finger-breadths; likewise in a six-cubit pit by ten, eight, and six;
and in an eight-cubit pit, they are formed by sixteen, twelve, and eight in number.
All [the altars] in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) are equal in width and height; they are surrounded by a border equal to themselves in length and are free from depressions or elevations.
Regarding this, King Bhoja states:
"In all fire-pits (kuṇḍas), three girdles (mekhalās) should be fashioned in sequence according to the dimensions of the pit.
One should fashion the womb (yoni) to the west of the pit, or alternatively to the south.
But they stand above all the girdles in the middle.
In the Ratnikuṇḍa, the yoni should be twelve aṅgulas in length from its base to its tip;
it should be eight, four, and two aṅgulas in width respectively, gradually rising in height and having its tip emerging sharply.

In sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit (aratni) and so forth, the yoni is prescribed to be formed by increasing the length and width by two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula) each in successive order.
Regarding this, King Bhoja states:
"Thus for the first fire-pit; for the remaining ones, the *yoni* should be fashioned with an increase of two finger-breadths.
And in the *Mañjarī*, concerning the fire-pit measuring one cubit:
Situated in the direction of the lord of waters (the west), it should be as long as a palm tree; then, it should gradually slope downward like an *aśvattha* leaf,
with the navel [depression] measuring ten or six finger-breadths in sequence.
"And in width, they have tips like four-finger-sized balls. Thus it is said.
"The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) may be either square or circular for daily rites and for rites of pacification (śāntika).
Others say that for all desires (sārvakāmika), it may be both square and circular. (6.23)
Having marked one portion of the boundary line outside as well as in front with water at the lord of the waters (the north),
and having fixed a cord from that measurement between the two interior squares,
one should rotate it from the center to the end of another diagonal, and further from the two corners to the previous mark.
But according to the Sūtra, by striking [the ground], the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) may also take the shape of a vulva or the leaf of an Aśvattha tree.
Having divided the square into sixteen parts (yuga-aṃśa), one should discard the final part toward the north;
then, by means of this [measurement], having placed two external marks from east to west, || 6-25 ||
In the same way, by rotating the thread situated in the middle from the south, there arises a beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a half-moon for the two [sides]. (6.26)

In a quadrangular area divided into four parts, having cast a cord measured by the length of one side outward from the eastern portion toward the north, and having rotated that cord twice when fixed at the central and western marks,
two "fish" (śaphara) figures shall be formed; then, three cords should be drawn from the front of those two.
Having cast [the cord] from that point, the pit dug to that same measure becomes known as triangular. || 6-27 ||
Having taken the sixth part previously established and situated at the southwest (nairṛta),
and having cast two threads ending at the northwest (vāyavya), there may be a triangle.
A thread fixed at the central point, extending two finger-breadths outward from the eastern arm, should be rotated around;
thus the circular pit (kuṇḍa) becomes most beautiful.

Having established the sixth external portion, which rests upon the directions of Indra and Varuṇa, in the center at the corner of the Veda (the northeast), one should then rotate the thread equally between those two on the outside;
there, four "fish" figures are formed, and subsequently, when the thread is placed in the south, in the direction of Kubera (the north).
When these marks are established there, a hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be formed by lines drawn from them. || 6-30 ||
In a circular pit (kuṇḍa), one should fashion lotus petals upon its rim;
eight petals, each half the length of the pit, should be made, and their center shall be the pericarp (karṇikā).
Having thus performed [the drawing] according to the characteristics taught for the lotus, there shall be the establishment of the lotus.

Having rotated around the interior and exterior in all directions by twelve parts (12) and nine parts (9), two fish-diagrams (matsya) shall arise from those two; and by means of the threads fallen in each direction from those two, [the layout] should be done correctly.

The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be octagonal and very beautiful; alternatively, it may be formed from the remaining portion after drawing the lines for the intermediate directions (ardhadik-sūtra), starting from the northeast (aindra) up to the southeast (śarāṃśa), or it may be produced by eight fish-shaped figures joined together.

On the site, having divided a circle measuring fifteen finger-breadths into three parts by means of three finger-breadths each, one should draw fifteen lines here; the spaces between the corners shall consist of three parts each.
Having established oneself upon this [mandala] at the central point (bindu), one should then lay five threads extending for twelve finger-breadths (sūryāṅgula) from the center of each side;
by means of these equally divided threads, the junctions of the two corners shall be formed.
Having rotated [the compass] from the measurement of the thread reaching the corners of the *bindu* by one-fourth of that field,
and having performed the rotation of the thread situated at the *bindu*, five junctions (*sandhi*) shall likewise be formed here by means of the threads.
The Chapter on the Five-Angled Pit:
Having first established a square, one should then divide it into eighteen parts;
thus, there will indeed be two hundred and fifty-six squares here.

One should draw a lotus with six petals using six squares in the center; outside of this, a pedestal (pīṭha) in a single row; and outside the pedestal, a pathway (vīthī) surrounded on all sides by two rows.
Outside that, in two rows, one should likewise [draw] the doors, the necks, and the adjacent areas in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
And likewise, the Gaṇḍas and Upagaṇḍas are located in the corners of the Night, Wind, Fire, and Śarva [directions].

Some say that from the neck (*kaṇṭha*) and its vicinity (*upakaṇṭha*), and from the cheek (*kapola*) and its vicinity (*upakapola*), there arise the primary beauties (*śobhā*) and the secondary beauties (*upaśobhā*).
Having fixed the directional lines within the lotus-field (*padmakṣetra*) and having smoothed out the rest, one should discard the outer twelfth part and rotate the other. (6.38)
One should divide the field into four parts by rotating a cord equally and sequentially to form a circle;
these [divisions] constitute the pericarp, the filaments, the joints of the petals, and the tips of the petals.
One should rotate outward that which was previously set aside as the twelfth part;
that shall become the fifth field, known as the void (vyoma), located at the tips of the petals.
Having extended two diagonal threads from corner to corner through the middle of the directions,
and having struck four [main] threads, there shall be sixteen threads.
For the successful completion of the petal, one should place a thread between the junctions of the petals measuring up to the tip of a petal;
thus, by means of crescent moon-shapes arising from the rotation of the space between two petals, the petal is perfected.
Having divided the center of the sixteen lotus-lines with threads,
there shall be thirty-two segment-lines equal to the circumference at the tips of the petals.
Then, drawing a line from the corner situated at the intersection of the petal-tip line and the side line down to its base, one should lead it to the end of the petal-tip line;
by drawing in this manner, the petal-tip will become beautiful.
Rice flour may be desired as white powder; turmeric may be slightly white, yellow, or combined with white;
safflower, vermilion, and mineral pigments may be used for red; and even burnt barley and other grains may serve as blue powder.
A dark-colored [mandala] is prescribed with sacrificial leaves such as those of the *śamī*, lotus, and *bilva*;
or indeed, one should fill the mandalas with grains of corresponding colors.
If one who is capable should desire the foremost accomplishment, he should indeed fill the mandalas here with gems of those respective colors:
with pearls, topazes, rubies, sapphires, and green gems.
Regarding such powders, King Bhoja states that one desiring success should prepare them with pearls, coral, and so forth.
All the lines everywhere should be white and measured according to the middle finger;
in a two-cubit [square], they should be the size of a thumb, or in a single cubit, equal to the ring finger.
In a space of two cubits, they should be the size of a thumb; in one cubit, they are measured by the middle finger.
Thus say others.
In the center, there should indeed be a very yellow pericarp; upon it, nine black seeds are to be placed.
Two by two, slightly curved at their tips, the filaments should be drawn separately in the spaces between the petals. (6.48)
At the base they are thin and yellow; in the middle, they are thick and reddish;
at the end, they suddenly become thin and yellow, and finally, they are indeed slightly white.
"King Bhoja says that there is a network of filaments which is yellow at the base, red in the middle, and white at the tip.
One should make those eight petals white, equal in size, with raised tips that are pleasing to the eye;
for the sake of worldly enjoyment they should have joined palms [at the tips], while for the sake of liberation in the sacrifices to Smara and others, they should have white tips. (6.50)
Regarding this [unconquered state]: one should cause all the tips of the petals to be red in color;
for Gaurī, Sarasvatī, and the others, the petals are like those of the *aśvattha* tree.
One should cause the tips of the cow’s ears to be fashioned for the lords of knowledge and the planets.
The tips of the lower [ends] belong to the guardians of the quarters (dikpālakas) as well as to the lords of the Gaṇas such as Nandin;
and likewise for Vighneśa, Padmodbhava, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Skanda, and others, just as in the case of Śiva. (6.52)
One should fill the joints of the petals with smooth, dark-colored powder;
the intermediate spaces and corners of the pedestal should likewise be made reddish.

The pedestal (pīṭha), however, should be adorned with feet that are white, reddish, yellow, and black, as well as blue pegs (kīla); it should have four limbs of various colors, or one may fashion it according to one's preference with any colors at all.
In this *Tattvasāgara*:
"One should erase two squares for the pedestal (*pīṭha*) in the cardinal directions, and likewise erase three squares each in the corners.
One should adorn the pathway with creepers, canopies, and so forth, as well as with leaves."
Outside of that, one should fill the four doors in the cardinal directions with white [color].
For the purpose of the doors, two squares in each of the directions are situated in the inner row for the sūtra-makers;
in the row outside that, there are two pairs [of squares]. One should thus contemplate these six squares in the cardinal directions.
There are three chambers each on the two sides of the inner doors;
for the sake of achieving aesthetic beauty, one should merge them into a single unit externally.
In this manner, eight [deities] known as Kaṇṭha and Upakaṇṭha arise, each possessing four separate compartments.
On their sides, there should likewise be Kapola and Upakapola, whose faces are turned in the opposite direction. (6.58)
Then, one should write the remaining six squares individually in the corners for the sake of liberation and the accomplishment of the corners, or else in the positions of the bulls.
One should cover those corners with blue and draw the branches with white.
One should cover both the neck and its vicinity with blood, and the cheeks and their vicinity with yellow, so that the ground is no longer visible. (6.61)
Then, one should draw the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas all around, following the sequence previously stated;
these should be measured by a thumb's breadth with red, white, and black powders respectively, and they should be separated in the middle by a barley-corn.
The Chapter on Auspiciousness:
Having divided the square into eight parts and thus formed sixty-four squares, one should draw a lotus and a pedestal in the center using four squares. (6.63)

Indeed, the pathway (vīthikā) should be formed by the outer row; then, in the four directions of the two outer rows, one should construct the doors using squares numbering four (vedasaṃkhyaiḥ), and having swept them clean, one should make them white and equal.
On both sides of the doors, in the outer row, one should join each individual square with the door and then erase it; thus the *kaṇṭha* and *upakaṇṭha* [sections] are formed. (6.65)
Having established one square in each corner, there shall be five separate squares remaining;
when these are joined together, they form the *vedas* (corners) and the *kapolakas* (cheeks), and an equal number of *upakapolakas* (sub-cheeks).

Regarding this, it is said: "In the Ajita [mandala], there should be a skull among them; the foot [mark] should extend from east to west, and the upakapola should likewise extend from south to north."
Having filled the pericarp and so forth, as well as the walkway, with the colors previously mentioned according to the path described,
the doors should be white, their jambs red, and the lintels below should be radiant yellow.
In this regard, it is stated in the *Ajita* and the *Bṛhatkālottara*:
"One should conceive of the cheeks and side-cheeks, starting from the southeast corner and proceeding in order,
as red, yellow, dark blue, and white."
One should fill the squares in the corners starting from the southeast with yellow, dark green, black, and red,
or else one should fill all of them with black.

On the exterior, however, having drawn the three qualities (guṇas) as before with white, reddish-brown, and black colors, this shall be the Sarvatobhadra; it is auspicious because of the unification of the six squares in each corner.
In all mandalas, however, the lotus petals shall be white;
likewise, the gates and the pathway (vīthī) are to be adorned with creepers and the like, without distinction.
The Chapter on the Sarvatobhadra:
In this square divided into thirty-two parts, there are one thousand and sixty-four cells.
One should draw a lotus in its center using as many cells as there are principles (tattvas), as described previously.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be formed by the outer row; outside of that, one should draw eight liṅgas on both sides of the lines of the cardinal directions using seven rows.

The auspicious pedestal, together with its neck, extending from Brahmā down to the water-base (jalapāda), should be laid out with lines that are horizontal and vertical, using proportions of six, four, two, and six units.

Indeed, above the pedestal, by means of the four squares situated in pairs within the middle rows, there shall be a liṅga; its top may be tapered toward the center from the central line passing through it. || 6-74 ||
One should draw inward-facing signs for those desiring enjoyment;
for those desiring liberation, one should make them the opposite, with the seats facing inward. (6.75)
The two auspicious side-pedestals situated on both sides of its neck-throne should be formed according to the division of four squares;
likewise, within the intervals between the liṅgas, creepers should be fashioned in the corners using twenty-five squares.
Just as the lines contained within those squares are touched together like a cow’s urine pattern (*gomūtrikā*),
so too, by the removal of other lines, there should be creepers extending toward the intermediate directions.
Alternatively, one may draw the leaves of creepers within the inner margins;
these should have their roots attached at the beginning of the creeper and possess curved tips and so forth. (6.78)
Outside of that, one should clear out a pathway with two rows as before;
likewise, having adorned the pathway with various *kalpalatā* (wish-fulfilling creepers), one should also [clear] the three outer enclosures.
Here, for the sake of the doors, one should omit squares numbering four, six, and eight, starting from the interior.
The primary ornament (śobhā) and the secondary ornament (upaśobhā) may also be formed by omitting two, four, or six [cells] respectively;
one should erase three times seven cells separately in each corner.
One should adorn everything, beginning with the lotus, like the *Bhadraka* [mandala], using five kinds of powders;
or one may fill the eight lingas according to one's wish with the colors prescribed for the five faces.
Thus has this circle of palaces been described by the beloved of Pārvatī,
adorned with eight liṅgas, creepers, lotuses, walkways, and ramparts.
The Chapter on the Temple of the Beloved of Pārvatī:
A square field measuring four cubits should be divided into twenty parts, resulting in four hundred squares;
in its center, a lotus is formed by twenty-five squares.
One row [of squares] shall be for the pedestal (pīṭha), then one for the path (vīthī);
thereafter, by four rows, there shall be the doors and liṅgas, with creepers all around; and by the outermost row, the outer path (bāhyavīthī) is formed.

One should construct the lotus seats and the pathways according to the ritual procedure, like that of Bhadraka; likewise, the gates in all directions should be formed by two squares each within a row of eight squares.
From the interior of the street, there are three cells connected by a doorway; then the floor-base (bhūpīṭha) consists of a single cell.
Next, the neck-base (kaṇṭhapīṭha) is formed, followed by the water-band (toyapaṭṭa) with three cells, and then the liṅga with one cell.
Below and above that square, within the four squares of the pedestal (pīṭha),
one should draw a thread reaching to the corners of the interior square, measuring half the length of the square-thread.
Having rotated [the thread] and cast it outside, one should leave four broken edges;
thus the pedestal (pīṭha) becomes beautiful, adorned with twelve corners.
Having filled the entire mandala, from the lotus to the edge of the path, with colored powders as previously described,
that mandala is known as the "Emergence of the Lata-liṅga," which is beloved by Śaṅkara.
The Chapter on the Emergence from the Embrace of the Creeper:
On a square field divided sixteenfold in the four directions, one should fashion four liṅgas using the compartments, like [the faces] of the Beloved of Pārvatī. (6.90)

In the center, with distinguished Veda-cells, and in the intervals between the liṅgas as well, with an equal number of those [cells], there shall be a four-petalled lotus by itself; it is contracted at the tops upon the liṅgas.
There should be eight auspicious syllables (bhadrāṣṭaka) at the necks and creepers in the corners as before;
having written this, that maṇḍala shall be designated as the Pañcabrahma.
In the center of the lotus, there should be a circular pericarp, yellow in color, with a thin row of filaments that are red.
Īśa is in the middle, while Puruṣa and the others are located in the directions according to their respective colors, situated within their lingas.

In this very *Gaurītilaka-maṇḍala*, however, having drawn svastikas in the places where the creepers would normally be, there shall be a pathway (*vīthī*) between the two rows of half-squares at the corners. (6.94)
First, one should mark a square near the navel that is curved and elongated; then, one should again erase two [squares].
This shall be a svastika marked with four paths turning to the right, provided with an inner pathway. (6.95)
One should decorate the paths in sequence with dark blue, yellow, black, and red;
however, in the Bhadraka layout, the cross-paths (khaṇḍavīthī) other than the central axis should be white.
The Chapter on the Gaurī-tilaka of the Pañcabrahma-maṇḍala:
When the field is thus divided eighteenfold, there shall be three hundred and forty-four squares in it;
indeed, with twenty squares corresponding to the number of the *tattvas*, one should draw a lotus in the center as described before.
In all eight directions, there should also be svastikas formed by thirty-six squares;
the procedure for omitting squares is traditionally taught as one, then three, and then five.

Indeed, this [design] is the Svastika-maṇḍala-lotus; or else, when this field is divided into twelve parts, there shall be a lotus in the center formed by sixteen squares, and likewise, svastikas shall be placed in the eight directions.
Having filled the svastikas and the lotus as before with colors,
the svastika is recommended for the sake of well-being, as it is a source of joy for all the gods.
The Section on the Double Svastika Lotus:
In this field divided into eighteen parts, one should first conceive of the navel of the svastika situated in its center;
then, one should erase five squares on all sides, which have the appearance of a crossroads. (6.101)
Lines extending across the squares, curved in the form of a svastika, should be established as mutually intersecting oceans by means of the omission of the remaining [lines]. (6.102)
In this [mandala], there are indeed fifty-seven *svastikas* together with the *arkabhadras*;
and in the center, there are fifty-two and two *sarvatobhadra* crossroads.
One should decorate the remaining single squares in the corners with white;
likewise, one should decorate the auspicious crossroads with blue, yellow, red, and dark colors.
This indeed is the mandala named Sarvatobhadrasvastika;
they call it Sarvasvastika because it is dear to the two, Śiva and Śivā.

Alternatively, when the site is divided into sixteen parts—either by the divisions of fourteen, twelve, two, ten, or six—the mandalas should indeed be laid out as before, in reverse order, so that they are auspicious and well-proportioned on all sides. (6.106)
The *svastika* and *sarvatobhadra* [mandalas].
In a square measuring two cubits, there should be a wheel and a lotus, devoid of a pedestal;
it should have a single nave, and its characteristics should follow the sequence of the measurement in finger-breadths (*mānāṅgula*).

Then, having placed the thread at the central point, with a measurement of nine finger-breadths—half of a lotus—one should rotate it three times by measures of eight and four [finger-breadths]; thus the navel, the spokes, and the rim of the lotus shall be formed.
Having drawn a lotus as before, one should fill the nave with yellow [pigment].
Then, having extended the lines of the petals upon the wheel which has spokes equal to the petals, || 6.109 ||

Then one should draw the spokes within them correctly; likewise, on the two spokes adjacent to each petal, the spokes here should be formed by extending the lines from the tips of the petals and the lines from the joints of the petals. (6.110)
Having divided the ground into three parts, one should mark two [sections] with a central line;
then, having struck out [the excess] like a fish-tail from among them, one should draw the spokes using threads upon these [lines].

They may resemble the petals of a blue lotus or an *aśvattha* tree, or they may have the shape of a *mātuluṅga* fruit; they may have the luster of a lotus leaf, or the shape of a barley grain, or be thin in the middle like an ant. (6.112)

The Arakas are red, dawn-colored (aruṇa), and dark (śyāma); they should be in alternating order. At the end, they should have the luster of yellow pigment (gorocanā); the joints of the spokes should be yellow.
Having divided the circumference into three parts, one should fill the middle with white and the exterior with black;
having filled the interior corners with yellow, they should be made beautiful with the svastika sign in black.
Standing within the interval between two spokes, one should revolve outside the felly;
but standing in the middle of the junction of the spokes, one should rotate the base of the spoke.
Standing in the middle of the spokes, one should rotate the center of the spokes;
in this way, the spokes are successively perfected, taking the shape of citron fruits.

A thread positioned at the tip of one spoke, extending from its center, joint, and root, and likewise positioned on both sides of the spoke, should be struck out separately; thus the spokes become like the petals of a wide-open blue lotus.

Situated in the middle of the spokes, having left a small portion at the tip of each spoke like a lotus petal, the spokes of the lotus petals arise from the rotation of the hub and the rotation of the tips. (6.118)
The roots should be tapered and broad in the middle; they should be made with a width of one-third from the joint of the *āra* [rib].
They should enter inwardly by what is called a "barley-grain's breadth" (*yavodara*), and they shall be perfected when their tips are gradually sharpened. (6.119)
Having divided the protective field into three parts,
one should stand in the middle of the second and first portions and, after circling around, [place the seed-syllables] in the third portion like the tips of petals.
One should draw the tips of the petals with two half-moon-shaped lines;
in this way, the spokes indeed come to resemble the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
Then, having stood at the midpoint of the junction of the spokes, by rotating transversely from half the length of both spokes,
there should be spokes with thin middles between the two lines, known as the *pipīlikā* (ant) and *kroḍa* (lap).
Having adorned it with various flowers between the spokes of the wheel,
one should then decorate the exterior of the *bimba*— or, if it has been smeared— with rows of flowers.
It has been stated that the lotus-wheel with a single nave is dear to Śiva, Āryā, Hari, and Bhāskara;
other lotus-wheel mandalas, beautiful with nine navas, should also be inferred. (6.124)
The section on the wheel and lotus:

By means of a measurement equal to half the pericarp, through the process of rotating the previously placed thread, twelve fish-diagrams (*matsya*) shall arise by joining the sides of those lines. (6.125)
By means of those [lines] falling upon the sūtras as they properly intersect with the sūtras, the lotus of the sun-maker [the central lotus] is formed;
through the equal division of the eight-petaled lotus, there shall be a lotus adorned with sixteen petals. (6.126)
From the thread at the end of the sky-line of the filaments, mark [the center] by means of a fish-diagram extending to the tips of those filaments; thus there shall be a five-petaled lotus.
From the junctions of the pericarp and the petals, as before, for the sake of accomplishing the six-petalled [lotus];
but in the seven-petalled [lotus], the tips of the petals are situated between the sky-line and the pericarp.
Having placed [the marks] at the junctions of the petals from the pericarp and the petal-junctions using the fish-sign, there shall be nine petals;
by stretching five lines, it shall become a row of petals.
Having placed the midpoint between the filaments and the sky (the center) within the void, one should mark it;
thus, by the laying of the lines, there shall be a lotus with eleven petals.

Having placed [the thread] at the tip of the petal and at the joint of the petal-tip, and having marked them, one should strike the threads across them; that shall be the covering for the lotus-diagram.
If one desires an increase in petals beyond this, one should follow this same method here in due order;
then, by means of lines drawn according to that calculation and based on the center, one should draw lotuses as desired.
The characteristics for the division of the [sacrificial] ground are as follows:
by means of the measurement and the laying down of the lines, one should fashion the forms of the half-moon and other kuṇḍas according to one's desire. || 6.133 ||

When the corners of the directions and intermediate directions are marked by sixteen long lines falling across, there are thirty-two divisions all around; then, from the rotation [of the cord], five fields arise within them. (6.134)

The half-lotus should be eight finger-breadths at the beginning; the pedestal (pīṭha) with three, the navel with three, the walkways (vīthī) with four, and the doors, as well as the beauties (śobhā) and sub-beauties (upaśobhā), should be six finger-breadths each.
As before, there is a lotus here with a circular pedestal; the navel is formed by the qualities (the three lines), along with a swan, arrows, a lotus, and a conch.
The path should be enriched with four rows, to be constructed according to the sequence of colors like the Bhadraka design.
In this case, there shall be a distinction regarding the doors and other elements; that field is divided in two ways by rotation.
The doors are formed by the outer portions of the inner *vedī* (altar) segments, consisting of six parts.
As previously stated, there should be primary and secondary ornaments; the corner-markings are also described.
Those pitchers are inward-facing; the corners have four parts for their mouths and two parts for their necks.
By turning them toward the sides of those corners, they should have broad bellies and curved bases.
Thus, this circle of powers (śakti-maṇḍala) is known as that which is called the Māyā-cakra.

The Chapter on the Māyācakra. Now I shall describe the Bimba known as Tripura; one should construct the field as a long quadrangle, according to the method previously stated, using the supreme lines, and it should be two or three cubits in length and breadth.
One should lay down thirty-three threads here extending from east to west,
and forty-seven in number extending from south to north.
In this [mandala], there are as many compartments (koṣṭha) as the number of the elements;
in its center, there should also be compartments equal in number to the elements,
forming a lotus, and around that, a row [of compartments].
Having abandoned those two [lotuses] to its east and west. || 6-142 ||
One should erase one row here around the three lotuses;
that long, square-shaped area is known as the *antarvīthi* (inner path).
Outside that row, one should construct a pedestal (pīṭha) all around using five squares from its corners;
furthermore, one should form the limbs (gātra) facing east, west, south, and north using [squares of] eight, eight, four, and four [units] respectively.
In the middle of the corners, one should erase five squares;
there shall be a single pedestal for the three lotuses, which is long and rectangular.
Outside of that, the markers for the south, north, east, and west shall be formed by six and seven squares respectively;
in those directions, within the squares as described, they are made with seven rows of horizontal lines.
One should erase [the lines] on both sides of the liṅgas in pairs within the square;
indeed, by means of thirty-six separate compartments, those [liṅgas] come into being.
In the same way, within the four corners, one should draw dancing swans using thirty-six square cells arranged in long rectangles.
One should make red lotus petals for the sake of attaining fortune, victory, wealth, and good luck;
white ones for the attainment of knowledge, poetic skill, and so forth; while the rest, beginning with the pericarp, is indeed as previously described.
Then, having drawn two conchs and two wheels with yellow [pigment] within the inner path in the eight squares, one should draw four lotuses.
In the street, there should be a creeper; by means of the remaining three rows, one should form the four directions, the four gates, and so forth.
One should erase six, eight, and ten squares on both sides of the gates, specifically on the south and the north.
For the sake of achieving the primary and secondary ornaments, one should erase four, six, and eight squares in the east and west, and two, four, and six in the north and south. (6.152)
The eastern and western gates should be formed by four, six, and eight squares;
the corners should consist of three and seven squares, and their bases by four squares.
The Chapter on the Maṇḍala of Tripurā:
Having divided the field twentyfold and then again into two, there are indeed six hundred and one thousand squares within this four-cornered [maṇḍala]; from the center of that—
With four sets of thirty-six [units], there shall be the great liṅga together with its pedestal (pīṭha).
The pedestal and so forth are formed by thirty-two, eight, and sixteen squares [respectively]. (6.154)
Having smoothed out a row around that [central area], the pedestal (pīṭha) shall be formed by an outer row;

outside of that, one should draw lotuses in the eight directions in sequence, using squares numbered according to the principles (tattva) of the sages' rows, separately as before, and also on the sides of the liṅga.
The walkways are formed by two rows [of squares] on all sides, consisting of six times twenty compartments.

In this [mandala], there should be lingas colored according to the castes beginning with Īśāna; these remaining lingas should be drawn from a lotus according to the prescribed method, using white, red, and reddish-white colors for the individual syllables on the lotuses starting from the east.

Then, having joined them in sequence clockwise along the path, one should draw conch shells of white luster; if that constitutes a mandala, it is called the "Garland of Conchs" (Śaṅkhamālā). If there are swans here, it would be the "Garland of Swans" (Haṃsamālā) with eight [swans] situated in the cardinal directions.
There are three doors and three-pointed projections arranged within the compartments, along with decorative elements in the three rows.
The corners should consist of twenty-seven squares arranged in three rows;
having covered them with black [powder], one should also draw svastikas, lotuses, and so forth therein.
The section on the liṅga, the belly-marked [liṅga],

the conch-shell garland, and so forth: other than the discus and lotus, these are prescribed for the worship of Śakti and Śiva, for initiation and the like, as well as for the Pavitraka rite and others, along with auspicious svastika-liṅgas.
The wheels and lotuses of the Sun, Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, and Brahmā are auspicious;
for the Śaktis, the conch, the pitcher, and the illusory lotus known as Tripura are prescribed. (6.159)
Just as it was stated for the Śaktis, so too here, in the Svastikas, Vighneśa, Anala, and Ṣaḍvaktra should be worshipped along with Indra, Smara, and Bhogin. (6.160)
"All [deities] are to be worshipped by all, or [only specific ones] according to their respective rites.
Thus has the procedure for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the mandala been primarily described, which is suitable for the worship of Śiva and the other gods.
Having examined various Śiva-āgamas in many ways here, [this work] brings delight to the minds of the foremost of practitioners (*sādhaka*). (6.161)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Rite of the Fire-pit and the Mandala, in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the seventh chapter:
I shall describe the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; furthermore, the *sruk* is one cubit in length.
It may be made from *pālāśa*, *khadira*, or likewise the excellent *śāmilī* wood.
The mouth should be four-cornered, measuring one *aṅgula* according to the vowels;
it is best when six or five [aṅgulas] wide, middling, and the lowest when less. Here, the interior of that [mouth] is covered with three parts.
The excavation should indeed be equal in width [to the base], and it should be circular;
there should be three external ridges (mekhalā), and likewise a lotus-like design all around them.
Outside of those, however, there should be a neck (kaṇṭha) measuring one finger-breadth in width and extending upward from it in length.
The tip should be four finger-breadths long, and its width should be equal to that.
Furthermore, the hollow cavity situated in the middle of the throat is indeed triangular and elongated;
it extends as far as that depression where the little finger can enter.
Its back is marked with a lotus, and its entire opening resembles an elephant's trunk.
The remainder of it should be a rounded handle, and its tip should be marked with a lotus. || 7-3 ||

The tip of the staff, measured by its circumference, should be one finger-breadth thick at the bottom of the lotus and gradually increase in thickness toward the base like a forearm until it measures eight fingers;
there, either a bull or a lotus of smooth form should be fashioned on all sides.
Having cut down trees grown in auspicious locations that are free from defects, one should have the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) fashioned.
The origin of the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles is as follows: one should fashion the *sruva* well-constructed with a length of two *tāla*s;
its mouth should be circular with a diameter of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and its cavity (*avaṭa*) should be half a finger-breadth.
A wall of the measure of a barley-corn (*yava*) is prescribed for the middle of those two smooth cavities.
The area from one *karṣa* [of earth] is the abode of clarified butter; it has the shape of a cow's footprint, and on its back, the two buttocks are marked by two barley grains.
A line measuring one barley-corn in thickness is drawn across the middle of the *sphiga*; below the mouth is the neck, marked with lotus-designs, and below that is the stem, well-rounded and even.
The tip of the stem is one finger-breadth in circumference, while its base is one-and-a-half times that.
It may resemble a cow's tail from the neck downwards, for its base is indeed thick like that. || 7-6 ||
Others say that the *sruva* ladles should be one cubit (*bāhu*) or one forearm (*aratni*) in length.
This concludes the section on the *sruk* and *sruva*.
If, having split a beautiful branch, it should emerge from a *śamī* tree or be made from *aśvattha* wood;
If not, then from a single *pippala* wood, the fire-drill (*araṇi*) should be as long as twelve finger-breadths;
its top should be six finger-breadths wide, the foot is said to be at the base and the head at the tip,
while the middle part, measured by four finger-breadths, should be suitable for the churning stick.
Likewise, the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇi) may also be made from aśvattha wood; one should fashion its rotating pin (bhrāmaka) with six finger-breadths.
The axle (netra) should be made of straight khadira wood, and the cord (rajju) must be firm.
Therein one should generate fire using fuel that is pithy and stripped of its bark.
One should also blow upon the fire using a fan made from split wood or other such means. || 7-8 ||
The rules regarding forest-grown wood and so forth:
wood that is crooked, with withered leaves, thin, worm-eaten, split, not harvested with an axe, short, with bark fallen off from being thick, damaged, long, burnt by fire, and so on [is unfit].
The sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) should be avoided if they originate from a place where impurities reside; the remaining ones should be cut evenly.
They are praised when their thickness is equal to that of the middle and ring fingers, while those as thick as the little finger are considered inferior.
Indeed, fuel sticks (*samidh*) that are as long as a palm are recommended for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and the like;
those measuring seven finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) are praised for rites of bewilderment (*bhramaṇa*) and subjugation (*cāṭana*);
and those measuring four finger-breadths are for the procedure of accomplishing the rite of enmity (*vidveṣa*).
Even those that are curved and measure six finger-breadths [are used] in rites of killing. || 7-10 ||

In matters of attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*) and subjugation (*vaśya*), the fuel sticks (*samidh*) should be the length of a finger; for rites where there is no specific distinction, they should be the measure of a span (*prādeśa*). For minor rites, one should offer the back of the stick into the fire, and likewise its tip.
And he indeed offers oblations into the fire during auspicious rites according to the instructions. || 7-11 ||

The sacrificial fuel (idhma) is declared to consist of eighteen kindling sticks (samidh), being one span (prādeśa) long, or in some cases measured by a cubit (ratni). There should be three enclosing sticks (paridhi), each a cubit in length;
the southern one is long, the western one thick, and the northern one thin and short.
In the north, those born in Kauśika are the best; indeed, the Pālaka and Kuśa types of Darbha grass are superior in their respective order.

Those that are torn, plucked by hand or nails, infested with worms, employed for other tasks, belonging to Yama, damaged by leaping over tigers, or those that are smoky-colored, upward-pointing, or dried out;
as well as those that are dark, tender, recently cut, fresh, or half-dried— these should be avoided.
If darbha grasses are to be used here in this chapter on fire-rituals, then the braided hair and so forth have been prescribed.

In that regard, there is a braid made of thirty *darbha* blades. Alternatively, for the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*), there may be *darbha* blades numbering eight, eighteen, sixteen, or twenty-eight. A *kūrca* (bundle) tied with *darbha* blades numbering the elements (five) is the "sword of knowledge. According to the *Saṃhitāṭīkā*, a general *kūrca* consists of two *darbha* blades, while a special *kūrca* consists of five *darbha* blades. For the rites of the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* vessels, there should be two *kūrca*s each made of five *darbha* blades; the *brahmakūrca* consists of seventeen [blades]. (7–14)
The staff shall be twelve finger-breadths long, with a single *brahmagranthi* at one finger-breadth from the top;
its tip should be fashioned with three finger-breadths of *kūrca* grass.

A pair of *darbha* blades tied together at their middle, measuring one *prādeśa* in length, is prescribed as the *pavitraka* for the consecration (*saṃskāra*); furthermore, a pair is used for illumination (*vidyotana*). For the wiping of the *sruk* ladle, there should indeed be four *kuśa* blades here in the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Two darbha tips, each one finger-breadth in length, are then placed here upon the sacrificial grass at intervals of twelve finger-breadths.
A *pavitra* for the twice-born should be knotted with two *darbha* blades as long as a palm and four finger-breadths in length; for minor rites, it should consist of three blades held in the hands.

For the twice-born, the *brahmagranthi* is prescribed for the hand-purifier; for those born in the natural order (*anuloma*), it is used alone; and for women and those in the fourth generation, it is the *dūrvā* grass alone.
"Thus, there should be one hundred and ten darbha blades, excluding the *prastara*;
this is the opinion of Baudhāyana.
This is the rule for the fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)."

The ground designated as a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) is that which has been immediately smeared with cow dung; it is traditionally held to measure eight "cow-ears" (gokarṇa), or six, or even the size of a cow-hide (gocarma).
Alternatively, for rivers and the like, auspicious white sand measuring five *prasthas* is prescribed.
Regarding that in general, Bodhāyana says in the context of the fire-oblation on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila): || 7-19 ||

The vessel for the clarified butter (ājya) should be like a shallow cup (śarāva), eight finger-breadths (aṅgula) in width and its height equal to half its width; its neck (nāla) should be four finger-breadths [in diameter].
The vessel for the praṇītā water should be six finger-breadths in width and equal in height.
The *prokṣaṇī* vessel should be eight finger-breadths in width and height, equal [in these dimensions], and provided with a spout.
In this regard, the Pauṣkara states:
"In all cases, vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or clay yield superior, middling, and inferior results respectively.
Furthermore, a cooking pot (sthālī) filled with eight *kuḍuba* measures of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) is considered the lowest.
A ladle made of copper is considered excellent when it measures twelve or eight finger-breadths;
those beginning with the best and ending with the inferior are measured by three or seven [finger-breadths].
Here, its length should be five finger-breadths, while the circular head is seven finger-breadths and the tail is two.

The white grains of *śāli* rice, along with *sakala*, *māsa*, wild rice (*nīvāra*), and *ṣaṣṭika* varieties—provided they are thoroughly cleaned, free from husks and grit, and acquired through honest means—should be used for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Furthermore, fresh ghee from one's own livestock is the best; that which is purchased is middling.
Clarified butter that is purchased and not freshly made is inferior; it should be of cow's milk and properly strained. (7.22)
