Honey that is not corrupted by smell or taste, even if purchased, should be accepted after being strained again; likewise, fresh white sugar-candy, sugar, and molasses from sugarcane should be taken.
Among these, each preceding one is more highly praised than the next, provided it is entirely pure and acquired through honest means.
And for the sake of the oblation (homa) and other rites, all grains such as sesame seeds and the like should be thoroughly purified and washed.
Furthermore, whatever other fruit, root, or substance is flavorful, pure, and fresh should be taken; for grains such as śāli rice, an oblation the size of a thumb is prescribed.
For liquid substances, it is said that the measure held by five fingers (the span) should be filled with a *sruva* ladle.
Indeed, for parched grains there is a mere handful; for flowers such as the lotus and others, there is only one at a time.
For creepers, it should be four *aṅgulas*; for sesame seeds and groats, it should be the "deer" (*mṛgī*) measure, which indeed consists of the middle finger joined with the thumb;
for fragrant substances, it is the size of a chickpea (*caṇakī*); and for *guggulu*, it is like the seed of a jujube (*badarī*).
And for edible foods such as large fruits and the like, the oblation should be measured by the size of an akṣa seed. || 7.25 ||

In the case of an oblation mixed with various kinds of food, one should take a single leaf each of dates, *iṅguda*, *goṣṭhanī*, jujube, and rose-apple fruits, as well as a single joint of sugarcane, and hold them with the five fingers.
Likewise, three tips of dūrvā grass and each individual fuel-stick (samidh) constitute a single oblation.
The measure of the oblation:
the *vardhanī* vessel may be filled with a full *bhāra* of water, the *kumbha* with a *khārī*, the *kalaśa* with a *droṇa* of water, and the *karkarī* should be completely filled by Śiva.
A full vessel (pūrṇā) consists of one āḍhaka; two kuḍubas make a śarāva.
Or, it may be half-full by one kuḍuba; likewise, the conch and the lamp should be proportionate to the spreading [of the offering]. (7.27)
The measure of the vessel:

I shall now describe here the purification regarding the vessel, as well as that of the substances and so forth; one should wash it with water until the scent, ointment, and other residues have completely disappeared.
One should also scrub with powders and then wash again with warm water;
this is the purification for vessels here, and now the specific purification is being described.
A golden vessel is purified by water so that the coating may be removed; likewise,
a copper vessel [is purified] by acidic water, one made of silver by cow-dung,
a bell-metal vessel by ash and water, and a gemstone vessel by the rays of the sun or by water.
If a clay vessel is [purified] by burning, it becomes as new; likewise, a wooden one [is purified] instantly. || 7-29 ||

The purification of iron from burning has thus been declared by those who work with metals; likewise, horse-faced [leather] is purified by touch or by contact with water, provided it is not excessively worn.
Regarding skins, ropes, and clothes, purification occurs through washing with alkaline water.
And there may be water and wind in a vessel made of bottle-gourd or bamboo due to the friction of cowherds' staffs. || 7-30 ||

Purification shall occur even for water-vessels by performing the *paryagni* rite; likewise, for grains, fruits, *darbha* grass, roots, and sacrificial fuel, it is by sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) and washing (*adhāvana*).
For silken garments, fine cotton cloths, silk fabrics, and dyed clothes—those which have not been touched [by impurity]—[the purification is as follows].
The eyes, which have become clouded by the passion for the sprinkling of nectar, are purified by white mustard seeds. || 7-31 ||

Furthermore, vessels made of wood, bamboo, and the like, as well as those made of clay, should be discarded if they are defiled by phlegm, food remnants, filth, or the like, or if they have been contaminated by the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
Regarding oily substances, purification is possible even if they are severely defiled; otherwise, they must be purified by heating.
One may be purified by [bathing] in lotus ponds and similar bodies of water at night, upon seeing the crest of a flame from a fire. || 7-32 ||

The ground is purified by being trampled by cows, or by having its surface dug up and scraped away, or by being thoroughly ploughed; likewise, a house or similar structure is purified when smeared with water and cow-dung.
Furthermore, a site is purified by the proclamation of a "meritorious day" (*puṇyāha*), by feeding Brahmins, and by scraping the earth.
One who has committed a sin is purified by speaking; the purification of words comes from speaking with the twice-born.

The body, together with the mind, is purified by breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma); likewise, one who has touched what should not be touched becomes pure by immersing oneself in water along with one's clothes. This also applies to one who has eaten such things, or after sneezing, spitting, or yawning.
One must perform the sipping of water (ācamana) upon seeing outcastes, Śūdras, and the like.
Water from wells and the like is purified by being drawn out; or, in this case, it may be purified by the rays of the sun when touched by their beams with great force.
A common fire is purified by sprinkling, or by having moved elsewhere.
And by means of the expiation and the rite beginning with the fire-mouth, he becomes one who has established the sacred fires. || 7-35 ||
The purification of perfumes and other substances is achieved by sprinkling them with water consecrated by mantras; in the case of milk and food, one should pour clarified butter over them;
and they are purified by the illumination of *darbha* grass, provided there is no excessive crushing.
In the same way, purification should be inferred even for those who have vomited. || 7.36 ||
This purity of the mind is common to all virtues and is the cause of them; it is the purity regarding actions, substances, the self, and so forth.
But that purity which is untainted by passion and the like belongs to the wise.
If these four human goals are also within his grasp. || 7-37 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the *Sruk* and *Sruva* Lladles," in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the eighth chapter:
Next, [the description] of the deities who are essentially composed of mantra, as is appropriate.
Worship should be known as that which brings about accomplishment, bestowing both visible and invisible fruits.
By that [worship], the deities become pleased and bestow the fruits of human goals;
that worship is to be known as threefold, according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior. (8-2)
The supreme worship consists of sixteen types of offerings; that which occurs here with ten offerings is middling;
while worship according to the rite of five offerings is inferior. One should resort to the worship among these according to one's means.

Whichever mantra has whatever kind of worship prescribed by the Guru of the Kalpatantra— be it the "excellent" (śreṣṭha) or other classifications— one should propitiate this [deity] with that and achieve success.

The seat, the invocation, the offering of water for honor (arghya), and so forth; the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya); likewise the bath along with its primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga), as well as the garments and ornaments.
Incense, flowers, as well as incense smoke, lamps, offerings of cooked rice, fire rituals, prostrations, and the dedication of recitation and worship. (8.6)
Thus, the sixteen modes of service have been briefly indicated:
namely, the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the bath (snāna), the fragrant paste (gandha), and the flowers (puṣpa).
Incense, lamps, food offerings, and prostrations— these ten are proclaimed as the ritual services (upacāras) in the middle level of worship.
Fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings—these five are the minor services (upacāra) in the Kaniṣṭha [rite].
Furthermore, the distinctions among these characteristics are here set forth for the benefit of practitioners. (8–9)
That which begins with Śakti and ends with the power of one's own limbs (svāṅgaśakti)— whether it be the lotus of the seat (pīṭhābja) or the lotus alone—
is declared to be the "seat" (āsana) as prescribed by the rules of the Mantras.
Or rather, the seat is the support for the deity; when seated upon it, the beloved deity is worshipped.
Since the root *ās* signifies "sitting," its accomplishment is "seatedness"; therefore, the seat is traditionally praised as being primary. (8.11)
Then, that which one brings forth from the sky-lotus, or from the *bindu*, or from the heart, or from the solar orb—
that is designated as "invocation" (*āvāhana*).
The manifestation of the reality that is inherently full before one, through worship and other rites performed with devotion, is intended here as its invocation (āvāhana).

Having filled his joined palms with flowers, and recollecting the all-pervading Lord residing in the heart and other centers, he brings Him up by way of the *suṣumṇā* channel, visualizing Him as having emerged from the *bindu*.
One should recite the mantra until it reaches the sphere of the partless (niṣkala);
then, having grasped that, one should remain confident and steady-minded before the [deity] standing in front.
Whether upon an image or even on a sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should perform that invocation;
and as constituent parts of the invocation, there are the rites of installation (sthāpana) and bringing near (sannidhāpana).
Furthermore,
for the purpose of worshipping the chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) who possesses form, there is the sealing, the immortalization, and the veiling upon the prepared seat.
Seating is designated as "sthāpana" (establishment) performed with devotion;
it consists of the deity's presence [invoked] until the conclusion of the ritual section. (8.18)
The continuous performance of worship is called "complete cessation" (sannirodha), which is the undifferentiated purpose of those things whose intrinsic nature is not divided. (8.19)
Indeed, that is the immortalization of the limbs together with the possessor of the limbs;
it is the reality that is the abode of bliss, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss. (8-20)
This very form should be meditated upon as that which constitutes the veil;
its splendor is like a covering that increases the radiance of the limbs. (8.21)
That which was described as the "enticement" (prarocana), rich with a flood of the nectar of aesthetic charm,
having received the grace and so forth while the worship is being performed— || 8.22 ||
That which has the capacity to bring something near is "sānnidhāpana" (invocation).
The authority over the seat and the invitation constitutes the rite; that which is offered to one who is worthy and has arrived is declared to be "arghya," meaning worshipful honor. (8-23)
That which is mentally conceived is offered in the various rites of worship and so forth;
and that [offering] of his should be known as threefold: Śaiva, Śākta, and Vaiṣṇava.
The Śaiva arghya is of two kinds: the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) and the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga).
[The six-limbed consists of] fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice grains, kuśa grass, the tip of dūrvā grass, and likewise water. (8.25)
The sixfold arghya described by Bhojendra, Brahmā, and Śambhu is proclaimed as follows:
kuśa grass, unbroken rice, sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, fragrance, flowers, and likewise barley. (8.26)
Milk and the eightfold water for the arghya offering should be consecrated with the Śiva-mantra as proclaimed in the Vijaya-tantra;
it consists of fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, kuśa grass, the tips of dūrvā grass, and mustard seeds. (8.27)
The *arghya* for Śakti is declared to consist of water and eight substances:
white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, tips of *darbha* grass, fragrance, flowers, barley, and fruit. (8.28)
Water joined with these eight ingredients, including sesame seeds, is known as the *arghya* for Viṣṇu.
It should be offered in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or, if these are unavailable, even one made of wood.
The vessel for the *arghya* offering should be filled with three *kuḍuba*s, or it may be a conch shell;
having filled it with the *arghya* water, one consecrates it with the root mantra and its limbs, transforming it into nectar.

Having meditated upon the all-pervading Lord, whose body is free from all limiting adjuncts, standing face-to-face before him, and who has whitened the quarters of the sky with the flow of supreme nectar; (8.31)
Having lifted up the vessel for the special *arghya* with the left hand,
one should subsequently offer the *arghya* with the right hand.
The ritual for the *arghya*:

The *pādya* (water for the feet), however, is common to all; having filled it with water containing *lakṣmī* (lotus) along with *dūrvā* grass, *śyāmāka* grain, and lotuses, one should offer the *pādya* at the [deity's] feet. (8.33)
Water cooled with nutmeg, cardamom, and cloves, which is declared in the *Prapañca* and other texts to be the standard water for ritual rinsing (*ācamanīyaka*). (8.34)
Having combined curd, honey, clarified butter, milk, and water,
and having placed them together in a bronze vessel along with gold, one should hold them with two bunches of kusha grass.
One should offer that madhuparka with the common mantra; however,
the presentation of madhuparka is not desired in the daily sacrifices (nityayajana),
but it is prescribed for occasional rites (naimittika) such as consecrations, ceremonial baths, and the like.
Thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"Furthermore, water that is fragrant is recommended for the rinsing of the mouth."
With the heart-mantra joined by the *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* syllables,
one should likewise offer the fourfold set beginning with the *arghya* in their proper sequence.
There should be three vessels for the *arghya* and likewise three for the *pādya*;
there should be six vessels for the *ācamana*, and one for the *madhuparka*.
The *arghya* is offered first, likewise at the time of bathing, and at the conclusion of the worship;
the *pādya* is offered at three times: first at the bath, then after the ornaments have been applied, and finally at the end.

One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) at these six points: at the end of the foot-washing (pādya), at the end of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), at the beginning and end of the bath (snāna), at the beginning and end of the garments and other items, and at the end of the food offering (naivedya).
Having offered incense, a lamp, and food offerings, as well as betel leaf or fruit and so forth, and having given water for sipping (ācamana), the subsequent ritual action should be performed. (8.41)
Having offered the honey-mixture (madhuparka) at the conclusion of the first round of water for sipping,
and having given a single sip of water for rinsing the mouth, one should then worship [the guest] with fragrant scents and other offerings.
The section on water for the feet, water for sipping, and the honey-mixture:
Having removed the withered offerings, one should worship with fragrance, flowers, and so forth;
having placed *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains upon the head, one should then commence the ritual bath. (8.43)
First, one should cause the bathing of the deity to be performed with meat and marrow;
then, having anointed [the image] with fragrant oil, one should likewise [bathe it] to remove that oil.
One may also rub [the body] with powders of barley, wheat, black gram, and so forth;
sprinkling with slightly warm water and cold water removes the application of ointments. (8.45)
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the root-mantra and the limbs, the offering of flowers and incense,
the food offering (naivedya) consisting of fruits, cakes, and so forth, and auspicious music such as singing and instrumental performance.
One should perform a bath with the nectar of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), followed by the removal of residual smears;
then, one should apply fragrant substances, myrobalan, turmeric, and saffron as unguents.
The sprinkling with fragrant waters using the root-mantras and ancillary Vedic mantras,
as well as the consecration with jars as may be available, should take place.
Likewise, there is the rite of *nīrājana* with auspicious flour, lamps, and so forth;
and the wiping away of the water remaining on the image with a clean cloth. (8.49)
Just as the head is always made non-empty with golden flowers and the like, so indeed is this twenty-limbed bath declared to be the general [rite]. (8.50)
If any of these should be unavailable, one should imagine them with the mind.
Then follows the entitlement to the bath, as well as pure, fine, and new garments.
Whatever garments there are, such as those made of dukūla, paṭṭa, cotton, or devāṅga, which have not been used elsewhere, are free of loose threads, and are unwashed; 8-52.
With devotion, one should cause to be offered here whatever is available that is auspicious,
as well as golden ornaments resplendent with various jewels.
One should properly adorn him with items suitable for his feet up to his hair, according to the extent of one's wealth; or, if these are unavailable, one should do so even mentally.
And here, one should place a stainless mirror in front of the Lord.
The procedure for garments and ornaments;
and scent is to be known as threefold: Śaiva, Śākta, and Vaiṣṇava. (8.55)
Sandalwood, saffron, costus, dalāśīra, as well as agallochum,
camphor, and hībera— these are declared to be the Śaiva fragrance.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, spikenard, saffron, yellow pigment, kakkola, and the fruit of the vānara tree— these are declared to be the ingredients of the Śākta fragrance.
Sandalwood, uśīra, toyāhva, māṃsī, kuṣṭha, murā, agaru, and saffron— these are known as the eightfold fragrant substances belonging to Viṣṇu.
And flowers are likewise described, as previously [stated], according to the divisions of Śaiva and so forth;
they are of three types: fiery (āgneya), lunar (saumya), and both lunar and fiery (saumyāgneya). (8.59)
In this world, those belonging to sattva are white, while those belonging to rajas are red;
those belonging to tamas are black, and the yellow is rajasa-sattvika.

Indeed, even on the leaves it is exactly thus: dark [leaves] are mixed with *tamas* and *rajas*, while from flowers that are *sāttvika* and so forth, the fruit shall likewise be *sāttvika* and so forth.
With white arka, karavīraka, lotus, durdhūraka, rājārka, white water-lily, tulasī, excellent aśoka, and campaka; with kalhāra,
baka, pāṭala, bakula, the two kinds of mallikā, and mālatī—
With leaves of the *pālāśa* tree, lotuses from a dry land, *darbha* grass, *damanaka*, *mārgacchada*, and *dūrvā* grass.
Similarly, [the ground] is auspicious when covered with *granthi*, *śamī*, large *maruvaka*, *punnāga*, *nāgāsana*,
*nandyāvarta*, *tamāla*, *kubja*, *vijayā*, *mandāra*,
and *kāśmīraka* flowers; likewise, it is auspicious with the blossoms of *utpala*, *karṇikāra*, *kādamba*, and *bilva*.
And the blue lotus—these flowers are said to belong entirely to Śiva.

And fresh *bilva*, blue lotus, *ketaka* and other such flowers, as well as *kunda* and *pāṭala*.
Lakṣmī, Devīsaha, Bhṛṅgamusalī, Bhītendravalī,
as well as Bhadrā, Śrīpatilaṅghitā as the tenth, Dūrvā, Jambūcchada, Kalhāra, Karavīra, Ekadalaka, Padma, Kuśa, and Kairava.
And if it is red, by way of reverse order, the flower shall indeed yield greater fruit for a Vaiṣṇava.
With *ambhoja*, *utpala*, *bandhujīva*, and *vijayā*; with *punnāga*, *nāga*, *jātī*, *kunda*, *karaṇḍa*, *campaka*, *japā*, *yūthī*, and *ramāpāṭala*;
and with *bilva*, *aśoka*, *hayāri*, *kubja*, *damana*, *mandāra*, and *dūrvā* leaves—
The flowers known as *rnandī*, *āhvā*, and *aparājitā* are said to be entirely suitable for the Śaktas. 8-66.
Those that are odorless, or possess a pungent and bitter smell; those that are untouchable or corrupted; those acquired through improper means; those marked by nails or worms;
those that are torn; or those that are faded and old due to contact with wool, thread, hair, and the like.
Furthermore, one should likewise avoid flowers that have passed their season or are out of bloom. (8.67)

Among the three types of flowers prescribed, those not explicitly mentioned should be avoided; furthermore, there should be a mutual exclusion where it is stated that they are to be used "except for" something else,
and likewise, those intended for another purpose should be avoided according to reason.
Whatever is specifically prescribed for this [rite] here, one should satisfy that deity.
Likewise, for the Sun and Agni, as well as for the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara), worship is performed with three kinds of flowers; likewise for Śakti, Śambhu, Skanda, Āryaka, Caṇḍa, and others.
For the beloved of Manojavā, Girisutā, Durgā, and the Eight Mothers, [the worship] consists of Śākta [offerings] alone.
Likewise, the lotus-throne of Viṣṇu, the king of gods (Indra), and Lakṣmī should be worshipped by the Vaiṣṇavas.
At midnight, one should worship with *nandyāvarta* flowers; at dawn, before the night has ended, with *mālatī* and *mallikā*;
by day, with lotuses (*abja*) or water-lilies (*utpala*); or always with golden flowers; or in the morning with *kesara* flowers, and at midnight likewise.

A lotus remains fit for worship until its filaments change color; a leaf from the Bilva tree and a wreath remain so for three nights; a Kārṇikāra flower remains fit for a fortnight; but a Bakula flower remains so for six months, after which it becomes withered.
Regarding the section on flowers: among all incense substances, black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru) is the best;
camphor is even more excellent, as is that which is mixed with agallochum.
Guggulu and uśīra along with sandalwood are prescribed for the middle [grade]; śrīvāsa and sarja are considered inferior, as are lac, clarified butter, and honey.
With all these ingredients combined with sugar, the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅgika) is described;
it should be offered upon smokeless, glowing embers that are without flame and without fuel.
One should offer incense slightly below [the vessel] and ring the bell with the left hand;
the wicks should be made from pure white thread or from cotton.
For the purpose of a lamp, cow’s ghee is the best; oil from a buffalo is middling or inferior.
A lamp with camphor as the tenth [ingredient] shall yield a fruit exceeding a hundredfold.
A lamp made of pure camphor alone is said to be a thousandfold more effective than ten, nine, or eight lamps filled with abundant oil.
The *ārātrika* rite should be performed with fresh lamps flickering nearby;
one should not, however, relight a lamp using a wick that has already been burnt down.
The procedure for incense and lamps should not be performed with leftover food, impure oil, and the like, nor with oils or ghee other than those [specified].
Five hundred grains of rice constitute one *tala*; two of those [talas] are known as one *prakuñca*.
Then those two [make] a *prasara*; likewise, two of those are a *kuḍuba*; two of those are half a *prastha*;
a *prastha* is a *pātra*; then an *āḍhaka* is auspicious; then a *droṇa* and a *khārī* follow in sequence.
Indeed, three *khārīs* are declared to be a *bhāra*; such is the measurement according to the scriptures.
The food offering (naivedya) is considered to be of two kinds: daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika).
That which is the most excellent of the excellent shall now be described according to its ninefold division.
Rice grains produced from the *śāli* variety are recommended, as are those from the *kalamā* and *rājaśāli* varieties;
those produced from *nīvāra*, *vrīhi*, and bamboo grass are of middling quality. (8.81)
Priyaṅgu, barley, wheat, and śyāmāka are progressively inferior to rice;
they should be one-eighth the size of the rice grains, and likewise for the condiments and the curd.
The clarified butter, sugar, and honey should each be one-thirty-second part [of the total]; therein, according to the daily rite, [the oblation] is made with eight *droṇas* of husked *śāli* rice.
At midnight and during the four periods [of the day], one should present offerings;
these consist of milk-rice, rice-and-pulse, and beef—thus the food is of four kinds.

It was accompanied by appropriate side dishes, clarified butter, curd, and excellent rice-pudding, along with singing, dancing, and instrumental music, and featured the offering of bali-oblations and auspicious rites.
In that regard, there should be five hundred lamps for the most excellent of the excellent;
having worshipped with six *droṇas* [of offerings] at four times of the day, one should present them.
There should be two hundred lamps along with incense, accompanied by song, offerings, and dance;
one should perform this according to the previous [prescribed] method, which constitutes the superior and middling [levels].
One should offer five *droṇas* [of grain] four times a day, as well as worship;
likewise, there should be one hundred and eight lamps, songs, instrumental music, and the performance of offerings (*bali*).

One should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya); thus indeed [the rite] is classified as superior or inferior, accompanied by an offering of four droṇas and worship appropriate for the four periods of the day.
There should be singing and the like, offerings (bali), oblations (homa), and seventy lamps;
thus shall it be for the middle-high [grade]. Now, the middle-middle is described.
The food offering (*naivedya*), worship, and other rites should be performed with half a *bhāra* of rice as before;
the fire sacrifice (*homa*) should take place at midday alone, while dancing and other such activities should occur twice a day.

There should be forty lamps in the inner-middle area, as well as an offering; the food offering consists of a khārī measure of rice, and the ritual offering is performed with worship at the four times of day.
There should be twelve lamps for a human [sacrifice]; song and the like constitute the middling and lowest [grades].
At evening and morning, two *āḍhakas* [of offerings] are for Śiva; at midday, there should be [offerings] during the day consisting of Vedic lamps.
At night, there should be eight; and worship at the three periods of the day should be performed with five musical instruments in the [rite] called the lowest-best (*kaniṣṭhottama*).

In the morning there should be one vessel, and likewise in the evening; at midday, however, there should be one *āḍhaka* of offerings and two lamps during the day. There are indeed four lamps for the night. This worship performed at the three times of day is said to be the "middling" [type], while the "lowest" is as follows: [8–94]
In the evening and in the morning, there is the offering of two sets of sacrificial food and worship by the Pratiprasthātṛ.
To say "there is a lamp by day and lamps by night" would be the lowest of the low. The Section on Daily Food Offerings (Nityanaivedya):
Beginning from eight *droṇas* up to twelve *bhāras*. (8–96)
The ritual offering (naivedya) should be of nine kinds, as before;
one should likewise assemble the worship, beginning with the most excellent of the excellent.

There may also be an offering (naivedya) made for a specific desire, or as long as it has been requested; there is no fixed rule regarding the time for that, though worship performed with all its constituent parts (sāṅga) is praised.
The rule for occasional and optional rites:
For milk-rice (pāyasa), there should be three parts of milk and one part of rice;
in the preparation of *kṛsarānna*, milk, ghee, rice, and sesame seeds should be in equal proportions.
The rice grains should be broken into pieces like mung beans and of equal size; there should be half as much ghee as that rice, and half as much jaggery as the ghee.
Six times the amount of milk relative to the rice should be added, along with the fruit of the plantain; this is indeed the most excellent *gulānna*. (8–100)
The twice-born, having cleansed their teeth and bathed in white garments, should silently wash the rice grains with water purified by mantras like the Vajra;
likewise, they should kindle the fire seven times with their limbs and with fans and other implements.

Having meditated upon the hearth, the Śakti, and the fire as Rudra, and having worshipped them with the seed-syllable of fire or the Tāraka mantra, they should prepare that oblation in that fire; and having consecrated the clarified butter (ājya) with the syllable Oṃ, they should take it up.
Bṛhatī, plantains, as well as kuṇḍahālī, along with kūśmāṇḍa, it is said that karkarī; likewise kāravella, those called cūta and ārdraka, large mung beans, mung beans, and coconut. (8–103)
Māṣa beans with their pods, as well as those called cidbhaṭa and kulastha, are recommended as excellent side dishes (upadaṃśa).
There should also be a soup made from boiled barley, combined with the juice of ripe plantains and the like, along with sugar, alkaline salts, and salt, and seasoned with cumin and curd. (8–104)
Likewise, one should prepare sweetmeats and side dishes made from barley flour mixed with ghee, the three pungents (vyoṣa), salt, and yavānī;
then, having cleansed the array of vessels outside, one should raise them along with the conch, banner, and parasol.

Having sprinkled water over gold and other items that have been washed with water from the heart-mantra, or having sprinkled water over leaves of plantain and the like, one should place the oblation there along with side dishes, such as ripe plantains, fruits, and sweetmeats. (8–106)

Then, having offered a portion of the colored liquid consisting of cow’s butter—fresh, fragrant, and mixed with sugar, honey, milk, and curd—one should bestow it upon this [deity] when flowers have been presented; thereafter, one should drench it with the nectar from the *dhenumudrā*.
Having sprinkled [the oblation] with the root mantra and offered water near the beloved of Agni (Agni’s wife),
one should touch the sacrificial food with the right hand while holding a flower and present it.
One should meditate with that mind upon divine food and clarified butter that cause satisfaction;
and one should offer him water that is pleasing, cool, and fragrant.

Having gone outside and offered the remainder of that food into the fire as well, the practitioner [should do so] according to the procedure for the root-mantra, the limb-mantras, and so forth, with their respective mantras. (8.110)
There, having offered some oblation, one should ask the fire for forgiveness with devotion;
one should propitiate it with circumambulations, prostrations, and hymns of praise. || 8.111 ||

Having thoroughly washed his feet and sipped water for purification, he should enter within; then, recollecting that the deity is fully satiated, he should offer water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīyaka).
Then, one should offer betel leaf accompanied by cloves, camphor, black pepper, and areca nut, and subsequently honored with fragrant flowers.
Having offered incense and paid homage, one should recite the root mantra according to one's ability.
The Chapter on the Food Offering (Naivedya): One should worship all the limbs and the entire host of attendants according to the rite of the five services (pañcopacāra) as they are available;
however, if these are unavailable here, one who is composed in mind should perform that worship mentally.
Furthermore, others [describe] different types of worship according to the distinctions in ritual practice (upacāra). || 8.115 ||

We shall speak of those [offerings] as well, though with some slight difference from what was previously stated; ten subsidiary offerings (upacāra) are prescribed at the conclusion of the presentation of food (nivedya) during worship.
At the conclusion of the fire offering (homa), sixteen services (upacāra) are indeed prescribed;
at the conclusion of the ritual offering (bali), they are likewise said to be twenty-five in number.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the dance, thirty-six modes of service (upacāra) are proclaimed;
these occur in the highest of the high worship, or indeed in the high worship itself.
The seat, the invitation, the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya),
as well as the bath with its ancillaries, and likewise clothing, the sacred thread, and ornaments.
Collyrium, fragrant flowers, incense, a lamp, a mirror, the waving of lights (nīrājana), food offerings, the fire ritual, and circumambulation. || 8-120 ||
Prostration, praise, instrumental music and song, the daily offering, and the presentation of worship—these are declared to be the twenty-five [elements]. (8.121)
Then follow the five [substances] beginning with the seat, the consecration with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
and [the offerings] of milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugarcane juice.
The consecration is indeed that bathing, performed with the formalities due to a universal monarch;
[it includes] garments, the sacred thread, ornaments, collyrium, perfumes, and flowers.
Then follow the incense and the lamp, the mirror, and the rite of lustration (nīrājana);
likewise, the display of the mudrās, the food offering (naivedya), and the worship of the book.
The fire-sacrifice (homa), betel, sandals, the fly-whisk and the banner,
the parasol, the daily procession, and thereafter the offering of oblations (bali).
Circumambulation, prostration, hymns of praise, and musical instruments;
likewise, song, dance, and thereafter the offering of worship and other services.
Thus, the thirty-six modes of service have been described in their proper sequence; alternatively, they may occur in a reversed order, as taught in various respective tantras.
The section on the three types of ritual service:

Sacrifices, processions, and festivals are recommended for the worship of fixed liṅgas and the like, but not for the rites involving temporary altars (sthaṇḍila), nor for those concerning mandalas, diagrams, and so forth. (8.128)
Thus have the ritual procedures been declared according to the paths described; they are seen here in their various sequences within the different tantras,
as well as those common rites for the diverse classes of humans and gods.
So that the practitioners may achieve the fulfillment of their desired goals. || 8-129 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānadeva.
Now begins the ninth chapter.

Next, the daily ritual (*naityaka*) is described here in general; it is the single necessary rite that brings success to mantras for all those belonging to the various castes, stages of life, and social orders. 9.1.

For when the stars are still radiant, the sages declare that twilight continues until the first sight of the rising sun; this is called the dawn-twilight (prabhātā), and during it, one should rise from bed and abandon sleep. (9.2)
On this point, the Grandfather (Brahmā) says: "Beginning from the stars and the luminaries until the appearance of the rising sun,
those sages who have mastered the Vedas call that the morning twilight (prātaḥsandhyā)."
Remembering the supreme Śiva-light, known as the Self, which resides within the hollow of the heart-lotus,
one should rise and proceed toward a pure direction where abundant and easily accessible water is found.
On this point, there is a Smṛti:
"Having placed the *nivīta* over the right ear and having covered the head with a cloth, one should perform the evacuation of waste while remaining silent."
At a distance from the path, water sources, and dwellings, on ground covered with grass,
having wrapped his lower garment around him, facing north by day or south by night, and having voided his excrement, he then holds his penis.
Having reached the water's edge and taken pure clay obtained from a spot dug eight finger-breadths deep,
he should place it to his right and perform the ritual purification according to the rules with the water held in his hands.
One application of clay should be used on the penis, three on the hands, and likewise five on the anus;
seven on the left hand and ten on both hands—this indeed is the procedure for purification according to the Kaniṣṭha method.
Two applications of clay on the two private organs, four on the hands, ten on the anus, ten on the left hand,
and twelve on both hands— this is prescribed as the medium rule for purification.
Then, there should be three applications of earth on the penis and five on each of the hands;
there should be fifteen on the anus, twelve on the left hand, and the same number on both palms—this is indeed the primary rule for purification.
Having risen and properly donned his garment, he washed his feet and hands up to the knees with pure clay and water, and purified his face with mouthfuls of water.
The Plakṣa, Āmra, Jambū, Kakubha, Aśvakarṇa, Mālūra, Kāśoka, Lavaṅga, Jāti, Vaikaṅkata, Udumbara, or Campaka trees are indeed recommended for one desiring to eat as tooth-sticks. (9–10)
Measuring twelve of one's own fingers, equal in girth to the little finger, and covered with bark,
he should sit facing east and, observing silence, eat it starting from the lower left tooth, moving clockwise.

For those seeking liberation, thorny trees are recommended; likewise, the *śirīṣa*, *arjuna*, and *naktamāla* are praised. Indeed, the *apāmārga* is also commended here; of these, an eight-finger-length twig is used for cleaning the teeth.

If one stands, speaks, lies down, or even eats after being anointed with oil, while holding nimba, dhātrī, dhava, śelu, śigru, vānīra, eraṇḍa, grass, or kuśa grass, he should not use a tooth-stick. (9.13)

One who has not fasted should not clean his teeth with fingers or nails before breaking the fast, nor on his birth star, nor on a festival day, nor on the new moon day, nor on the days of the eighth lunar day or śrāddha ceremonies. (9.14)

Moreover, in this *Kālottara*, consisting of three hundred and fifty verses, it is stated: "O Guha! On the first lunar day, on festival days, on the sixth, or even on the ninth, a great fault is said to arise from the contact of a tooth-stick [with the teeth]."
In the same manner, having cleansed the tongue and discarded that tooth-stick and so forth at a distance,
one should afterwards perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with twelve mouthfuls of water and then commence the bath.
Bathing in the Ganges and other principal rivers, as well as in other chief holy fords (tīrthas) and rivers, is the best;
bathing in lakes, ponds, and the like is middling; while bathing in wells or at home is inferior.
One should bathe in wells and similar sources using water collected by twice-born men who have themselves bathed with pure vessels;
however, one should not bathe in hot water, for that is not considered suitable for ritual acts, as it is intended for the sick.
Having dug the ground to a depth of eight finger-breadths and having discarded the soil from below while remaining unsullied by water,
one should take that excavated earth and completely fill the pit with it.
Having placed it again on the shore of the milk, which has been washed with the *śiras* [mantra],
and having purified it with the *śikhā*, one should divide it into three parts with the *varman*.
Having smeared one portion [of the ashes] up to the navel and washed [the hands], one should sip water and, remaining silent,
smear the limbs with the second portion joined with the *astra* mantra while it is blazing.
If he is a twice-born, he should pray to the earth with the mantra "uddhṛtāsi" (you are lifted up);
another [should do so] with that which is about to be described.
O Goddess, the sustaining and nourishing of all beings always proceeds from you!
"By that truth, O Upholder, release me from sin, O Sinless One!
Having thus restrained his breath and submerged himself in the water, he should meditate upon the Lord. (9.22)
Then, at the water's edge on the bank, which resembles the fire of cosmic destruction,
the twice-born man, having sat down before the sun has risen, should perform the twilight worship.
Having first performed the Brahma-sandhyā and then the other known as Astra-mantra-sandhyā,
and having offered water upwards, he should perform the ritual bath according to the rules.
Having armored one's body with one's own mantra and visualized oneself within the lotus of the heart,
one should take the third portion of the previously prepared earth and place it in water reaching up to the navel.
Having stood and placed it in the left hand, one should divide it again into three parts:
the southern portion with the weapon-mantra (astra), and the northern portion first with the root-mantra (mūla).
Having consecrated it with the limb-mantra and taken hold of it with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, the wise one should cast it toward the ten directions for protection. (9.27)
Having first practiced with the root mantra, one should cast water with the right hand into the water and swirl it about while recollecting the Śiva-tīrtha.
Having smeared the entire body with the remaining portion ignited by the fire of the limbs practiced, one should invoke that sacred site (tīrtha) by its own name and worship it.
With perfumes and flowers as they may be obtained, or with a concentrated mind even in thought, one should bathe at principal rivers, oceans, and sacred fords; one should not praise other fords.
Through such recitation, that [act] would become fruitless, and one might even become angry; therefore, one should not recite it.
The recitation of holy places such as the Gaṅgā is prescribed only when there is pure water. (9.31)
Therefore, one should proclaim the various sacred fords (tīrthas) there, as each bestows its own specific fruit;
then, having restrained the vital breaths, one should immerse oneself three times with a concentrated mind.
Immersed [in water], he should recite with his heart the root mantra of his own [deity] along with its ancillaries by means of the Śakti-mantra.
Furthermore, if he is a twice-born,
he should recite from the beginning the hymn "hiraṇyaśṛṅgaṃ varuṇaṃ prapadye" with his heart.
Remaining in the Aghamarṣaṇa [mantra], he removes the entire flood of sins from within the waters by his power, as if submerged in water itself. || 9.33 ||

Just as even a vast accumulation of salt dissolves instantly when poured into a flood of water, so too even a great heap of sins goes to destruction through the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite; this is certain. (9.34)

Then, standing in the water, having visualized his left and right hands as being of the nature of the two deities Śiva and Śaśāṅka (the Moon), he should consecrate himself on the head with the root mantra using the *kumbha-mudrā*, and then likewise with the limb-mantras (*aṅga*). || 9.35 ||

The twice-born man, having consecrated the *pavamāna*, *puruṣa*, and *śrī* hymns with water according to his ability, went to the bank; there he put on two garments for himself that were pure, white, and free from the defect of tearing.
Having bathed, one should not wipe one's limbs with the hand or with a wet garment.

Likewise, one should not look upon heretics, those who have committed mortal sins, outcastes, or the impure; nor should one look upon a funeral pyre, wood from a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, or a *caṇḍāla*.
Having touched even a *devalaka*, one should enter the water with one's clothes on;
likewise during occasional rites such as eclipses, the waning of the moon, and so forth.

One ought to bathe with one's clothes on at the two solstices, at sacred fords and the like, during the twilight hours, after vomiting, and after contact with those who have discharged semen, feces, or urine, or with those who are defiled by food remnants or afflicted by leprosy.

Upon contact with, shaving by, or touching the waters of the ocean on an improper lunar day (aparvan), as well as upon contact with Śūdras, those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), or even a cat; 9.41.
After performing the rite of shaving, one should perform the Vāruṇa rite;
likewise before giving gifts, bathing, reciting prayers, offering libations, or performing fire oblations.
In all cases, one should be accompanied by the *pavitra*; otherwise, it would be demonic (*āsura*).
Or [it is demonic] if one has loosened one's topknot, is naked, is talking incoherently, or has not wrapped the sacred thread around the neck. (9.43)
One should know that all rites beginning with those for the gods are performed [with water]; however, that which is for the asuras involves earth.
Earth should be used once for washing the feet, and always for both hands.
At the beginning of all duties such as bathing, and at the time of eating, one should sit down;
and at the conclusion of purification after urination and so forth, one should wash the hands and feet. (9.45)
Now, the procedure for sipping water (ācamana) as prescribed in the general Smṛtis is stated here,
as well as the Vedic Sandhyā and the Tantric one called Astra.

For the twice-born, the divine (daiva) tīrtha is at the tip of the finger, the brahman tīrtha is at the base of the thumb, the ṛṣi tīrtha is at the joints of the fingers, the prājāpatya tīrtha is at the little finger, and the pitrya tīrtha is at the base of the forefinger. (9.47)
It is said that on the right hand is the *tīrtha* called Āgneya, while on the other [the left] is the Saumya;
one should perform rites beginning with those for the gods from one's own *tīrtha*, but one should sip water (*ācamana*) using the waters of the Brahma-*tīrtha*.

In the right hand of the Brahmin, the deities are thus assigned to the fingers: Agni is at the tip of the thumb (jyeṣṭhā), Vāyu at the tip of the index finger (tarjanī), Arka (the Sun) at the tip of the middle finger, Surendra (Indra) at the tip of the ring finger (anāmikā), and Prajāpati at the tip of the little finger (kaniṣṭhā).

Facing either east or north, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, having tied his topknot, with his arms placed between his knees, well-seated, raising water [in his hands], remaining silent, and bowing low while desiring to offer the oblation, he should be single-mindedly focused. (9.50)

One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with pure water that is not hot, which is free from foul tastes, smells, and the like, and devoid of insects, foam, or bubbles, and which has been properly inspected. (9.51)

Water reaching the heart, the throat, and the mouth purifies the twice-born in sequence according to the rule when drunk three times; it likewise purifies even Śūdras, women, and those born of inverse unions such as the Kuṇḍa and Anuloma castes.
By sipping water (ācamana) three times, one gratifies the three Vedic Puruṣas; furthermore, that which one wipes away [from the face] [purifies].
Twice [the merit of] the Atharva-veda and the six auxiliary sciences; may the sacrificial Puruṣas and even the fires be pleased. || 9-52 ||
One pleases the Sun by touching the ring fingers and eyes with the thumbs;
likewise, the thumb joined with the index finger, when measured against the two nostrils, [pleases] the Maruts;
and the little fingers with the thumbs at the ears [please] the Directions; from the navel [one pleases] the Vasus.
One should touch the self [with one finger], the heart and shoulders [with two], the sky [with three], and the sages [with four]; from the head upward, all [limbs] are touched with all five fingers.

One should sip water (ācamana) twice in this manner for purification after all instances of becoming impure (ucchiṣṭa), as well as after washing the feet, loosening the girdle, untying the topknot, spitting, yawning, or sneezing. (9.54)
One should drink water three times, recited over with the principles of Self-knowledge and Śiva, ending with "Obeisance to Īśvara"; this is remembered as the Śaiva ritual of sipping water (ācamana).
Having wiped the lips with a cloth, one should touch all the sense-orifices with one's whole being;
thus, in connection with the twilight rites, the Vāruṇa bath is described.
This is the section on the Varuṇa bath and sipping of water (ācamana).
If possible, one should also perform other baths, such as the Āgneya and so forth. (9.57)
The fire-related bath with ashes destroys all sins;
it is by means of this very [bath], born from his own radiance, that Śiva himself has bathed.
Having first performed the Varuṇa bath, one should afterwards perform the Āgneya bath;
likewise in times of distress, or when capable, one may perform only the Āgneya bath for the body.
And at the three junctions of the day, at the beginning of recitation, and at the start and end of one's conduct;
after eating, sleeping, drinking water, or having performed the necessary bodily functions—(one should perform purification). || 9.60 ||
Having touched a woman, or those born of inverse unions (anuloma), or a mouse, or impure things,
one should perform the fire-related bath (āgneyasnāna) exactly as prescribed in the Atharva Veda.
In the presence of gods, fire, teachers, or elders, when seeing an outcaste,
or while standing on impure ground or on a path, a wise man should not shake off the dust from his limbs.
According to the divisions of *kalpa*, *anukalpa*, and *upakalpa*, ash is likewise said by the Śaivas to be of four kinds; each preceding one possesses greater merit than the one following it.
One should take cow dung from a healthy cow that has a calf, which has not fallen upon the ground, using either a lotus leaf, a Palāśa leaf, or any other suitable vessel. (9.64)

Having taken it, however, that other twice-born one of purified soul [should apply] it with the root mantra of Gāyatrī together with its limbs in the Śaiva fire; that is proclaimed as the ritual for the sacred ash (bhasma).
One should fetch pure cow-dung from the forest at a distance from villages and the like;
that which has been burnt by the Śiva-fire as previously described shall serve as a secondary alternative (anukalpa).
Having taken ash from forests consumed by fire and having formed it into a ball bound with cow urine, one should then purify it in the fire of Śiva.
That which has been burnt should be prepared as ash; or else, it is said to be "unprepared" (akalpaka), having been produced from a distinguished Brahmin's cow-pen or from a temple of the deity.
Having taken it and processed it as before, that ash becomes free from conceptual construction (akalpaka).
And that ash is of four kinds, devoid of any confusion of classes (jātisaṅkara).
The white ash, which others have not claimed as their own, which is untainted by contact with [impure] actions and the like, smooth, pure, and free from disease, should be placed in a vessel. (9.70)
The ash suitable for the Agni-bath is as described by Brahmaśambhu; it has been repeatedly empowered with the Śiva-mantra and well-protected by the Śakti-mantra. (9.71)
Having taken [the water] from the vessel with the right hand, one should consecrate it with mantras;
then, having purified it by means of meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) according to the procedure for the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having first consecrated [the water] with the six-limbed mantra and placed it in the left hand,
one should perform the impurity-bath starting from the head and proceeding in sequence by means of the weapon-mantra.
Then, by means of the [mantras] of Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Sadyojāta, in sequence, one should [worship] the entire body from the head, face, heart, and private parts down to the shanks.

A twice-born man should smear [the ashes] over his entire body, while others should wear the triple marks (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, shoulders, heart, and other parts; likewise, Brāhmaṇas and the other castes should do so.
"One should maintain the *triyāyuṣa* because it is seen to be authoritative according to the Veda;

for the *Śruti* declares: 'The *triyāyuṣa* of Jamadagni, the *triyāyuṣa* of Kaśyapa and Agastya, the *tryāyuṣa* of the ṛṣis, that which is the *triyāyuṣa* of the gods—may that *triyāyuṣa* be mine! O auspicious one, your name is *Triyāyuṣa*.'"
The section on the Āgneya-bath:
When the sun is shining in a cloudless sky, having seen rain [falling], one with upraised arms... [9.76]
The Māhendra bath should be performed starting from the northeast (Īśāna) for a distance of seven steps,
using dust raised by the hooves of cows and carried along by the wind.
A twice-born man standing in the midst of cows should recite the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra or the *Go-sūkta*;
others, however, should utter the praise of cows or the words "Salutation to the cows."
One should perform the Vāyavya bath, which destroys all sins;
among all baths here, the Vāruṇa is both the root and the most excellent.
Therefore, having first performed the Vāruṇa bath, one should then proceed to the subsequent bathing;
for the Vedic mantra-bath is indeed performed with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
According to the ritual procedure for sprinkling, one should perform the Tantric rite with the root-mantras of one's own limbs;
thus, through rising, the necessary purification, and the cleansing of the teeth.
For one who has been purified by bathing, the performance of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana) is prescribed;
the twice-born should first perform the Vedic twilight devotion, and thereafter the Tantric one.
Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas likewise, as well as others, may practice the purely Tantric [form]; therefore, the Vedic [form] is described first. (9.83)

Having washed both his feet and hands according to the manner prescribed for those who have performed their ritual ablutions, he [performs] that which is declared in the Smṛtis of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and others, as well as the Tantric rite proclaimed in the Āgamas.

Having sipped water and holding the *pavitra* grass, the twice-born should sprinkle [the materials] with that mantra, as well as with the mantras for the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), deities (*devatā*), and applications (*viniyoga*) of those mantras. (9.85)
If the performance [of a rite] were otherwise than for the sake of its fruit, it would be demonic;
indeed, Vāmadeva is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of the hymn beginning with "dadhikrāviṇṇo akāriṣam. (9.86)
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, and likewise the waters and the Viśvedevas are the deities;
having sprinkled [the water] with this [mantra], the twice-born should then drink the consecrated water.
The meter of the mantra beginning with "sūryaśca" is indeed Gāyatrī; Savitṛ is the deity, Agastya is the seer, and Agni is also [the deity]. (9.88)
Having drunk that water and sipped it, one should sprinkle oneself with mantras dedicated to the waters and the deities,
beginning with "dadhikrāvṇo" and likewise with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and so forth.
For the verses beginning with "āpo hiṣṭhā," Sindhudvīpa is remembered as the seer;
the waters are indeed the deity, the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the rule is for sprinkling.
Then, having filled his joined palms with water and remaining facing the east,
he should meditate upon the supreme Brahman as light, abiding in the hearts of all worlds.
One should know that the city consisting of the body resides within the solar orb;
one should project it upward by means of the *tāra*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*, according to the sacred tradition.
Those waters, having become like thunderbolts, slay the Rākṣasas in an instant.
Then, having circumambulated [the water] clockwise and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should recite that mantra.
On pure ground, remaining silent and facing the sun while seated upon *kuśa* grass,
one should recite the *Gāyatrī* ten times along with its head (*śiras*) and the *Vyāhṛtis* three times;
at the beginning of the procedure for recitation, one should be intent on breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) according to one's capacity.
The thief shall have his body purified of stain and become fit for the recitation of prayers and other such rites. || 9-94 ||
The sage of the Praṇava is Brahmā, and its metre is indeed the Gāyatrī;
at the time of meditation it is the Supreme Brahman, and at the time of oblation it is the Fire-god.
At the time of recitation, the deity is the Triple Veda (Trayī); elsewhere, however, it is the Universal Deity (Viśva).
Its application (viniyoga) is at the beginning of the Vedas and as the very utterance of speech.
The Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh,
and Jagatī are said to be the meters of the seven Vyāhṛtis;
furthermore, their seers are Atri, Bhṛgu, Kutsa, and another, Vasiṣṭha.
Likewise, Gautama and Kāśyapa were also there, with Aṅgiras as the seventh.
Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Vāgīśvara, Yādonātha, Vāsava, and the Viśvedevas—these seven renowned deities are said to be the abodes of the vyāhṛtis; they correspond to the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr.
One should remember that Viśvāmitra is the seer, the divine Savitṛ himself is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter; these three belong to the Sāvitrī mantra. (9.99)
This [Vidyā] of twenty-four syllables is to be understood as having three feet when recited according to the division into eight syllables;
however, in the context of fire-offerings (homa) and worship, it has four feet, with each foot divided into six of its own syllables.
The sage of the Gāyatrī-śiras beginning with "oṃ āpo jyotiḥ" is Brahmā; its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the Supreme Self is its presiding deity. (9-101)
Prajāpati is likewise the deity of the head or the end;
Vāmadeva is the sage of the beginning of the *āyāhi* [verse], the meter is *anuṣṭubh*, and the deity is that very goddess.
Having thus properly invoked her with the mantra, the wise man, holding *darbha* grass in his hand, should then recite it. 9-102.
One should meditate upon the Mother of the Vedas, who has six bellies, three feet, and five heads; she is white in complexion, lotus-eyed, and possesses crests blazing with the brilliance of fire.
She rests upon a footstool of the earth, and her belly extends from the directions of Indra (East), Yama (South), Varuṇa (West), and Kubera (North), as well as above and below.
One should meditate upon the primordial navel, which faces [the practitioner] and has encompassed the three worlds within its embrace.
The Śikṣā, Kalpa, Jyotiṣa, Śabdaśāstra, and Nirukta are its five heads;
Vāyu is its breath, Viṣṇu its soul, Brahmā its forehead, Rudra its crest-lock, and Speech its tongue. (9–104)
She has the *Chandas* as her variegated garment, the two *Tantras* as her breasts, the *Dharmaśāstra* as her heart, and thick hair;
she has the *Nyāyavistara* as her arms, fire as her smile, the moon and sun as her eyes, and the *Uḍu* (stars) as her necklace. (9–105)

Mīmāṃsā and the Atharvaveda are her movements; Vedānta is her mind; Yoga and Sāṃkhya are her ears and nose; the mantras are her sacrificial rites; and the excellence of the radiance of her own limbs is all her [other] sacrifices. (9–106)
Having meditated upon the Goddess in such a form for the sake of all accomplishments at all times, one should practice her through recitation and other means.

Due to the distinctions of the divisions of the junctions (sandhyā) and the specific differences in the objects of meditation, they are here described in detail for the purpose of achieving perfection in recitation.

One should meditate upon the Mother of the Three Worlds, who is mounted on a swan, seated upon a white lotus, adorned with ornaments of radiant rubies, possessing eight eyes, and having four faces; she holds a rosary, a sacrificial ladle, a water-pot, and a staff in her four arms— she who is to be saluted at the morning twilight.
The Sāvitrī verse, the Savitṛ [mantra], and the maiden of fresh youth within the orb of the fierce-rayed sun.
Mounted upon Tārkṣya, lotus-eyed, possessing the luster of Indra’s crest-jewel,
holding the conch and discus with her four arms, she who is the very foundation of the worlds, pouring forth the Yajurvedic mantras,
radiant and beautiful with the shimmering light of many swaying necklaces— such is the Goddess Vaiṣṇavī at midday.
Sāvitrī, whose form is that of the object of meditation, shines within the orb of the sun, clad in yellow garments.
One should meditate upon her who has five faces and a circle of matted locks beautiful with streaks of tawny lightning; who bears the moon upon her crest;
whose smearing of ashes is made manifest by the rays of clear jewels from the dancing serpents that serve as her ornaments;
who holds a skull-topped staff and a trident, who grants boons and removes fear, and who is clothed in a tiger skin.
She bore Sāvitrī, who possessed three eyes, was advanced in age, and was the mother of the Sāman hymns.
One should meditate on her during the other twilight [the evening] while mounted upon a bull;
thus, in the three twilights, Sāvitrī is to be meditated upon in three forms. (9–111)
Now, for each of its colors, there are indeed presiding deities:
Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Īśāna, and Sūrya. (9.112)
Likewise Bṛhaspati, Indra, Bhaga, and Aryaman;
then Sāvitra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, and then Indra, Agni, and the Maruts.
Īśvara, Mitra and Varuṇa, Skanda, the Viśvedevas, and then Cakrabhṛt;
the Vasus, the Maruts, Artheśa, the two Aśvins, and Pitāmaha.
The deities of the syllables beginning with *tat* are considered to follow in sequence.

Previously, the Savior (*tāraka*) was revealed in a general sense through the order of the seven *vyāhṛtis*. Now, the union with reality according to the rule is explained, together with *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*, *mahaḥ*, *janaḥ*, and *tapaḥ*. (9.115)
That alone is the Truth: for the light situated within the orb of the sun is indeed the *bhūḥ* by its own existence;
the *bhuvaḥ* exists through the existence of its cause and effect; and the *suvaḥ* is the world, which is impelled by the Self through its own self-possession. (9.116)
Because it is of the nature of great light and because of its greatness, it is called *jana*; likewise, because it is the inner self of all people, it is called *sarvajana*.
Because it dispels darkness and shines forth, it is called *tapa*; for that supreme reality is indeed said to be *satya* and infinite. (9.117)
Now, the connection of the vyāhṛtis with the praṇava is stated here.
*Bhūḥ* is the letter *a*, while *bhuvaḥ* is indeed the letter *u*; *svaḥ* is the letter *m*, and *mahaḥ* is the *bindu*.
*Janaḥ* is the *nāda*, and *tapaḥ* is the *śakti*; the state known as the end of *nāda* is here the *satya*.
Now, for the sake of understanding the meaning, the etymology of that *sāvitrī* is explained:
the word "that" (*tat*) is the second case singular, denoting Brahman. (9.120)
The splendor residing in the solar orb is indeed that which is the supreme Brahman;
the word *savitṛ* ends in the genitive case, derived from the verbal root meaning "to bring forth. (9.121)

And [he is] the most excellent (*vareṇya*) because he is to be chosen (*varaṇīyatva*) by those seeking the fruits of the four aims of life, being the manifest progenitor of the rain and of all classes of living beings, O All-pervading Lord. (9.122)
Of this first eight-syllabled [mantra], the earth-element is traditionally held to be the pervading *vyāhṛti*.
*Bharga* is that which is accessible through devotion, or it is so called because it shatters evil. (9.123)
And the word "devasya" (of the god) ends in the genitive case, referring to the giver or lord of rain and so forth;
or it refers to that which is playing, or rather, to that which shines by virtue of its own self-luminosity.

Let us meditate upon that state which is established through the root *dhyai*, meaning "to contemplate"; we contemplate that splendor whose nature is the sun, which is to be known as identical with Śiva. (9.125)
For this second eight-syllable mantra, the vyāhṛti *bhuvaḥ* should be the pervader;
the statement that "dhiyaḥ" refers to the intellects and the mind is explained as being due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
And a change of gender has been made [in the commentary] from the sūtra, because of the case endings, verbal suffixes, and auxiliary verbs;
however, in the word "ya" (which), the genitive case ending "yat" [is used] for our [word] "tejas" (light), and [the forms] "yuṣmad" and "asmad" [are used] for the genitive.
Therefore, the meaning is "for us"; [the word] *pracodayāt* is used in the sense of a prayer.
It is traditionally taught that even for the third eight-syllabled [Gāyatrī], the *vyāhṛti* is *svar*. (9.128)

Thus, let us contemplate that one stainless splendor of the Lord of the Universe—the source of the world—which is worthy of being chosen, which shatters evil, and which grants all desires; may that Blessed Maheśa bestow wisdom upon us. (9.129)
The meaning has thus been stated here regarding Sāvitrī; now her head is being described.
"Water, light, and essence"—this is said to be the splendor of Soma and Agni.
"For that fire is indeed the immortal Brahman; 'The Sun is the Self'—such is the injunction.
Having understood these in this way according to their true meaning, one should assign them to the body in the proper sequence. (9.131)
Then, one should place her [mantra] syllables upon the head, between the eyebrows, the eyes, the face, the throat, the heart, the navel, the secret place, the two knees, and the two feet.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these are, in order, the mantras for the limbs associated with the universal self (sarvātman). || 9-133 ||

Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *Gāyatrī* and having paid homage to its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes, one should recite it while restraining the breath; thereby, one shall partake in infinite fruit. (9.134)
If one recites the Sāvitrī joined with its head (śiras) and preceded by the seven vyāhṛtis each followed by the praṇava, the fruit is a hundredfold.
One should recite this mantra one thousand and eight times with undistracted mind;
or, if unable to do that, one hundred times, or even just ten times.
In this matter, each preceding one is more primary; one should not let go of the power of recitation (*japa*).
Now, for the mantra of dismissal (*udvāsana*), there is the verse beginning with "uttame śikhare. (9–137)
Sāvitrī is the deity and Anuṣṭubh the meter for these; Vāmadeva is considered the seer (ṛṣi). For the mantras of worship beginning with "mitrasya," Kauśika is the seer. || 9-138 ||
Mitra is the deity; the meters are Gāyatrī and Anuṣṭubh.
Then, having circumambulated clockwise, [he honors] the directions together with their presiding deities.
Then, having paid homage to the five deities beginning with Sandhyā in their proper order,
one should worship the thousand-rayed Sun as he rises.
Having meditated upon the Self as the Supreme Self, and having performed prostration at the feet [of the deity],
one should then carry out the worship of the deity, the fire-oblation, and the recitation of mantras.
Now, therefore, the application and so forth of the Sāvitrī mantra shall be described.
Standing in a recommended place, with a disciplined mind, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while gazing at the solar disc;
having offered oblations of sesame seeds mixed with cow-products into the fire for that same duration, the high-souled devotee becomes perfected in the mantra.
Indeed, by reciting ten thousand times while standing in water up to the navel, one destroys sins;
by a hundred thousand, minor offenses (upapātakas); and by a million, one shall surely destroy all major transgressions (pātakas).
By reciting it one million times, even those who have committed great sins attain purification in the waters up to their necks;
by reciting it three thousand times, one is purified from the fault of eating what should not be eaten, as well as from evils committed through speech and mind.
Through the oblation of thirty thousand sesame seeds and clarified butter, one destroys untimely death, diseases, and sufferings by the tens of thousands;
through the oblation of three hundred thousand *dūrvā* grasses sprinkled with the three sweets (*madhuratra*), one overcomes death at its appointed time.
One obtains a son by offering rice; Lakṣmī by bilva and lotuses; cattle by palāśa flowers;
food by cooked rice with ghee; garments by white water-lilies; rain by reeds;
and a streak of cow-dung, stone-paste, and gorocana by blue lotuses.
What was performed? Three thousand repetitions of the *lilaka* mantra, which subjugates the world, were touched [performed]. || 9-146 ||
By performing a *puttalikā-homa* using the dust from the feet of a tree, one may kill even a Brahmin who has transcended others;
one should cause him to hate by means of fuel-sticks of the *kalivṛkṣa*, and one should subdue him in that fire with leaves of the *kali*.

By offering *kundapuṣpa* flowers, one obtains a maiden; furthermore, from the oblation of *karavīra*, supernatural powers (*siddhis*) arise. Indeed, by ten million recitations (*koṭijapa*), one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*), equal to the gods and the lords of sages.
One should offer oblations with milk-rice, as well as with clarified butter, sesame seeds, and sprouts of dūrvā grass.
And with four kinds of milky wood fuel, three thousand oblations for each;
whatever one aims for, all that is accomplished without delay. (9.150)
One should perform oblations with milk-rice, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and dūrvā sprouts;
by reciting the thousand-syllable mantra for each syllable, one shall obtain a long life. (9.151)
He who offers ten thousand oblations with red lotuses sprinkled with the three sweets shall obtain prosperity;
furthermore, by offering cooked rice with ghee according to the prescribed rules after performing the rites beginning with the invocation of the fire's mouth, he shall become wealthy in food.
Having established the fire according to the rules and invoked the Sun into its mouth,
and having worshipped him according to the rules, one should [worship] Sāvitrī in the lotus of his heart.
Having invoked her with the mantra, one should meditate upon her as possessing the characteristics described for the twilight worship;
having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, she is bathed in the nectar from the dvādaśānta.
Having also resolved upon his own specific duty, he obtains the fruit by performing the oblation;
then he should perform the midday rite preceded by bathing. (9.155)
The ritual bathing is as previously described; however, the specific Vedic procedure is now being stated.
Except for the morning bath, one who intends to bathe at other times should not clean their teeth.

Having submerged oneself and sipped water (ācamana), one should recite the hymn beginning with "hiraṇyaśṛṅgam" and ending with "punantu," while holding water in the hollow of both hands (añjali). || 9.157 ||

Having recited the mantra beginning with *sumitra* and ending with *santva* toward the direction of the enemies, and having thrown [the water] while reciting the mantra beginning with *durmitra* and ending with *dviṣmaḥ*, he should sip water and remain silent.
Having recited "yad apām krūram" and so forth three times while submerged in the water until it reaches the end, he should then emerge from the water to the bank with his hands. (9.159)
Having sat down and likewise performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), one should consecrate the water held in the hand with the mantra beginning "āpaḥ punantu" and drink it again, ending with "svāhā."
One should sip water [with this mantra]; its seer (ṛṣi) is known as Brahmaṇaspati, its deity is Water itself, and its meter is proclaimed to be Anuṣṭubh. (9.161)

One should sprinkle [the materials] with water using darbha grass in hand while reciting the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," as well as the verses "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ" and "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ. (9.162)

Having sprinkled [the disciple] with these and other mantras, he should then submerge his body in water while reciting the three verses beginning with "Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca" and ending with "khari. (9.163)
Having restrained the breath, one should mentally recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
if one is capable, then one should do so with these waters preceded by Varuṇa.

Having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* with the concluding mantras beginning with "suvāna indur," and having emerged from the water, he should wring out his garment in the air until it is clean and spotless.
Then, having put on [clean garments], washed his feet, and sipped water while restraining his speech,
he should offer libations as at the morning twilight and recite the Sāvitrī mantra according to his ability.
Standing and gazing at the sun, one should sit facing the east and recite [the mantra];
then one should offer a handful of flowers or merely water to the Sun.
Then, with arms raised, he should worship the sun while reciting these [hymns]:
"ud vayaṃ tamasaspari," "ud u tyam," "citraṃ tad," and "cakṣur ādityasya."
The sage proclaimed for these [verses] beginning with "ud u tyam" is Hiraṇyayūpa;
their meter is Triṣṭubh, and their deity is the Sun. (9.169)
The third [verse] is Gāyatrī, and the fourth is considered Jagatī;
the Uṣṇik is that of the mantra beginning with "Taccakṣuḥ," and Savitṛ is the presiding deity. (9.170)
Thereafter, one should perform the *brahmayajña*; that is declared to be *svādhyāya*.
After the *brahmayajña*, Āśvalāyana prescribes the time for the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
But others maintain that immediately after the *upasthāna*,
one should perform [the rite] with the mantras beginning with *sāṅga-mūla* according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *āgama*.
For those who have been initiated should indeed gratify the gods, the sages, the ancestors, and others;
at the time of bathing, they should not cause agitation in the water with their feet or other limbs.
If one should, through negligence, perform the removal of internal impurities or the cleansing of clothes and so forth [inappropriately], the expiation for this is stated here.
The twice-born should mutter the mantra "Namo 'gnaye 'psumate" and then approach the water;
if he is a member of the twice-born caste, he should perform the ritual worship (upasthāna), whereas another should merely say "Namo 'dbhyah."
Then, having received permission and having dismissed the deities who were present for the purpose of the rite,
and having also dismissed the sages and the ancestors, one should then proceed to the sacrificial hall.
There, having worshipped the desired deity according to the teachings of one's own tradition and teacher,
one should mutter the respective mantra and perform the fire-oblation, the Vaiśvadeva rite, and the offering of bali.
Having completed his duties and fed guests, those dependent on him, and others according to his capacity, he himself should eat together with his sons and others, not disparaging the food. (9.178)
Having eaten, one should remove any traces of food, odors, or smears and cleanse [the mouth];
then, having sipped water (ācamana), one should also employ mouth-perfumes.
Then, one should spend the remainder of the day happily with the diversion of learning and other such pursuits.
Then, when the sun has half-set, one should perform the evening twilight ritual (*sandhyā*).
One should perform the worship as before, omitting the cleaning of the teeth;
having bathed, sipped water, and then sprinkled oneself while reciting the Agnicam mantra, one should drink water. (9.181)
Having likewise cast water upwards, one should mutter the Gāyatrī as much as possible; then, having performed the worship with the hymns beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa," one should proceed as before.
Having worshipped the deity with perfumes and other offerings according to the previous procedure and to the best of one's ability,
and having performed the recitation of mantras and paid obeisance, one should then perform the Vaiśvadeva and Bali rites.
Having finished [the rites], if the householder eats together with his guests, dependents, and others,
he should lie down on a pure bed well-spread with a white cloth.
One should not sleep over cows, Brahmins, gods, or fire;
nor in a cramped space; nor along the length of a lineage (or beam); nor with one's head toward the north or the west. (9.185)

One should not [perform it] naked, nor with wet hands and feet, nor smeared with oil, nor while impure; rather, when there is the means to do so, one should perform it in a place adorned with canopies, lamps, and jars.
With his body armored by mantras and adorned with protective perfumes and the like,
he [should approach] his own wife, who is endowed with virtuous character, devoted to him, and well-adorned.
A householder may approach [his wife] on days other than the forbidden lunar phases for the sake of progeny.

Thus has been briefly stated the cycle of obligatory duties— enjoined by sacred law and consisting of the performance of the twilight prayers— as prescribed in the Śrauta, Smārta, and Tantric traditions for those belonging to the social orders.

"May the virtuous, who walk upon the path of the righteous, accept this work as their own wealth—just as friends do—since it has been practiced by the sages here and bestows the attainment of desired goals both seen and unseen. (9.188½)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Daily Rites," in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānadeva.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Having prostrated before Śambhu, who is crowned with the crescent moon, Bhava, the one who brings about the cessation of worldly existence,
the purification of the self along with the sequence of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is briefly described for the sake of attaining success in yoga, recitation, and other practices.
Having bathed according to rule and performed the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), he went to the sacrificial hall and purified his feet;
having sipped water (*ācamana*) and entered within according to the injunctions, he sat down upon an auspicious seat, restraining his speech. || 10.10.2 ||
Meditating upon his own body from head to both feet as containing a very subtle cavity within it,
he then places that pure power, which has the luster of the sky, externally and then within the middle of the body.

Having meditated upon the radiant seed-syllable *huṃ*, and having restrained the vital breaths and fixed the mind, one should then, at the end of that exhalation (*recaka*), perform the gradual breaking of the knots by means of the weapon-mantra ending in *phaṭ*. (10.4)

Those five knots, well known to be stained by darkness and situated at the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and in the head—through their piercing, however, the path of the channels is perfected. (10.5)

Having restrained the breath within oneself at the end of inhalation, one should contemplate through retention (kumbhaka) that form of the individual soul (jīva), which consists of the essence of consciousness and peace,
as having become a drop (bindu), free from all affliction, within the lotus of one's own heart.
