There, by the upward flow of the breath, one should lead the individual soul—placed at the crown of the head via the path of Suṣumnā—to Śiva, who resides in the Dvādaśānta, merely by means of the upward thrust (uddhāta) through the function of the seed-syllable. || 10-7 ||
At a distance of twelve finger-breadths, one should contemplate a white thousand-petaled lotus, auspicious, filled with the nectar of space, facing downwards, and its center occupied by Śiva. (10.8)
Absorbed in Śiva, his self protected by the limbs [of the mantra], having visualized the tree of the body with its face turned downward,
he then leads the thirty-six principles (tattvas) in reverse order into dissolution within their respective causes.
From earth, water, fire, air, and ether, there arise smell, taste, and form;
touch and sound are also declared [to arise from them]. Furthermore, the generative organ, the anus, the feet, the hands, speech, and the nose [are the organs]. (10.10)
The tongue, eyes, skin, and ears; the mind, along with ego (ahaṅkāra), intellect (buddhi), and primordial matter (pradhāna);
the person (puruṣa), passion (rāga), necessity (niyati), impurity (aśuddhi), knowledge (vidyā), limited agency (kalā), and Māyā conjoined with time (kāla). || 10–11 ||
Saṃśuddhavidyā, likewise the one called Īśvara, the one named Sādākhya, then Śakti, and Śiva;
thus, in reverse order, there are thirty-six principles (tattvas), each being the cause of the one preceding it. || 10–12 ||

Then, the five elements beginning with space (ākāśa) are to be purified within one another in reverse order, by means of those [five] eyes presided over by Īśāna and the others, which are the presiding deities of the letters, the phonemes, and the digits. || 10–13 ||
The sphere of earth, which is square, yellow, marked with thunderbolts, possesses the quality of fragrance, and is eternal;
that is the sense of smell, joined with the *nivṛtti* kalā and presided over by the four-faced deity. (10.14)
Then, through the inhalation and retention [of breath] originating from the seed-syllable *hlāṃ*, the area from the soles of the feet to the head is pervaded;
one should contemplate that it is purified by the five *uddhātaka*s once the vital air has entered therein. (10–15)
The reflection [of the deity] has the marks of the crescent moon and the white lotus; it is white, rich in the [taste] element, and represents the sense organ of taste.
Situated on the left, accompanied by Viṣṇu, it should be joined with the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā and purified.
The seed-syllable *hrīṃ* is at the end of the four extractions; having become that [seed], they enter afterwards.
There should be a triangular, reddish orb of fire, which is the base of the Vidyā and marked with a svastika. (10.17)

The visual faculty, possessing the quality of form, together with Rudra and the seed-syllable *hrūṃ*, conjoined with Aghora, should be purified. One should contemplate it as having entered into the water through three *udghātas*, pervading the entire body. (10.18)
Then, there is the wind-element (vāyubimba), marked with six dots, black, hexagonal, and situated in the Puruṣa;
it is endowed with the sense of touch and the quality of tranquility, joined with the Lord (Īśvara) and the syllable *Aiṃ*, and is produced from two *udghāta*s. (10.19)
The circular form of one's own reflection, white as crystal, together with the ear, the sound, the bindu, and the śakti,
joined with the seat of Īśāna and transcendent, is indeed to be purified by the *uddhāta* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) by flooding everything with the streams of lunar nectar-water from the root mantra situated at the *dvādaśānta*, and having established the principles (*tattva*) in their proper order; 10.21.

Having had his pure body produced by the will of Śiva, and having offered a seat in the heart with the *praṇava*, he should install the all-pervading power (*śakti*) of Śiva, placing his own seed-syllable as the individual soul (*jīva*) within that which is called Śiva. (10.22)

Then, having brought [the deity] from that dvādaśānta by means of inhalation through the channel into the center of the heart-lotus, and having established it there, one should bathe it with floods of the root-mantra's nectar-water and begin the worship and other rites. 10.23.
The Section on the Purification of the Elements:
Herein is described another clear purification of the self, which purifies the body through the sequence of drying and so forth;
by bestowing the purity that results from the total destruction of all defects, it destroys disease, old age, and even death. (10.24)
As before, having visualized a hollow space within one's own body and the inner-and-outer power pervading it,

with the mind and life-force situated in the midst of the syllable *huṃ*, one should restrain the vital breaths by means of the inhalation (*pūraka*) drawn in. Having burst open the knots until the end of the exhalation (*recaka*), one should turn back the wind from the inhalation by means of the Weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Having drawn forth consciousness along with the tranquil individual soul (jīva), [one should contemplate] the heart-casket known as the stainless light.
Then, by the force of the upward movement of the *kumbhaka*, having drawn that [consciousness] upward through the path of the *suṣumṇā* to its own beloved [abode],
and having joined it with Śiva residing at the *dvādaśānta*, one leads the *tattvas* to dissolution in reverse order.
Having dissolved the sequence of letters in reverse order, beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*, along with the stream of sounds, into the Power (*śakti*),
one should then contemplate the body as empty, consisting of nothing but impurity and sin, and black in color at the navel-center.

But for the [yogin] of wind, having visualized the syllable YAṂ, which is of an exceedingly smoky color, as the fierce wind, he should meditate upon his own body as the tree of saṃsāra, with its branches below and its roots above. (10.29)
On this point, Brahmaśambhu says:
"There, the tree of worldly existence (bhavapādapa), whose self is the body and which hangs face downwards, is to be meditated upon.
One should dry it up by means of the wind emerging from the navel, having visualized it, while the impurity and stain are being dried.
Having subsequently brought about its drying up by means of the five *uddhātaka* [breaths] through the restraint of the vital air (*vāyu*), [one should proceed]. || 10.30 ||

In the heart-lotus, one should contemplate this seed-syllable known as Cintāmaṇi—the final letter (KṢ), joined with poison (Ū), fire (R), and wind (Y), together with grace (Ī) and the half-moon (Bindu), and endowed with sound (Nāda); it is the form of fire within the image of the sacrificial fire.

Having placed [the deity], one should contemplate that [deity] completely burning away the mass of sins known as the physical body with the spreading thousands of flames from the six-cornered fire-trident, until it has been reduced to ashes. (10.32)
Or one may burn it with the Pāśupata weapon, since it is stated in the *Parākhyatantra* and the *Pauṣkaratantra*: "One should burn [it] with the Pāśupata weapon.

Having driven away all that ash by scattering it in all directions with the seed-syllable of the wind, *caṇḍānila*, and having contemplated the body as empty and equal to space, it remains pure, consisting of nothing but a residue of merit. (10.33)
Regarding this, Brahmaśambhu says:
"One should contemplate [the body] as dried up by the fire of the *kumbhaka* [retention],
and then as reduced to ashes by the wind from the *recaka* [exhalation], spreading through the ten directions."
One should meditate on the pure, stainless void as dissolved by the final [breath].
Thus, O wise one, one should burn the body until it is situated as a heap of ashes.

Thus, in the *Śrī Kālottara*: "When Śiva, who resides within the lotus of the sky, desires to emit [the universe] by virtue of His powers of will, action, and knowledge, He produces the principles (*tattvas*) through the groups of phonemes and letters according to the capacity of that power, and then constructs a body with them. (10.34)

Having created the world of the universe consisting of that egg, and having contemplated the pure [Self] freed from the bonds of fetters, he should draw forth the living soul (jīva) whose seed has been placed at the previous dvādaśānta, mixed with the air of that filling [breath]. || 10-35 ||

Having led that [Self] through the path of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) into the center of the heart-lotus, one should contemplate Śiva, whose nature is the Self, enriched by the digits of the moon in the center of the sky-lotus, and by the nectar-drops supported by the sixteen-petaled lotus. || 10.36 ||
One should fill [the channels] individually and correctly through the *sauṣumna* path in reverse order of the vowels:
Amṛtā, Mānasī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭī, Prīti, Rati, Śrī, Śānti, Svadhā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Haimavatī, Prabhā, Pūraṇī, and Vāmā; the sixteenth is Amā. (10.37)

From the right thumb, one should place [the digits] in sequence upon the ankle, knee, hip, abdomen, wrist, and right arm, and finally half [of the last digit] on the head; the locations for the left side are said to be the reverse of that, where the *kalās* are to be placed.
"Aḥ, salutation to Amā; Aṃ, salutation to Vāmā; Auṃ, salutation to Pūraṇī.
Having thus deposited the sixteen digits (kalās) from the thumb to the top of the head, one should fill them with their respective nectars in sequence—this is the instruction.
One should contemplate the water in one's own lotus as having the luster of the half-moon and the full moon, and as possessing the sounds of those digits.
Having filled one's own body with the nectar that is as white as a conch shell, a jasmine flower, the moon, cow's milk, and Brahman, along the path of the *nīḍa*.
On this point, Brahmaśambhu says:
"Having sprinkled it continuously with a flood white as that nectar.
And in the Śrī Kālottara:
"There, one should visualize the lunar disc situated upon a white lotus,
flowing with divine nectar, the cause for the arising of the body"— thus [it is said].
[One should meditate on the deity] having the form of a sixteen-year-old, whose body is pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), and whose form is being drenched by the flood of that nectar.
He who, even once, should thus remember with his intellect this pure [state] acquired through a multitude of merits—he would become a yogi. (10.40)
Thus, through such practice, one whose being is purified attains the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) by the grace of the Lord.
Then, through recitation, worship, and other means, the desired perfection is achieved; and the Goddess of Speech, being well-pleased, shall issue forth from his mouth.
For this most defiled body cannot be rendered pure merely by washing and other means with specific waters;
rather, the wise have taught that purification is twofold, including internal spiritual purification along with the prescribed rites—I worship that [internal purification] constantly.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, beginning with the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the eleventh chapter. Now is described the initiation (*dīkṣā*) which brings success to mantras; it is of four kinds:
namely, the Mantra-initiation, the Śaiva, that called Śākta, and the Vaiṣṇava.

Because it bestows here a divine state, because it exhausts both the impurity of illusion (māyāmala) and karma, and because its fruit consists of the four aims of life (caturvarga), it is therefore designated as "initiation" (dīkṣā). || 11-2 ||

Indeed, the initiation pertaining to mantras is traditionally held to be common to all groups of mantras; likewise, it applies to the castes beginning with the twice-born, as well as to the Śaiva, Śākta, and Vaiṣṇava traditions. (11.3)

When the sun has entered the northern quarter, during an auspicious constellation, on a favorable lunar day and a good lagna, and in the bright fortnight—which bestows prosperity upon both teacher and disciple—one should perform the initiation. || 11-4 ||

During initiations, for the construction of temple pavilions, houses, and so forth, as well as for the pacification of obstacles, one should first perform the worship of Vāstveśa; by doing so, one shall accomplish all desired objectives. (11.5)
Indeed, the asura named Vāstvīśa, who possessed a massive body and had long ago been granted boons by the gods, was highly honored;
he used to lie upon the earth with his feet and hands spread out, always with his face turned downwards. || 11-6 ||
Indeed, those deities residing within that body are thirty-two, while others are enumerated as being of the nature of Prakṛti;
they are to be worshipped by Brahmins in sixty-four squares, and by kings and others in eighty-one squares.
In the designated place, having first smeared it with fresh cow-dung water and made it square, one should then divide it eightfold; thus, as described, it shall consist of sixty-four squares.
When that [space] has been divided ninefold and the lines have been drawn, one should apply a mixture of flour and powder;
that which consists of eighty-one squares is said to be for temples as well as for kings.

Having divided that [area] into sixty-four squares and having fixed the cords at the corners, one should then place the worshipful deities beginning with Brahmā in the four central squares. || 11-10 ||

Likewise, in the pairs of squares in the directions starting from the east, there are the teachers Vivasvat, then the one named Mitra, and the one called Mahīdhara; I shall now describe the deities in the pairs of half-corners between them.
Sāvitra and Savitṛ should be in the direction of Agni (the southeast), each occupying half a square;
Indra and Indrajaya should be in the direction of the Rākṣasa (the southwest);
likewise, Rudra and Rudrajaya in the direction of Īśa (the northeast); and those called Āpa and Apavatsa in the direction of the Wind (the northwest).
Furthermore, I shall describe the eight deities in the four external corners as well.
Śarva, Skanda, Yamāha, Jambhaka, Pilipiñjaka,
Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the evil Rākṣasī.
Now, the deities of the thirty-two squares in the outermost row should be known to be arranged in four groups, proceeding in order starting from the east in each of the four directions. (11–14)
In the eastern direction, there are eight deities: Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Indra, Arka, Satya, Bhṛśa, and Antarikṣa; these are the presiding deities for every moment.
Agni, Pūṣan, Adhivithatha, Yama as the guardian of the house, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and the one called Mṛga are also in the south. (11–16)
Nirṛti and Dauvārika, as well as Sugrīva and Varuṇa, Puṣpadanta and Asura, Śoṣa and Pāpayakṣman are in the west. (11.17)
Māruta, the two chief Nāgas, Bhallāṭa, Niśākara,
Argala, Diti, and likewise Aditi are situated in the north.
The head was placed upon Īśāna; the two hands were on Vāstoṣpati and Agni; the pair of feet was stationed on Naktamcara;
Parjanya was in the eyes; Diti was in the mouth; and Āpavatsa was in the throat.
Aditi likewise occupied the two ears along with the bolt, and Jayantī took refuge in the shoulders. || 11.19 ||
Then Śakra and Niśākara are on the backs of his two arms; Rudra and Sāvitra, along with Savitṛ and Roga, are stationed on his hands;
Caturānana (Brahmā) is at his navel; likewise, Bhūbhṛt and Aryaman are at his two breasts.
And Mitra was also born from Vivasvat; and another, Guhyendra, was born from his belly. || 11-20 ||
The worship of Īśāna should be performed with ghee, unbroken rice grains, and water; that of Parjanya with water scented with blue lotuses.
The banner of Jayanta should be yellow; one should worship Mahendra with red food offerings and lamps.

The worship of Sūrya should be performed with yellow food and canopies; likewise, that of Satya with ghee and boiled rice; that of Bhṛśa with wheat cakes; and that of Antarikṣa with black gram and meat. (11.22)
Having worshipped Agni with the sacrificial ladle (sruc) in that same manner, and having offered to Pūṣan with parched grains (lāja) and to Vitatha with gold;
one should worship the Guardian of the House with honey and boiled rice, and Yama with meat and boiled rice.

Having worshipped the Gandharvas with fragrant flowers, one should then offer the *pakṣijihvā* plant to Bhṛṅgarāja; the worship of the Mṛga should be performed with sesame and barley, and the offering for Nirṛti, pertaining to the ancestors, should consist of *kṛsara* according to the prescribed rule.
Having worshipped Śobhanadanta with auspicious tooth-sticks and grains of barley along with incense,
and likewise Puṣpadanta with pillars of *kuśa* grass, one should worship Jaleśa with white lotuses.
Worship for the Asura should consist of honey and unbroken grains; for Śoṣa, food mixed with ghee should be offered.
For Pāpayakṣman, however, there should be food made of nīvāra grain, and for Vāyu, cakes prepared with clarified butter.
One should perform the worship of Nāga with *nāgapuṣpa* flowers, and that of Mukhya with sweetmeats (*modaka*).
For the one named Bhallāṭa, the food offering should be *samudga*; for King Soma, it should be honey, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and clarified butter (*ājya*).
Having worshipped Argala with unbroken grains of śāli rice, Diti with red-colored śāli rice and ghee,
and Aditi duly with food offerings of black gram, one should thus worship these thirty-two deities in sequence.
The Waters (Āpas) should be worshipped with milk, and likewise the Apavatsas with curd, ghee, and sweetmeat balls;
having sacrificed to Sāvitra, one should then perform the worship for Savitṛ with offerings of Kuśa grass, keys, and food.
For Indra, yellow rice with ghee is prescribed; for Indrajaya, pure rice alone is recommended. For Rudra, cooked meat is ordained, while for Rudrajaya, raw meat is likewise prescribed.
Here, Samarīcaka and the others are to be worshipped with sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka) and red and white rice offerings;
likewise, they should be properly placed in their respective positions in sequence, four at a time, along with cooked grains and clarified butter.

Having first worshipped Brahmā with clarified butter, unbroken rice, the five products of the cow, flowers along with perfumes, sacrificial porridge (caru), and sesame seeds, one should then worship the one named Śarva, that is Skanda, with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
To Yama and Aryaman, one should offer meat with ghee; then to Jambhaka, yellow garlands and meat;
and to Pilipiñja in the northwest.
One should thus cause the bali-offering to be presented with thick red flowers and food;
in the northeast, the bali for Carakī consists of meat, rice, ghee, and cakes.
Outside, one should offer a bali to Agni in the southeast with bile and meat;
and to the Rākṣasī Pūtanā in the south with curd, blood, and cooked rice.

One should worship the sinful Rākṣasīs of the Vāyavya direction with milk, bile, unsteady blood, and food, using their own names followed by "namaḥ" (salutation) along with the ritual offerings. || 11-36 ||
Then, outside, one should offer oblations (bali) to the eight classes of beings;
if the aforementioned substances for each are unavailable, [one may use] flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata).

The *bali* offering is prescribed with fragrant incense, lamps, and pure food. Having performed worship to these [deities] with their own names, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should present the *bali* at night, dressed in white garments and with a pure disposition, using the five types of ritual offerings (*pañcopacāra*). || 11-38 ||
Thus, when the deities residing within the body of the dwelling have been properly worshipped, they grant success in their respective undertakings as well as peace. (11.39)
Having placed this [deity] as before within the eighty-one squares, one should worship Vāstoṣpati in the center and the Creator (Vedhas) in the nine central squares; then, outside of that,
in the corners and in the pairs of squares there, are the gods beginning with Savitṛ, residing in the Agni-square.
In the middle of that [square], four deities preceded by Samarīca are said to be situated in sequence. || 11-40 ||
In the directions starting from the east, thirty-two deities headed by Īśa (Śiva) are to be worshipped in sequence as before, each situated in a separate square on the outer perimeter.
Outside [the inner circle], the others are without squares; Carakī is in the northeast (Īśāna), and Vidārī in the southeast (Agni).
In the corner is the Rakshasi Putana; and from the direction of the wind comes the Rakshasi. || 11-41 ||
The four [deities] beginning with Śarva and Skanda, excluding Pāda, are situated outside; one should worship them in order in the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions.
Having invoked the deity of the site (vāstupa) by resorting to one of these two paths,
one should worship, in due order, the deities residing in its constituent parts as well.
This is the section on the worship for the layout of the site:

Having thus propitiated the Vāstu deities, the twice-born should then perform the Vāstu-homa sacrifice according to the path seen by Bodhāyana, so that the Lord of the Site (Vāstupati) may be pacified. (11.44)
One who is about to enter a new house should first decorate it with archways and other ornaments;
having prepared a sleeping place for the architect and purified it with the *tāra* mantra, one should worship Gaṇeśa.

Having established the center of that site, one should smear an area the size of a cow-hide (gocarma) in the north-eastern direction from there with cow-dung, forming a square mandala, and having performed the ritual scraping and other preliminary rites. || 11.46 ||

Having established the fire there according to the ritual procedure prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, and having performed the *agnimukha* rite therein, he offers the sacrificial porridge (*caru*)—prepared with cow’s milk and sprinkled with clarified butter—into the fire with the mantras, duly and in the proper sequence. (11.47)

Having recited the *puronuvākyā* beginning with "O Lord of the Dwelling (*vāstoṣpati*), recognize us," he should then offer the oblation while pronouncing the *yājyā* beginning with "O Lord of the Dwelling, may there be peace for me through this assembly."

One should perform [the rite] with the mantra beginning "O Lord of the Dwelling, a firm pillar is your essence," and so forth; and with the mantra beginning "Whatever fear of the house... and so forth, as well as with the mantra beginning "The twitching of the eye... and so forth. (11.49)

In the case of a bad dream or a sinful dream, [one should perform expiation] by means of consuming the dream-food and so forth, as well as with the mantra beginning "O Lord of the Dwelling, be our furtherer," and so on. (11.50)
And he indeed offers oblations with the mantra beginning "amīvahā vāstoṣpate," having sacrificed with clarified butter using the *sruva* ladle while reciting these Vedic mantras.
Then one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering up until the gift of the cow and the granting of boons.
Then, having spread *darbha* grass in front of the fire, [one should place] the remains of the oblation upon it.
One should pour [the water] out with the mantra beginning "Namo rudrāya vāstoṣpate," and having washed the vessel with this very mantra, [one should discard] that water. (5.53)
Having poured the remaining clarified butter and the remaining water into some vessel,
one should mix them together with a mantra, using either a branch of the udumbara tree.
Alternatively, with a branch of the *pālāśa* tree or again with a handful of *darbha* grass,
one should perform three circumambulations to the right around temples, houses, and so forth, in every such case.
Then, sprinkling water around [the fire], he circumambulates; thereafter, having honored the twice-born, he should feed them with this mantra: "Thou art the Brahmin, thou art the Kavi. (11.56)

Having caused [the officiant] to recite the benedictions, one should then cause him to recite, "May there be auspiciousness for the dwelling" (śivaṃ vāstu). This concludes the section on the Vāstuhoma. [One may perform this rite] for a temple, a residence, a water-station, or even a sacrificial hall.
Having fashioned them from *takṣaka* wood and taken hold of them, one should wrap them with three threads; then,
having encircled them on all sides with a garland of *kauśī* grass and scattered unbroken grains of grain everywhere, one should place a full water-pot and a lamp in the center.

Then, one should recite the hymn beginning with "kṛṇuṣva" here, verse by half-verse; at the end, however, one should join the first half of the verse "daha" and so forth and recite it in its entirety. Thus, in recitations and other such acts, it shall be a destroyer of demons.

Having again prepared a sacrificial mound in the fire-quarter and having established the fire there according to the prescribed rule, he should first offer oblations to the mouth of the fire with both [verses] beginning with "rakṣohaṇaṃ vājinam. || 11.60 ||

Furthermore, having offered oblations of clarified butter (ājya) here with the mantras beginning with *kṛṇuṣva* in their proper sequence, one should likewise offer with the four distinct Vedādi mantras. (11.61)
With "iṣe tvā" and so forth, and likewise with "agnim īḷe" and so forth;
with the preceding "agna ā yāhi" and with "śanno devīḥ" and so forth. (11.62)
Then he performs oblations with the five Durgā mantras declared in the Vedas;
the first Durgā mantra is the Ṛg verse beginning with "jātavedase. (11.63)
The second Ṛc is declared to begin with "tām agnivarṇām"; the third is "agne tvam pāraya arvān asmān. (11.64)
The fourth mantra is declared to be "viśvāni no durgahā," and the fifth mantra is said to begin with "pṛtanājitam. (11.65)
One should offer oblations separately with clarified butter using these five Durgās;
then likewise with the Vyāhṛtis, and again with the Aghora-weapon mantra.
Thereafter, he should offer one hundred oblations with apāmārga fuel-sticks and ghee, and then one hundred with food mixed with clarified butter;
subsequently, he should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering one hundred and eight times, and then take the remaining clarified butter as well as the remainder of the water.
Having taken that ash and mixed it with the juice of *apāmārga* in a vessel,
one should wipe the entire house with it and sprinkle water around it with *darbha* grass.
Having taken that fire and placed it in the northeast corner, or else at a crossroads,
one should then dismiss it after offering the aforementioned water and food-balls (piṇḍas) and having completed the bali-offering in all directions.

Thus has been described the pacification of the slayers of demons (*rakṣohaṇa*), which destroys the afflictions of disease, untimely death, and malevolent planets; when performed according to the rules, it provides protection and bestows prosperity, victory, long life, and increase. (11.70)

In connection with the initiation (dīkṣā), the worship of the site (vāstupūjā), the offering of oblations (bali), and the fire sacrifice (homa) established by the Tantras, as well as the rite for the pacification of demons (rakṣoghnaśānti), have been duly described after understanding the doctrine of the teacher Baudhāyana. (11.71)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā), in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.

In various festivals, including initiations, the installation of deities, and the rite of the sacred thread (*pavitra*), that ritual action which is performed preceded by the sowing of auspicious sprouts becomes auspicious. (12.1)
On the seventh or ninth day prior to the auspicious day of the sacrifice,
or even on the fifth day, at a favorable moment during a propitious time, one should perform the rite for the auspicious sprouts (maṅgalāṅkura).
In this context, three types of vessels are prescribed: the *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva*.
These three, dedicated respectively to Viṣṇu, Brahmā (Padmabhava), and Śaṅkara, should be prepared individually in their proper sequence.
The height is clearly measured in finger-breadths (aṅgula), as is the width of the mouth of the *pālikā* vessel;
furthermore, the best [size] is said to be according to the number of fingers, while the middling and inferior methods are indeed described accordingly.
The height above [the base] should be equal to the width of the foot; the neck-opening should measure one-third of that.
The remainder of the entire structure is like a staff, with a circumference as pleasing as the neck.
Equal in height to the width of Vyāsa, the one called Ghaṭikā should be five-faced here, measuring a palm’s length;
its four faces are toward the cardinal directions, while the single middle face has a symmetrical, rounded portion.
The mouth of the shallow bowl (śarāva) should be as wide as a palm tree and its height equal to that; its base should measure half of that.
The handle (daṇḍaka) should have a thickness of four finger-breadths, and its neck should be raised, excluding the cavity.
When available, they may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even new earthenware;
having been washed with water from one's own weapon, they should be placed with their necks wrapped in thread. (12.8)

One should place the vessels, filled with pure clay, sand, and powdered cow dung, and provided with bundles of *kuśa* grass, within the charming house of auspicious sprouts that is covered by a canopy. (12.9)

Having smeared the ground with cow-dung water, having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the root-mantra of one's own deity, and having drawn a square according to the prescribed characteristics using threads coated with flour; || 12-10 ||
Having worshipped Vighnanātha in front, one should also have the auspicious day recited by those distinguished in the Vedas;
furthermore, for the eighty [syllables], there shall be a square arrangement of four squares.
In the center, one should draw a white lotus with nine squares, adorned with a pericarp, eight petals, and filaments; it should be well-constructed with raised center and colored with rice-powder.
There, having placed upon *kuśa* grass a jar wrapped with thread and fumigated with incense,
one should fill it with the nectar-water dripping from the "twelfth" [cakra], together with *kuśa*, a tuft of hair (*kūrca*), and gold.
With the fragrances of the fresh sprouts of *pippala* and mango trees, with garlands, flower-wreaths, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and cloths;
with an arrangement rich in *śāli* rice and fruits, and made beautiful by pairs of garments and blossoms. (12–14)

One should meditate upon that [deity] situated within the lotus of the Mātṛkās, endowed with the sixteen digits (kalās) together with the sixteen vowels; he who is like the cool-rayed moon with its upward-shooting beams, the Lord of the Stars accompanied by the circle of constellations.
One should worship with special offerings, presenting milk-rice, sacrificial porridge, and clarified butter;
then, upon the auspiciously marked squares delineated with colored powders, one should place the individual vessels for the sprouts.
In Āditya, in Samarīci, in Vivasvat, and likewise in Yama; in the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), in Mitra, in Soma, and in the Supporter of the Earth (Bhūdhara). || 12-17 ||
One should place eight *ghaṭikās* in their respective positions in due order:
in Agni, Pūṣan, the one called Citrā, Dauvārika, Roga, and Nāga. (12–18)
Furthermore, one should place eight shallow bowls (śarāva) in the northeast corner of the Aditi [section],
and eight in their central squares according to the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should place eight locations for the *pālikās* as they have been described; having first drawn out the squares within these, one should fill them with white powder.

Having separately placed one *āḍhaka* measure of each type of *śāli* rice upon separate mats of *darbha* grass, and having set down the water-clocks (*ghaṭikā*) and other instruments, he should sow the seeds therein.
Black gram, mung beans, horse gram, flat beans, sesame, rice, mustard, millet, wheat, śyāmāka, vrīhi rice, and barley; || 12-22 ||
Priyaṅgu, āḍhakī, and vaiṇava—
these seeds of the three and five groups are declared, in order, to be the most excellent for sprouting.
The two groups [of mantras] should be in the middle [position], and the five seed-syllables in the lowest;
having washed the seed-syllables with water, one should thereafter wash them with milk.
Having tied it firmly in a piece of cloth and kept it in water for one day,
one should remove it and sow it when two watches (yāmas) have passed.
Soma is the presiding deity of seeds, for he is radiant during the night;
therefore, one who desires to enjoy the harvest should sow the seeds only at night.
Having first consecrated it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should sow it with this mantra:
"Oṃ, to Tryambaka, to Śarva, to Śaṅkara, and to Śiva. (12.27)
Homage, homage again and again to the eternal one, the foremost of all worlds!
With this very mantra, one should sprinkle [the disciple] with water infused with turmeric.
Having worshipped with the five types of offerings and having clothed [the deity] in white garments,
one should present the bali offering for seven nights according to the sequence that will be described.
The Brahma-bhūtas, Indras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rakṣases, Piśācas, and the seven Gaṇas of the meat-eaters (Balibhujs) are designated respectively by those names. || 12-30 ||
In the first watch of the night, the bali offering consists of food, flowers, and kuśa grass;
likewise, food, curd, powdered atisīsa, parched grain, flour, and sesame seeds.
One should cause the rite known as Bhūtakrūra to be performed at night on a Bhūta-day;
[the offering consists of] food mixed with Indravallī and garlic, along with barley meal, milk, and curd.
On the third night, dedicated to Indra, the preceptor should offer an oblation consisting of rice cooked with bamboo shoots mixed with milk; on the fourth night, it should be for Gāndharva.
In the fifth [night], called Yakṣarātra, the bali offering consists of flowers, cooked rice, clarified butter, and water;
but in the sixth, the Rākṣasa [night], it consists of red rice with husks and mixed with clay.
Furthermore, in the seventh [birth], that of a Piśāca, one should cause to be given black gram rice, kṛsara, honey, turmeric powder, and meat, all richly mixed with oil.
Otherwise, some teachers indeed declare a group of seven qualities;
those are described here as the Bhūtas, the Pitṛs, and the Guhyakas. (12.36)
The Nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and all the deities— on every night,
one should cause the bali-offering to be given with their respective names, preceded by the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ."
On the first Bhūta-night, one should cause [the offering] to be given with the Bhūtakrūra [mantra];
on the second Pitṛ-night, with sesame seeds mixed with rice.
On the third night, one should offer coconut water with rice;
on the night of the Yakṣa, with milk, flour, and parched grain; and on the fourth night, with ginger.
In the fifth Brahma-watch, one should offer food with lotus seeds, rice, and clarified butter;
in the sixth, which belongs to Śiva, one should cause [the offering] to be given with food accompanied by cakes and clarified butter.
On the seventh day, during the rite dedicated to Viṣṇu, an offering (bali) should be made with pure boiled rice mixed with clarified butter;
when nine days have passed, milk-rice and kṛsara should be offered in succession.
One should worship the designated group of deities with the designated offerings;
no one else whatsoever should ever look upon the sprouts.
Either the preceptor himself or his disciple, by his command, should enter;
then, by means of well-grown sprouts, one should indicate the auspicious or inauspicious results for the patron.

One should declare loss of wealth from dark or black sprouts, disease from those growing sideways, and suffering from those that are reddish; one should predict death from those that have grown crooked, and loss of one's position, country, and desired objects from those that are broken.

With sprouts that are white, yellow, fully developed, abundant, quickly produced, beautiful, and extensive, the performer shall obtain fortune, nourishment, complete success in his desires, and auspiciousness. (12.45)
If the teacher perceives that the sprouts there are unfavorable, he should perform a rite for pacification (*śāntika*).
Having offered oblations with the root mantra, the limb mantras, and the Brahma-mantras, ending with the *vyāhṛtis*, he should use sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Offering of Sprouts," in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter:
Now, the sacrificial hall should have four doors and corners, marked with four archways, enriched with canopies and banners;
it should be smeared all around with cow dung and water, draped with garlands, fragrant, and perfumed with incenses.

Having adorned the sacrificial pit with lamps, sprouts, and full vases, and having prepared it in the direction of Indra (the east), one should establish the fire within that quadrangular pit endowed with the proper characteristics, and having offered oblations here into the mouth of the fire; || 13-2 ||
Then, having worshipped Vighnarāja with perfumes, edibles, and foods, one should sacrifice to him in the south;
having purified that spot in the center of the house, one should construct a square there using the prescribed lines.
Furthermore, dividing that [remaining space] into two and eight parts, there should be two hundred and fifty-six squares here;
one should draw a lotus in the center with squares numbering two and eight, and three circles outside with squares numbering seven (the number of *darbha* grasses).

The wheel of the zodiac (rāśicakra) consists of eighty squares; here, with the remaining squares numbering fifty-two, one should draw the door-decorations (dvāraśobhā) and the intermediate decorations (praśobhā), along with the corners, using squares numbering six, four, four, and six respectively. (13–5)
One should draw a circle, which shall be in the middle of the two paths; there should be a set of four threads in the cardinal directions.
Thus, there shall be twelve spokes, which are the zodiac signs, equal [in size], resembling *mātuluṅga* fruits and having the luster of blue lotuses.
In the outer pathway, there should be wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadruma) with nets of creepers, leaves, fruits, and birds;
and according to the beauty of their respective places, there should be lotuses, water-lilies, and the like, together with buds, flowers, and clusters.

Having rotated the lotus-base fourfold to make it even for the sake of the pericarp and its filaments, the joints and the tips of the petals should likewise be made equal; thus one should then fashion the eight petals.

White [is the color] from powdered rice-flour; well-yellowed from turmeric; and red from safflower. It becomes dark-colored with *palāśa* leaves; likewise, it becomes deep blue with parched grains of rice. (13.9)

Its pericarp should be yellow and subtle, and likewise the filaments at the beginning should be thick in the middle; they should be reddish-brown at their tips, yellow at their base, and white at their ends; these should appear in pairs upon the petals.
All the lines should be white, equal in number to the petals, and the petals themselves should be red with clear powders;
the junction of the petals should be dark-colored, and the three concentric circles should possess white, reddish, and blue hues.

Likewise, the zodiacal signs belonging to Varuṇa (the western quarter) should be dark green, while those on the path (vīthī) should be bright yellow; their junctions should be of colors that are beautiful to behold.
The wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas) should be made variegated and pleasing to both the eye and the mind. || 13-12 ||
One should draw white door-surfaces, with beautiful decorations reddish like safflower and yellow secondary ornaments;
on the deep blue areas, one should draw white conch-shells, or white svastikas in the corners, or whatever pleasing designs one desires.

The preceptor, together with his disciples, having first fasted for one night, performed his ablutions and daily rites, washed his feet, sipped water for purification, and put on white upper garments; having performed the ritual worship of the door and discharged the weapon-mantra, he stood ready. (13–14)

Having stepped here with his foot and struck the ground three times with his heel, and having touched the threshold with his right foot, he entered and took refuge within the northern branch; then, having worshipped Vāstunātha and Vidhi.
Having established a rampart of weapons and performed protection on all sides, he should then sit upon the prescribed seat in silence;
he should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) arising from the restraint of breath, and having worshipped the elephant-faced [Ganesha] in the south and the Guru in the northeast.

Then, having empowered his own body with mantras and become one with Śiva, he should worship Śiva—the singular light—residing in the heart-lotus with offerings accomplished by the mind; likewise, he should sacrifice into the fire-pit of the navel with mental oblations.
Having filled the *arghya* vessel and worshipped [the deity] together with the root-mantra and its limbs, one should sprinkle one’s own head with the water from the *kūrca* and the *arghya*.
Likewise, having sprinkled the entire collection of ritual materials used for worship, and having likewise sprinkled the sacrificial ground (*yāgabhūmi*) with those waters; || 13–18 ||
Then, reciting the mantra ending in the *niṣkala* form along with the three *tālas* and the *astra* ending in a protracted vowel (*pluta*), one should perform the purification of the site;
thereafter, having sprinkled the image with water flowing from one's own lotus-heart and from the moon, the water of the *astra* should likewise be purified.
One should place the *vardhanī* vessel filled with water to the north, and likewise, the fragrant powder, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) to the south.
One should cast a drop of that *arghya* water along with fragrance and a flower [into the fire], and mutter the root mantra over the circle of ritual substances.

Having lit as many pleasing and pure lamps as one is able, according to the prescribed methods, one should worship that maṇḍala—either individually with fragrant unbroken rice and other offerings as described, or according to the sequence to be explained hereafter. (13–21)
Likewise, one should install the Support Power (Ādhāra-śakti), who sustains the worlds and resembles a lotus sprout; one should worship her beneath the earth.
Then [one should worship] Ananta, the Earth, that which is called the Seat of Ananta (Anantāsana), and the four-cornered pedestal known as the Union (Yoga).
One should worship the one called Dharma, red in color and bull-shaped, in the southeast; Jñānasiṃha, black, at the foot of the western [direction];
Virāga, bright yellow, likewise; and Īśvara, transparent, in the northwest, on the two elephants situated on the earth.
One should know that *rajas* is the bulbous root, *tamas* is the stalk therein, and the lotus is called *sattva*, being perfectly white;
from that [lotus], one should understand the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire, joined with the petals and other parts representing Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (13–24)
In the same manner, one should worship the principles (tattvas) known as Śiva, which consist of self-knowledge, as well as the lotus of the Mātṛkās, according to the prescribed rule;
having thoroughly worshipped that golden or other vessel, one should wrap it with a triple-stranded thread after it has been well-washed.
One should place an incense-filled vessel facing downwards upon the pericarp, together with grain and darbha grass, on the side containing the bodhi leaves.

Having placed it with its opening facing downward, one should then set down a bundle of kuśa grass (*kūrca*) upon the back of the jar, its interior filled with [grains] numbering according to the *kalās*.
Then, having ascertained that within it resides the primordial, throbbing Power (Śakti), the source of the entire phenomenal world along with all the principles (tattvas),
one should lift up that jar, place a bundle of kuśa grass (kūrca) therein, and recite the Mantra of Power (Śakti) which contains the Praṇava (Oṃ).

Then, having first filled [the vessel] with the waters of sacred sites (tīrtha) mixed with the nectar-essence from the moon-disk of one's own lotus, combined with the letters of the Mātṛkā in reverse order, along with the water of medicinal herbs of corresponding colors and fragrances.
But if all these medicinal herbs are unavailable, one should instead use the barks of trees that yield the four milks along with water;
or one may properly cast in the eight fragrant substances well-ground, as well as sweet-smelling flowers in the same manner.
One should cast into the sovereign jar pure and auspicious rubies, coral, diamonds, emeralds, pearls, topazes, and likewise pure sapphires originating from beryl, as well as moonstones. (13.30)

Having adorned it with fresh garlands and flowers, as well as with leaves of *aśvattha*, *bilva*, and *pānasa*, and having bound fresh, pure, upward-pointing shoots of *śakravallī* to the tree, one should meditate upon that Pārijāta tree.

Having placed a vessel completely filled with white rice, along with betel and areca nut, into his mouth, and having adorned him with two very fine, new, white garments, as well as garlands, perfumes, and unbroken grains of rice; || 13-32 ||

Having invoked Śakti, the source of the phenomenal world, as well as the pure Vidyā and Cit in her subtle form, [one should worship] separately with the letters of the Mātṛkā placed between the *tāra* (OM), and also the fifty *kalās* born from the *tāra*. (13.33)

One should duly apply the thirty-eight digits previously mentioned in sequence to this jar, which represents the power of will (*icchāśakti*) and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*); furthermore, one should manifest the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), which is the manifestation of independent awakening. (13.34)

Likewise, when the power (śakti) has been pacified, one should employ the living being called Haṃsa; having performed the installation of the living being in that [liṅga] with the root-mantra and its own limbs, one should contemplate the presence of all the sense organs through the mantra. (13.35)
The twice-born should employ five *ṛc* verses spoken by Tāraka: first, "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" and so forth;
another is "pra tad viṣṇuḥ," which is an *anuṣṭubh*; likewise, "tat padādyā" and "viṣṇornukam" as the preceding one. (13.36)

In that same manner, one should appropriately employ the limb-mantras and the root-mantra within that [deity], maintaining the state of its having form. Having worshipped it thoroughly with the prescribed services, one should correctly meditate upon the Śakti who bestows desired objects and possesses a beautiful form—
rosy-red like a hibiscus flower, for the sake of attaining visible goals, holding a noose and a goad, and with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
She was adorned with variegated garments, garlands, and saffron-colored unguents, her mass of hair shining with the luster of trembling bees.

Having meditated upon her—the source of the phenomenal world and whose nature is the phenomenal world—who bears in the sky the splendor of separate parasols and rainbows through the radiance of her crown and ornaments of shimmering gems, and having worshipped her in the lotus of the heart, one shall become [established]. 13.39.

Having invoked [the deity] and meditating upon the chosen deity—who conforms to the disciple’s preferred mantra and possesses the desired form, color, and other attributes—one should place the six limbs with the four limb-mantras in the intermediate directions, the weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions, and worship the eye-mantra in the center. (13.40)
The Śakti situated upon the tips of the petals of that lotus is said to worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and the deities of the weapons (astradevas) in the directions;
their complexions are, in order: tawny, yellow, white, smoky-grey, white, honey-colored, pale-white, white, and red.
And Sarojaprabha—these are the lords of the worlds; and the ten [lords] beginning with Indra, together with Brahmā and Śeṣa, [are present].
The vajra is bright yellow, the śakti is deep red, the staff (daṇḍa) is white in appearance, and the sword is the color of a sword [or black]. (13.42)
The noose and the goad are said to be like lightning and white in luster; the mace is like fire, and the trident is like the sun.
The lotus is like the sun, and the discus is likewise; thus they are described in order according to the colors of their respective weapons and fires.

One should worship Gaṇa, Vīrabhadra, and the Seven Mothers in the south; [one should worship] the yellow elephant-faced one, and the very dark-blue Bhadra, as well as the seven Mothers, who resemble their respective deities and are equipped with their mounts, weapons, and so forth.
To the east of Kubera, one should worship Caṇḍa, as well as Kṣetrapāla and his own vehicle in the eastern direction;
these are to be honored with offerings according to the proper sequence and application, using their names preceded by "Satāra" and ending with "Namaḥ."
Then, one should place the *pālikās* and other vessels at the front of the mandala, enriched with sprouted shoots, and worship them in the cardinal directions;
likewise, one should offer fresh cow-ghee, *caru*, black sesame seeds, rice flour, and white mustard seeds.
Having uttered the letters of the alphabet along with the stars, the syllables of the script, the Śakti, and the Haṃsa, ending with the pair of *ṭha* sounds, he offers each of those;
having offered with his own mantra and its limbs (*aṅga*), and with the desired mantra, the twice-born should likewise offer the Mahāvyāhṛtis and the Vyāhṛtis.

Reciting the mantra for the sake of abandoning the fourfold bondage of karma, one offers sesame and clarified butter as described below: "The word *baka*, followed by the syllable *sa* with the vowel *ū*, then the syllable *agni* with the nasal *ṅ*, then the syllable *ṭīṇa* with the vowel *ā*, and finally the word *prāṇa* joined with the third [vowel]. (13.48)

Whatever has been done by me through thought, word, or deed—whether in waking, dreaming, or deep sleep; whether by mind, speech, or action; or by my two hands, two feet, belly, or genitals—may all that be an offering unto Brahman. Thaḥ thaḥ.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations there with this [mantra], and then having offered the *bali* and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to the north,
he should give the *bali* there to the lunar days (*tithi*), the constellations (*uḍu*), and the zodiac signs and planets, using their own names followed by the word "namaḥ."
Then, having seated there upon this pedestal a disciple who has been purified by ritual bathing and has performed the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana),
and having placed dūrvā grass, a bundle of kuśa (kūrca), unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth upon his head, one should worship him with fragrant flowers.

Having prostrated before that deity, saying, "Be gracious so that this sacrificial animal may be released from its bonds and attain the fulfillment of its desires," and having obtained permission, the preceptor himself unites the deities residing in the image with those in the water-pot (kumbha).
Holding it with both hands and standing upon the tips of *kuśa* grass, he should sprinkle the disciple with that water;
by means of the path of the *suṣumnā*, the streams of water flowing into the disciple’s body through those mantras mixed with nectar [should be applied] in due order. (13.52)
Then, by means of the radiance of the throbbing power (śakti) of that deity, one should contemplate its entry into the heart-lotus;
likewise, one should effect the release of the bees [of the senses] three times with the weapon-mantra (astra), and having brought about the state of Śiva within that [lotus] via the channel (nāḍī).

Having risen, the disciple, wearing a pair of pure white garments and having washed his feet again, should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), offer the arghya oblation to the Sun, and after bowing down, proceed to the entrance of that [temple]. || 13.54 ||

Seated upon *kuśa* grass with palms joined in reverence, he should face the northern direction by the command of the preceptor. The preceptor, seated facing the east, should sprinkle his head with water for the *arghya* offering while reciting the *astra-mantra* and using *darbha* blades.

Having worshipped his body three times with the *bhūti* [ashes] upon its head, and having purified it in three ways through emaciation and other means, one should then perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) once more; having personally brought about this purification within the disciple's body through the activity of the mind, [one should place it] in the vessel.
Then, having worshipped with the special *arghya* offering and having sprinkled it again with the water from that *kūrca*, one should place the letters of the Mātṛkā therein.
Thereafter, having brought about its embodiment, one should place the mantra of the deity to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and its limb-mantras (*aṅga-mantra*) within it.

Then, having again enveloped it with armor, and having taken a new white cloth marked with his own root-mantra and limbs, he should bind it over the eyes of the image; then, having first worshipped the chosen deity within that [image], || 13-58 ||
Then, one should cause him to cast that handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) upon whichever form [of the deity] it falls, according to the *bāṅga* mantra;
for it is said that one should give him the mantra by that [deity's] name, and he too should recite that mantra three times.

Then, seated upon a darbha-grass mat on the Tāra-pīṭha, having gazed at the disciple while reciting the root-mantra and its ancillaries, and placing his own hand upon the disciple’s head, he should touch every limb with the root-mantras of the limbs.

Then, having placed the root of a *darbha* blade into the hand of the disciple and sat down previously in front of the fire, he should press it between his own thighs and gradually effect the union of the life-channel within himself with that [channel] of the disciple. || 13.61 ||
One should contemplate the vital breath as having issued from the two channels known as *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, and also from the *suṣumnā* path at the crown of the head;
then, one should visualize that threefold light as well as the life-force (*jīva*) within the body of the disciple with its connection unbroken.
Having brought about the state of oneness between the disciple and one's own self, one should offer oblations three times with ghee while reciting the root mantra;
likewise, the disciple’s *jīva* enters the [teacher’s] self, and then, having emerged again, it enters his own body.
By manifesting the birth of the Self in this way, the disciple, through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), will clearly become Śiva, equal to himself;
just as a grasshopper, having enveloped a caterpillar in mud, undergoes a transformation of sound and, becoming six-legged, brings it to its own species. (13.64)
In this manner, the preeminent teacher makes the ordinary disciple a manifestation of the mantra through the initiation of ritual action (*kriyādīkṣā*).
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, he offers five [oblations] for each of the limbs (*aṅga*) with clarified butter, using a tenth part of that amount.
If the twice-born performs the *jaya* and other oblations here, let him offer the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with all the root-mantras and their ancillary mantras;
having offered with fuel-sticks, milk, parched grain, white mustard, cow-products, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and the ancillaries, he should sacrifice with the root-mantra.
Just as clarified butter offered here with Vedic mantras according to the path prescribed by one's own Sūtra serves as atonement, so too, O twice-born ones,
the expiation for you is performed by a mantra-knower who offers oblations from the root [mantra] twenty-eight times.
Then, one should elevate his birth by means of three oblations of clarified butter with the mantras to be described hereafter:

"The Praṇava (Oṃ), Śakti (Hrīṃ), and the Mūlamantra; being the source of this self within its own [nature], may he become a twice-born one whose body is mantra, purified in seed, food, state, and place—Ṭha Ṭha."
Thereafter, having offered oblations with the vyāhṛtis, || 13.68 ||
"O Blessed One, may his self become the essence of mantra; *ṭha ṭha*.

Having offered three oblations with this [mantra], and having subsequently offered the *vyāhṛtis* there, one should sprinkle and strike him with the *astra-mantra*, and immediately enter within him through the *recaka* breath to [sever] his bonds. (13.69)

Having separated [the disciple's consciousness] from this [body], one should then sever the weapons; having again formed the mudrā called the goad (aṅkuśa), one should draw forth that consciousness residing in the body of the disciple from it and join it to the moon at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta).
When the beloved lotus has entered the heart during inhalation (pūraka), one should unite this with one's own self through retention (kumbhaka).
Then, having cast off the human state, one should lead it to a state of equal flavor (samarasa) as Śiva during exhalation (recaka).
Having worshipped that [consciousness] with the *haṃsa-japa*, one should again cast it out and lead it to the heart of the disciple;
having established that consciousness from one's own lotus into the lotus of the disciple's heart via the path of the channels (*nāḍī*).

Having bathed him with streams of water from the moon’s mansion poured by the *sūtas*, and having visualized his mantra-body as free from ailment and possessing undiminished power, one should contemplate the disciple thus and then perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the letters of the *mātṛkā*.

Having established that son of tender body with his own physical form seated upon the root-limbs of the desired deity, one should perform for him the birth-rite (jātakarman) and other ceremonies. Then, from the root-mantra, that [rite] should be performed three times separately;
while reciting the root-mantra along with its limbs, one should invest him with the sacred thread (upavīta) and unite him with the vows prescribed according to the root-mantra.
The Guru should first satisfy the fire with oblations according to his capacity, and having again offered the final *pūrṇāhuti*,

he should proclaim to him these bridges of dharma pertaining to the conduct of the tradition (*sāmayācārika*), so that the practitioner may protect them. Thus, from the Preceptor, he receives the mantra-initiation which purifies the sins of seven lifetimes and bestows desired fruits.
Having obtained that which bestows success in recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and mantras, the wise person shall immediately become fulfilled for a long time.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the Initiation into Mantras, in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Next, the Agneya rituals (kalpas) are described, which bestow the objects of one's intentions.
The first ritual is Vaidika, followed by the Śaiva and the Vaiṣṇava.

The ritual procedures for the sacred fire (agni-kalpa) prescribed in the Tantras are fourfold: obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), optional (kāmya), and that which is to be accomplished (sādhya)—these being the rites performed by those versed in the Vedas.
That [rite] may be accomplished by the twice-born with Vedic mantras and the Vedic fire;
or likewise, the rite prescribed in the Śaiva Āgamas may be performed with Śaiva mantras. (14.3)
One who follows the Śaiva path should accomplish rites performed according to the Pāśupata and other such traditions by means of the Śaiva fire;
one should accomplish Vaiṣṇava rites with their respective mantras by means of the Vaiṣṇava fire.
The fire-god shall accomplish the four aims of human life and those six rites performed for specific desires by means of Vedic and Tantric mantras.
Fire is divided into thirty-two types, distinguished by thirty-two kinds of ritual action; such is the doctrine of the Aṅgirases, renowned among those who know the Atharva Veda. (14.6)

The worldly fire is Pāvaka; Marutta is for the ceremony of conception (garbhadhāraṇa); Pavamāna is for the rite of generating a male child (puṃsavana); and the one named Maṅgala is for the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana). || 14-7 ||
In Tuṅga, the one named Śobhana is powerful for the birth-ceremony;
Pārthiva is for the naming ceremony, and Bhadra is considered suitable for the first outing. (14.8)

Śuci is prescribed for the consumption of food; Sabhya is declared for the tonsure ceremony (caula); Jātavedas is indeed for the initiation (upanayana); and Saṃbhava occurs during the three vows (vratatraya).
At the gift of a cow, he is named Sūrya; at the completion of a vow, he is Saumya;
at the establishment of the domestic fire, he is Āvasathya; and at the Anvāhārya sacrifice, he is Maheśvara.
Viṣṇu is in the Āhavanīya fire, while Brahmā is in the Gārhapatya;
Vītihotra is in the Prāyaścitta fire, and the one named Mṛḍa is in the Pūrṇāhuti.

The Kravyāda fire is for the cremation of corpses; the Vaḍavāmukha fire is in the ocean; the Vardhana fire is for forest fires; and the Saṃvartaka fire is considered to be at the time of universal destruction.
The boon-granting [mudrā] is prescribed for pacification (śāntika), and the strength-increasing [mudrā] for nourishment (pauṣṭika).
The smoky-colored [mudrā] is for eradication and expulsion, while the black [mudrā] is considered for inciting enmity (vidveṣaṇa).
In the rite of subjugation (vaśya), it is named Kāmada; in killing (māraṇa), it is called Śoṣaṇa;
in paralyzing (stambhana), it is known by the name Piṅgala; and in the stomach, it is considered to be Jāṭhara.
The section on the thirty-two varieties of fire:

In a pure place, either in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on an altar (*sthaṇḍila*) as prescribed, smeared with cow dung and made of gold, silver, copper, or other materials, [one should perform the rite]. (14–15)
Having sprinkled the ground that has been cleared by the fragments, and having thrown sand upon it,
one should then fashion a square measuring one cubit (aratni).
One should then draw three lines facing east and three facing north;
one should not do so with pebbles, grass, wood, clods of earth, or with the fingernails.
Nor with charcoal, nor silently; there, with Brahmā as the presiding deity, one should draw the eastern line in the middle with the mantra "brahmajajñānam."
From the *nāke suparṇa* [hymn], one should place [the line] toward the east; then again toward the south and the north.
With the verse *āpyāyasva*, [one places a line] with its tip pointing eastward; with *yo rudraḥ*, [one places a line] extending toward the north. (14–19)
Reciting "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and likewise "indraṃ vo viśvataspari," one should sprinkle water toward the east and the north and discard the wooden chip.
Having touched water from the vessel and examined the fire with the *vyāhṛtis*,
one should cast it into the center with the *praṇava* and cover it with excellent fuel.
Having kindled [the fire] with the *tāra* mantra, with his hands joined together and filled with *darbha* grass,
and having recited "juṣṭo damūnā" and so forth, he should then sweep around [the fire].
Having sprinkled water with *darbha* grass as prescribed,
one should perform the rite in the east with the mantra "devasya tvā" and in the south with the *vyāhṛtis*.
"Rising up from behind the darkness, O Agni, come hither to the north;
one should place the southern ones above and the northern ones below. (14.24)
Having spread darbha grass to the north of the fire, he should set down the vessels in pairs:
the vessel for the clarified butter and the sruva-ladle, as well as the prokṣaṇī-vessels and the sruc-ladle.
The vessel for the *praṇītā* water, the fuel wood, the sacrificial pot, the stirring-ladle,
the sacrificial grass together with the mats, and whatever else is required for the oblation.
But in the case of the pouring out of the rice, the pestle and mortar,
as well as the winnowing basket and the black antelope skin— all of these should likewise be turned face down.
Having taken the *pavitra* grass-blades crosswise into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and having filled it with water,
one should grasp it with both hands using the thumb and ring finger.
Having cut [the grass] three times, purified it thoroughly, and sprinkled the vessels with water,
one should turn them face upwards, sprinkle them three times, and then untie the fuel and other materials once more.
With darbha grass blades measuring a span (prādeśa) and with unbroken tips,
the seat for Brahmā is placed to the south, and the seat for the Praṇītā vessel is to the north.
Afterward, having consecrated the seat for the vessel of clarified butter (ājyasthālī), one should seat a pure Brāhmaṇa upon it for the sake of the Brahmā priest;
if no Brāhmaṇa is available, a blade of kūrca grass should be placed there.
O Brahmin, having invoked [the deity] with the Tāra and the Vyāhṛtis at the beginning, one should worship;
and having filled the vessel intended for the Praṇītā water with water, just like the Prokṣaṇī vessel.
Having lifted up [the seat] which rests on *darbha* grass and is covered with *darbha* grass, reaching as high as the nose,
and being authorized by the Brahman priest, he should place it upon each respective seat.
Saying "Thou art Varuṇa," and having propitiated [the deity], he should then place rice grains or even husked grains—
either with a *sruva* ladle or a *sthālī* pot— silently between [the fire and the offering], and then [offer] with the *yājyā* verse.
Having designated "of such-and-such a one," he should offer it to the deity;
if it be rice, he should thresh it, sprinkle it with water, and wash it three times.

Afterwards, one should pour [the remainder] into the vessels; then, having cooked the sacrificial porridge (caru) in this fire according to the prescribed instructions, one should sprinkle it with clarified butter and remove it from the heat.
Having approached the fire from the north, one should pour clarified butter into the vessel;
having drawn out the embers to the north and placed the vessel containing the butter upon the seat.
Having illuminated that [oblation] with two *darbha* blades, he should again touch water;
having illuminated it three times over the clarified butter (*ājya*), he should then cast the tips of the *darbha* blades into it.
Having performed the circumambulation with fire, one should cast darbha embers into the fire;
then, having purified [the clarified butter] three times with the central-knot strainer using drops of clarified butter.
Having offered [the oblation] into the fire, having washed [the vessel], and having untied [the knot], one should throw back the washed [portion].
Then, into the fire, one should place four *darbha* blades and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with their faces turned upward.
Having taken [the grass-blades] and heated them in the fire, one should wipe [the ladles] three times with them;
then, having wrapped those [blades] around the fingers individually, one should do so again for both the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

One should wipe the tip [of the ladle] with the tip of the *darbha* grass, the middle with the middle, and the base first with the base; then, having washed those two again, one should cast the *darbha* blades into the fire.
Having placed two [pieces of wood] face down on a seat of darbha grass to the south, one should worship;
then, having laid the thick enclosing stick (paridhi) in the west, and again the thin one.
Having placed the long one to the south and the short, subtle one to the north,
and likewise having placed two upright fuel-sticks in the south, north, and east [corners].
Thinking, "May this serve to ward off the Rākṣasas," the twice-born man,
having sprinkled water toward the south with the mantra beginning with "adite," should then sprinkle it toward the east.
Likewise in the west, with permission;
then in the north, [beginning] with "Sarasvatī" and so forth, all around, preceded by the deities.
Having uttered "O Savitṛ, impel! and having sprinkled water around, the wise one should then meditate upon the god Anala, who holds a spear and a svastika in his hands.
Three-eyed, with the luster of saffron, adorned with divine ornaments and garments,
possessing a serene countenance, and wearing a beautiful crown of matted hair.
Encircled by a golden garland and joined with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness—Kālī, Karālī, Manojava, and Sulohitā. (14.49)
Then there are the tongues Sudhūmra, Viṣphuliṅginī, and Viśvaruci;
these seven, situated in the directions starting from the east, are to be worshipped again in their respective order.
In the northeast is the one called Vasudhārā, who is indeed a secondary tongue of the Fire-god;
Kālī is for the rites of a Śūdra, while Karālī is for malevolent magic (ābhicāra).
One who is as swift as thought should effect the pacification of diseases caused by spirits, planetary influences, and the like;
likewise, the wise person should also perform the pacification during the Sulohitā [period].
In the Dhūmrā [Kalā], there is the raining of water and so forth; in the Sphuliṅginī [Kalā], there is hatred and eradication;
the goddess Sarvārthasādhanī is considered to be the tongue Viśvaruci. (14.53)
One who desires prosperity or seeks nourishment should offer oblations into the Vasudhārā fire;
thus there shall be seven tongues of flame, with Vasudhārā as the eighth.

Since a fire oblation performed without knowing the different tongues of the fire would be fruitless, one should know the tongues of the consumer of the oblation; thus, through such offerings, the attainment of results occurs here in this world.
Then, having prepared the oblation with clarified butter, he should offer it equally with the mantra "svāhā.
Taking the clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, he should offer it at the northern junction of the two enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Having touched [the base], one should cast a straight stream of water into the fire for Prajāpati;
likewise, having touched the southern joint with the mantra "indrāya," [one should do so].
Then one should offer the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) in the southern and north-eastern parts;
these two shall be for Agni and Soma, and they are indeed his two eyes.
Then, according to the instruction, one should offer oblations equally into the eastern mouth of the fire;
thus, being disciplined, one should offer four oblations with *āghāra* clarified butter and likewise four with *āditya* clarified butter.
From *ā no bhadrāt* [to] *virūpākṣāt*, from *virūpākṣāt* again [to] *yāti r̥cīnī*, and from the preceding [mantra] *saṃrādhanyā* again. || 14-60 ||
Having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* using the *prasādhani* ladle, the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*) is accomplished;
then, having sprinkled that *caru* offering with clarified butter from its eastern half and its western half...
Having performed two *avadāna* (cuttings) and having held the *sruk* ladle over the fire, one should set it down;
then, having again held it over the fire, one should offer the oblation separately for each according to the traditional injunction.
Then, for the sake of Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, he makes a single portion from the northern half of the sacrificial oblation;
having sprinkled it with clarified butter, he offers it into the fire using the very same ladle.
Having offered that in the eastern and northern halves of the fire and having lifted up the oblation,
one should sprinkle the stirring-spoon with the residue of the offering, and then, having taken that water into the ladle— 14.64.
Having poured those offerings for the Pitṛs, who are prescribed within the enclosing sticks, with the *sruva* ladle,
he should indeed wash it inside the enclosing sticks and heat it over the fire.
Having filled it with water, he should sprinkle it outside the enclosing sticks;
then, having cast into the fire that fuel-stick which was previously set aside.

In that same manner, one should strike the fuel-belt (*idhma-saṃnāha*) with the *ukṣita* mantra; thereafter, one should offer the oblation beginning with *jaya*, followed by the thirteen mantras beginning with *cittam*.
From that [the mantra], then fire, and the eighteen elements (bhūtas) in sequence;
however, if no specific instruction is given, one should offer oblations ending with the word "samāva."
For specific rites, the presiding priest offers oblations for years, having uttered:
"May he protect this [person] in this Brahmanhood; may he grant this in this Kṣatriyahood. (14.69)
Then, after *asyām* and *ante*, there is the word *śiṣyasya*; after that, *purodhāyām* and *padam*;
then *asmin* and *karmaṇi*, and after *asya*, the two *ṭha*s in *devahūtyām*.
Having reduced [the materials] to a paste, one should offer eighteen oblations in sequence;
then, having offered with the twelve mantras beginning with *ṛtāṣāṭ*, [one proceeds].
Likewise, having offered oblations to the ministers, one should offer twenty oblations ending with Agni, using the mantras beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam. (14.72)
"O Prajāpati, nothing other than you"—with this [verse], one should cast the fuel and the wood-cutter's blade;
and also with "The mind is the light, the oblation for Agni," and "Whatever in this rite... (14.73).
Then, having offered oblations with "svasti naḥ" and so forth, as well as with "yan ma ātmanaḥ," and again with "punar anyat" and so forth, and likewise again with the *vyāhṛtis*.
With these verses, that which was unknown is likewise measured by the person;
then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, he throws it toward the east for the sake of clarity.
Having wiped the enclosing sticks (paridhis), he should pluck darbha grass from the sacrificial seat (prastara);
having dipped the tips, middles, and roots into the vessel of clarified butter (ājyasthālī), [he should offer them].
Starting from the tip and proceeding upwards, one should then burn it down to the root;
one should not blow on it, nor should one throw it outside the fire, nor scatter it.
Having gathered them together, one should slowly cast [the fuel] while likewise separating the grass;
however, the *śamyā* sticks should not be discarded, and one should throw the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) [into the fire]. (14.78)
One should cast the other two [ladles] simultaneously after having offered the two upright fuel-sticks;
then, having also offered the residue in the fire, one should perform the sprinkling around and release [the ritual].
One should silently sprinkle consecrated water in each direction; or else, one should sprinkle it in due order with the mantras beginning with "In the eastern direction," and so forth.
One should pour the remainder on the ground and give a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin;
one should give it if available, or otherwise feed the Brahmins according to one's ability. || 14.81 ||
One should eat the remnant of the oblation, or touch the belly while reciting "May there be long life";
then, having sipped water, one should recite the hymn beginning with "yat indra" and the following verse.
"The remainder should be given to one learned in the Vedas," says the omnipresent Bodhāyana. This concludes the section on the ritual for the Vedic fire.
Now, the ritual for the Śiva-fire, possessing the characteristics previously described, is being told here. (14.83)
Whether approaching the sacrificial pit or the consecrated ground, he should circumambulate it clockwise while muttering the Śiva-mantra and gazing at the oblation materials with his eyes.
Having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should look toward the Kuṇḍayoni while facing north and sit down,
reciting "Hauṃ Śivāya," preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "Namaḥ."

Having observed that pit in Japan and having dug it with the Astra-mantra, the Preceptor [should know] that the limbs of Śiva are seen therein for the sake of attaining the rites to be described. (14.86)
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva, salutation to the heart.
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Śiva, svāhā to the head.
Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to Śiva, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to Śiva; for the armor, huṃ. Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva; for the three eyes, vauṣaṭ.
Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to Śiva; for the weapon, phaṭ.
Having excavated with the Astra-mantra and filled [the pit] with the Hṛdaya-mantra,
one should level it with that same mantra and sprinkle it with water using the Kavaca-mantra.
Having pulverized [the vessel] with the *śara* mantra, swept it, and smeared it with that [substance], one should recite:
*oṃ hauṃ śāntyatītāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ haiṃ śāntyai namaḥ*.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Vidyā. Oṃ hīṃ, homage to Pratiṣṭhā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nivṛtti.
Thus, one should worship the Kalās in the directions of the center, east, south, west, and north.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the pit (kuṇḍa) consisting of the [thirty-six] kalās.
Having meditated upon the pit as being entirely composed of the kalās and having worshipped it,
one should then encircle that pit with a triple-thread and a kuśa blade empowered by the Astra-mantra.
One should draw three lines from east to west using the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva;
and one line from north to south in the middle, starting from the root and ending at the tip of the sacrificial fuel.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—Śiva—is their presiding deity;
then, having made them adamantine with three blades of darbha grass using the Astra-mantra, [one should do so] again with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having created a crossroads in the pit with two darbha blades whose tips point eastward and northward,
one should then [proceed] with kuśa grass over the pit purified by these eighteen consecrations.
Having consecrated the cloth as the seat for the vessel,
one should place the darbha-seat with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvarīvāgīśvarāsanāya namaḥ*.
Oṃ hāṃ, I invoke Vāgīśvarī—the dark-hued goddess, adorned and embellished with all ornaments. || 14-93 ||
Having meditated and invoked her with this [mantra], one should worship her when she has bathed after her menses;
then, with this [mantra], one should worship Vāgīśvara as one full of passion toward her who has bathed after her menses.
Having worshipped the fire with flames, smoke, and fuel as prescribed— without [using those that are improper]—
