one should bring it [the oblation] placed in a shallow dish or similar vessel and then discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda).
Having sprinkled [the site] with the root mantra, gazed upon it with the weapon mantra, and then bound it with the armor mantra,
one should protect it from the weapon mantra while recollecting it as having the form of light.
Having taken [the seed-syllables] beginning with *oṃ hoṃ rauṃ hāṃ*, one should join the fire of the eyes on the forehead with that;
[one should join] the fire arising from the navel-pit, which resembles a falling sun.
By means of the *recaka* [breath], one should draw [the breath] out through the path of the *piṅgalā* and direct it into the fire;
thus [one unites] the elemental, the divine, and the digestive fire—the threefold fire.
Having unified [the limbs] with the sixfold [mantra]:
*oṃ rāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *oṃ rīṃ śirase svāhā*;
*oṃ rūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; *oṃ raṃ netratrayāya namaḥ*.
Oṃ raḥ astrāya phaṭ;
Tāraṃ (Oṃ) hauṃ śaktaye vaṣaṭ. Having thus rendered [the substance] nectar-like by means of the Dhenu-mudrā, one should conceal it with the Kavaca-mantra. || 14-99 ||

Having protected it from the weapon-mantra and worshipped it with his heart, the preceptor should lift it up with both hands and stand upon the ground above the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) on his two knees.
Having whirled three times for the purpose of agitation, one should meditate upon the two gods, the goddess and the god, naked and with Īśāna as their head,
[reciting]: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seed-syllable of Śiva*.
Recalling it as the seed-syllable of Śiva. || 14-101 ||
One should cast that fire, facing toward oneself, through the path of the womb of the Goddess;
having unified the scattered [elements] by means of the weapon-mantra, one should lead that casket to the navel.
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī. Having thus clothed [the deity] with garments, and having provided for purification and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
one should kindle this [fire] from a fan, which has been covered with some kindling wood.
"Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the fire of the womb. Having thus worshipped, one should then bind the purified kusha-grass bracelet upon the right hand as the auspicious mark of Vāgīśvarī.

"Oṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta. Having thus invoked Sadyojāta, one should offer five oblations of sesame seeds with the Heart-mantra ending in *svāhā*, and thereby complete the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*). || 14.105 ||
Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva.
Having invoked him and offered oblations with the head [mantra], the *puṃsavana* rite is accomplished.
Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Aghora.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the body consisting of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka). One should cast a drop of water from the *kuśāstra* for the sake of the body and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), up to the point of the *arghya* with the *śikhā* [mantra].
Having offered oblations with sesame seeds and the like, one should then assign the faces and limbs [of the deity].
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the purification of the [five] faces, having likewise offered five oblations,
one should meditate upon Vāgīśī as she has brought forth [the child], as well as the infant and the fire.
Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa.
Having thus invoked Puruṣa and offered five oblations with the armor-mantra (varma),
one should then sprinkle both the exterior and interior with the water of the guest-offering (arghya) while reciting the weapon-mantra (astra).
Having discarded the darbha-grass bracelet for the sake of ending the period of ritual impurity,
he should bathe and adorn the Goddess, and likewise sprinkle the God with water consecrated by mantras.
Then, having mentally adorned those two with garments, ornaments, perfumes, and so forth,
he offers oblations of palāśa wood produced from the *astra* mantra for the purpose of removing the stake.

Five tips of sacrificial fuel-sticks, each a span in length and sprinkled with clarified butter, should be placed upon the Darbha grass to the north; there, one should set down the vessels and ritual materials.
Having also performed the strewing here with the *veṇī* and *kuśa* grasses, and having arranged the seats of *darbha* grass for the Prokṣaṇī vessel as well as for the Brahman priest; || 14.113 ||
Having placed the enclosing sticks (paridhi) of refined wood, he should perform the sprinkling;
having filled the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with water through the two strainers (*pavitra*), he should sprinkle [the sacrificial ground].
Having sprinkled [the site] in due order with the *kalās* beginning with Nivṛtti, and likewise having swept around it with a blade of *darbha* grass while reciting the Śiva-gāyatrī; 14.115.
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the presiding lord of sacrifice.
Having thus invoked Brahmā, one should worship either a twice-born Brahmin or the *kūrca* grass-bundle.
Then, having filled the *praṇītā* vessel with water for its purpose by means of the *pavitra*, [one worships] Jaleśvara.

Having meditated upon [Viṣṇu], extracted him from [the heart], and worshipped him upon his own seat, one should worship Viṣṇu—placed upon the *kūrca* grass—with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the slayer of the enemies of sacrifice," in the *praṇītā* vessel. (14.117)

Then, one should worship Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Hari, and Ananta upon the darbha-grass placed on the enclosing sticks (paridhi) in the four directions, using the syllable "Tāra" (Om) and their names preceded by "Hāṃ."

Having worshipped the world-protectors (lokeśas) in their respective directions in due order for the sake of protection, as well as their weapons in those same directions, one should then proclaim the command of Śiva.
O gods, Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the others, together with your weapons, by the command of Śiva,
stay each in your respective direction and protect the abode of the fire.

Having taken up both the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and inspected them with the Heart mantra, one should heat the well-prepared ladles with the Weapon mantra, wash them with the Head mantra, and hold them facing upwards.
Having heated [the vessel] and then washed it with *kuśa* grass from the base, the middle, and the top, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of the self (ātmatattva).
Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva)."
"Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the principle of Śiva.
Having thus wiped, rinsed, and worshipped those three in sequence, [one should proceed].
Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śakti.
Having thus worshipped the *sruk* ladle, [one says]: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva.
And with this [mantra], one should worship the *sruva* ladle;
its neck should be encircled by a triple thread, or, if not, by a blade of *darbha* grass on the right side.
Having established those two upon a seat of kuśa grass, he then [prepared] fresh,
auspicious cow-ghee, consecrated by the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (nirīkṣaṇa).
Having visualized one’s own form as Brahmī, and having heated it in the fire at the northeast corner above the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should offer oblations with this mantra:
*oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*.
Furthermore, having attained [it] in the northeast, however... || 14-125 ||
"One should offer oblations to Viṣṇu," thus [speaking], the form of Viṣṇu himself [is present];
having offered in this manner, one should heat a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade. || 14.126 ||
Then, having whirled that ghee three times around the fire with the body of Rudra,
and having offered it with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ rudrāya ṭhaṭha," he should place it upon the kuśa grass in the womb [of the fire-pit] using the tip of a kuśa blade.

Having ignited the tips of two *kuśa* blades and cast them into clarified butter while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should then throw those *darbha* blades back into the fire; that is the rite of purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*).
Having gazed at the clarified butter while reciting the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should cast the remaining darbha-torch into the fire;
then, having washed both hands while reciting the mantra for coloring the fire (tad-rañjana), one should take up the kuśa grass.
Having kindled the fire and performed the ritual circumambulation, one should cast [the oblation] and perform the illumination,
while recollecting one's own right and left hands as the two wings, white and black respectively.
Having placed the purifier into the clarified butter with the thumb and ring finger turned upward, one should place it in the eastern part, and then in the southern and northern portions.
One should contemplate the two wings, the preceding and the following, as the waxing and waning of the moon within the clarified butter (ājya);
likewise, one should visualize Piṅgalā as the iḍā and Suṣumnā in the middle.

Oṃ hāṃ agnaye ṭhaṭha. With this [mantra], having offered from the southern portion of the clarified butter into the right eye with the *sruva* ladle, and having addressed it with the *bhaga* [mantra].
Oṃ hāṃ somāya ṭhaṭha.
[This is] in the left eye of Vahni.
Oṃ hāṃ to Agni and Soma, ṭhaṭha.
Having thus offered with the portion of honey and clarified butter, [one offers] to the eye on the forehead:
Oṃ hāṃ to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, ṭhaṭha.
Thus, by offering the three portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), the visualization of the mouth of the fire is completed.
This sequence would apply in the *pūrvapakṣa* (the waxing fortnight), whereas there is a distinction in the *asita* (the waning fortnight):
*Oṃ hāṃ agnaye ṭhaṭha*, *Oṃ hāṃ sūryāya ṭhaṭha*, *Oṃ hāṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ ṭhaṭha*, *Oṃ oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte ṭhaṭha*.
In this manner, there should be the three eyes of Agni as well as the opening of his mouth. (14–135)
The placement of the three channels within the clarified butter (ājya) is likewise conceived for both fortnights;
then, having consecrated the clarified butter with the limbs [of the mantra], one recites: "Oṃ hauṃ, to Śakti, vauṣaṭ."
Having consecrated it with this as well, || 14-136 ||

Having rendered it nectar-like with the *dhenumudrā*, and having again concealed it with the *varman* (armor) mantra, one should protect it from the *astra* (weapon) mantra; such is the stated consecration (*saṃskṛti*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

If one should drop a drop of consecrated clarified butter (*ājya*) into other substances such as ghee, those [other substances] shall likewise become consecrated by means of the recitation of the *hṛdaya* mantra. (14.138)
Then, one should meditate upon the auspicious Śivāgni, who has five faces beginning with Sadyojāta, three eyes in each face, and a countenance endowed with seven tongues of flame.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Pauṣkara:

"In the four-faced [liṅgas] there are four tongues, and three in the middle one. Among these, those used for initiation, consecration, and so forth, are sāttvika; those for minor rites are tāmasa; and those for rites performed for specific desires are rājasa. These have already been mentioned. [He is] holding the gesture of fearlessness, the svastika, the spear, and the boon-granting mudrā with his arms.
Clad in white garlands and garments, anointed with unguents, and adorned with divine ornaments.
Having worshipped with offerings such as *arghya*, fragrance, and flowers according to the prescribed ritual, one should perform the oblation for each face individually, saying:

*Oṃ hāṃ sadyojātamūrtaye ṭhaṭha |* *Oṃ hāṃ vāmadevaguhyāya ṭhaṭha |* *Oṃ hāṃ aghorahṛdayāya ṭhaṭha |* *Oṃ hāṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya ṭhaṭha |* *Oṃ hāṃ īśānamūrdhāya ṭhaṭha |* In this manner, there shall be the invocation of the faces after having offered oblations separately into each respective mouth.

Oṃ hāṃ, to the form of Sadyojāta, the secret of Vāmadeva, ṭhaṭha. Oṃ hāṃ, to the secret of Vāmadeva, the heart of Aghora, ṭhaṭha. Oṃ hāṃ, to Aghora, the heart, the face of Tatpuruṣa, ṭhaṭha. Oṃ hāṃ, to the face of Tatpuruṣa, the head of Īśāna, ṭhaṭha.
Having thus joined the faces, one should offer ghee in pairs.
Oṃ hauṃ heṃ huṃ hiṃ haṃ, to Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, ṭhaṭha.
Thus, from the southeast to the northwest, and from the northwest to the end of the night-walkers (the southwest).
With the *sruva* ladle, [he should offer] a single stream of clarified butter from the Rākṣasa direction (southwest) up to the Īśa corner (northeast).
Because it is primary among the daily rites, one should perform the oblation immediately upon speaking.
Having meditated on that face as being the size of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
one should remember the unification of the faces through the entry of the other [faces] into the *sadyojāta* face.
And so it has been stated in the *Saṃhitā* regarding the daily obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) performed with water:
"The upward-facing [mouth] is declared to be primary; the other, however, possesses only secondary quality.
Furthermore—
In both the occasional (naimittika) and the optional (kāmya) rites, whichever face holds primacy, wherever it is specifically designated, its unification with the others [is prescribed]. (14.146)

Likewise, for one seeking liberation, the upward-facing [consecration] is traditionally held to be the primary initiation; the eastern [facing] is for the attainment of visible perfections, and the southern [facing] is for minor rites.
The [face] called Vāmadeva is the northern one; it bestows peace, nourishment, and desired results.
That which is called Sadyojāta is prescribed in the Saṃhitā for daily rites. (14.148)
Up to this point, the completion of the birth rite (*jātakarma*) has been described.
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna"—having thus invoked Īśāna, [one offers] five oblations of sesame seeds (*tila*). (14.149)
Having offered the oblation, one should give him a name, saying:
"Oṃ hāṃ! You are protected by the fire of Śiva. Having spoken thus, one should worship the fire.
Oṃ hāṃ, to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara, ṭhaṭha.
Having dismissed the two parents with this [mantra],
[one offers] Oṃ hauṃ, to Śiva, vauṣaṭ.
Having offered the full oblation with this [mantra], however, || 14-150 ||

In a fire consecrated by the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*) and protected for the purpose of incense and other offerings, the sacrificial oblations (*caru*) and cakes (*puroḍāśa*) should be cast. (14–151)
As it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*:
"The sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and the cake (*puroḍāśa*) are to be offered into a fire that has been consecrated by the five purificatory rites;
however, the oblation (*homa*) should be performed in a fire into which the deity has been invoked."
Then, one should perform the eleven sacraments,
beginning with the *upanayana*, by offering oblations of clarified butter three times each, using the root mantra followed by the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.

Namely: the departure from the womb, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, the initiation, the preparatory rite, the observance of vows, the gathering of vows, the concluding of vows, the gift of a cow, the return home, marriage, and the establishment of the sacred fires—these and so forth.
Then, having placed the *sruva* ladle face down upon the *sruc* which is full of clarified butter;
Having placed a flower on the tip of the sacrificial ladle with both hands in the śaṅkha-mudrā gesture, || 14-153 ||
Holding those two [sticks] with their handles joined together and standing with feet even,
he should fix his gaze on the tip of the *sruk* while reciting the root mantra and the mantras for the heart and other limbs.

At the end of the mantra, ending with *bauṣaṭ*, one should pour an unbroken stream of clarified butter the size of a barley grain into the fire; in this manner, the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) is accomplished.
Immediately after, [he says]: "O Śiva, in the lotus of your heart! Having invoked Śiva in this sacrifice, we shall perform the worship with your permission. (14-156)
Thus, having received permission, he should then invoke Śiva into the fire by means of his own seat, limbs, and form, and perform the concentration upon Śiva (śivasandhāna).
By means of the pure, severed radiance emitted from the tip of the nose of Śiva residing in the *baindhava* [knot],
together with the light issuing from the tip of the nose of Śiva residing in the *liṅga*.
One should visualize the connection through the piṅgalā-nāḍī up to the end of the āyāga;
having worshipped with the aforementioned offerings such as clarified butter and other oblations, one should satisfy Śiva.
The oblation that is being offered into the sacrificial fire as prescribed by the injunctions [is conveyed] by Agni through the path of Suṣumṇā to the head of Śiva via the Suṣumṇā.
Having focused [on the Lord], one should satisfy the Sovereign with streams of nectar in the form of cows, so that Śiva may become pleased and grant his own desired boons. (14–161)
The Chapter on the Conjunction of the Channels:
Now, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and food with clarified butter are prescribed for the daily oblation (*nitya-homa*).
For special rites (*vaiśeṣika-kṛtya*), one should offer oblations with the materials specified [in the scriptures]. (14–162)

Let the oblation of clarified butter offered to the limbs of the ten forms [of the deity] from Śiva on the festival days be double that of the daily offering; or let the recitation (japa) be equal to the fire-oblation.

Saying "Oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā," one should sprinkle the three portions of the sacrificial oblation (caru) with clarified butter, offer them with the large ladle (sruc), and then offer them once each to the Mūrtis and the Aṅgas.
Having offered the rinsing water (ācāma) with the prokṣaṇī waters and the arghya with the Astra mantra,
one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and also with betel.

Having prepared the fire and touched the ashes, one should release the connection of the channels (nāḍī-sandhi) while reciting the seed-syllables and so forth, the vyāhṛtis, and the mantras of the forms and limbs, each once.

Having offered the clarified butter and drawn it out with the Astra-mantra, one should assign the limbs of the Mūrti to Śiva according to their proper positions; then, having placed Śiva who resides in the fire into the heart-lotus of the fire, [one should proceed].
Alternatively, having restrained [the fire], one should protect it or release it every day.
Reciting "Oṃ hauṃ haiṃ hūṃ hīṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva," one should take that form of Śiva from the fire into a handful of flowers. (14–168)
Oṃ hauṃ, oṃ hoṃ, oṃ heṃ, oṃ huṃ, oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Śiva.
With this [mantra], one should unite [the self] with Śiva residing in the liṅga, or within the lotus of the heart.
However, if the liṅga exists [externally], the connection of the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna) must first be performed toward that Śiva in the liṅga. (14–169)

In the case of the non-concrete (aliṅga), one should perform the union [of the deity] with Śiva within the lotus of one's own heart; likewise, one should conceive of the extraction [of the deity] from the tip of its nose.
One should also infer the ritual procedure for the dismissal (udvāsana) in the same manner.
In the case of rites performed for specific purposes, if he is a twice-born, he should offer oblations with the *jaya* and other formulas,
as well as the expiations for the ministers and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

Oṃ hāṃ to Agni, ṭhaṭha. Oṃ hāṃ to Soma, ṭhaṭha. Oṃ hāṃ to Agni and Soma, ṭhaṭha. Oṃ hāṃ to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, ṭhaṭha. With these mantras one should offer oblations; by these very [mantras] among the twice-born [castes]. Or, having prepared two mandalas to the east or in front of the fire for Agni... [14-172]

One should offer the oblation (bali) with one's own names preceded by "Tāra" (Oṃ) and "Hṛt" (Namaḥ), ending with "namas," using the remainder of the sacrificial porridge (caru) along with perfumes and other offerings, according to the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions.
And for the Rudras, the groups of Mothers, the Yakṣas, the Grahas, the enemies of the gods (Asuras),
the Rākṣasas, and the Nāgas, [the offerings] proceed in order starting from the east and Īśāna (northeast).
And among the constellations, and again from the midst of these,
and further from the zodiac signs, ending with Īśa (the North-East), and also from Vahni (the South-East) to Viśva (the All).
To Kṣetrapāla in the southwest and to Durgā in the northwest;
having thus offered the internal bali, one should again [offer] in the second maṇḍala.
One should offer bali to Indra and the others in the ten directions as before; having dismissed them, one should again offer bali outside the mandala and so forth.
Having scattered [the offering] in all directions for the crows and others who violate the covenant, [say] "ṭhaṭha.
Then one should take away the bali-mantras.
Furthermore, at the edge of the courtyard section, one should offer an oblation upon the mandala.
Those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in fierce abodes, as well as those who are gentle and dwell in gentle abodes— || 14-179 ||
May the Mothers of fierce form and those who are the lords of the Gaṇas—
all of them, with well-pleased minds, accept this bali offering.
"May they quickly grant me success; may they always protect me from fears.
Homage to all beings! Having thus cast the *bali* offering, [he says]:
"Furthermore, O Yoginīs, terrifying ones, fierce ones, Vetālas, and Brahmarākṣasas! (14–181)
May they come and accept this offering given by me, acting in accordance with the will of Śiva;
may they swiftly protect me always from all fears.

Oṃ hāṃ haḥ huṃ phaṭ. With this [mantra], one should cast the bali offering. Having given the bali, then having washed the feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), remaining silent, and having paid homage to Mahādeva, one should perform the rites in their proper sequence.
The section on the Śaiva fire-ritual.
Now, the Vaiṣṇava fire-ritual as enjoined by the Tantras is described:
having bathed, washed his feet, sipped water, performed breath-control, and restrained his speech... (14.184)
Then one should draw three lines facing east and three facing north;
having recited the twelve-syllable vidyā in the proper sequence. (14.185)
Having cast away the scrapings, washed his hands, and sprinkled [himself] with water while reciting the Vidyā,
he should perform the placement of the syllables upon his hands and limbs, while meditating on the Tāra-mantra.
There, having invoked the supreme Śakti while remembering Lakṣmī as being in her menses,
and likewise having invoked Viṣṇu as one who has bathed and is adorned, he should worship those two.
Having brought forth one of the three sacred fires (āraṇeya), or fire contained in a shallow vessel and the like,
and having sprinkled it with water while recollecting the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu, [he should proceed].
Having cast the embryo into the womb of the Goddess and meditated upon it with fuel,
one should kindle it with ignorance as before and sweep around it.
Having placed the vessels upon *darbha* grass and strewn them around in due order,
one should fill the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with water while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having invoked Hari into that [fire] and sprinkled those vessels with its water,
he should then turn the vessels face-upward and loosen the fuel and the sacrificial grass (vedhas).
Having invoked [the deity] on the south as before and worshipped it, one should again fill the *praṇītā* vessel with water from the north,
and place it there as before.
Having invoked Viṣṇu along with his limbs (retinue) and worshipped him, and having set aside the clarified butter,
he should cook it over the northern embers and heat it three times with kuśa grass.

Having purified them three times and placed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with *darbha* grass at the front, one should heat them again and wash them; then, from the syllable *TĀR*, one should wipe their tips from the front.

One should cast the middle [blade] with the middle [finger], and the root [blade] with the root [finger], into the fire; having placed the enclosing sticks (paridhi) and the two upright fuel-sticks as before, one should do so with the Vidyā-mantra.

Having sprinkled [water] around and taken the fuel, having sprinkled it with ghee while reciting the *Tāra* mantra, one should offer it once; likewise, having offered two oblations (*āghāra*) with the twelve-syllable mantra.

Having offered oblations with sesame seeds three times for each mantra during the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony (*garbhādhāna*), he should dismiss the deceased's two parents by reciting the *praṇava*.
One should meditate upon the Vaiṣṇava form of Fire seated upon a golden lotus-throne—
five-faced, four-armed, golden-hued, and three-eyed.
The earth became his feet, the sky his head, and the vital breaths his wind;
the sun was his eyes, the ether his chest, and the seven worlds were his tongues.
The Gārhapatya fire should be in the heart, and the Āhavanīya fire in the mouths;
the Anvāhārya fire should be in the stomach, and the Vedas are the mouths in their respective order.
That which consists of the Ṛgveda is golden-hued, faces the east, and is the means for rites pertaining to the gods;
that which belongs to the Yajurveda resembles crushed collyrium, faces the south, and performs minor rites.
The western [Atharvaveda] is considered suitable for rites of pacification, resembling the rising sun;
the northern [Sāmaveda], resembling the moon, is the means for accomplishing rites of desire.
Having thus meditated upon Him—who consists of all the Vedas, who is radiant like crystal, and who bestows liberation—and having worshipped Him in His heart-lotus, [one should proceed]. (14.203)
Having invoked Vāsudeva, who has four arms and bears the conch, discus, and mace, according to his described form, and having worshipped him, one performs oblations with the prescribed mantras.
If he is a twice-born, having offered oblations with the *jaya* and other mantras, as well as the *sviṣṭakṛt*,
he should conclude that rite after giving the sacrificial fee (*brahmadakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmin priest.
Then, having likewise released the *praṇītā* waters and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*),
one should cause Acyuta, who resides in the fire, to flow away into either the image or the lotus of one's own heart.

One should also cause the fire to proceed as before, together with its primary and secondary limbs (sāṅgopāṅga). This is the section on the Vaiṣṇava fire-ritual; now follows the ritual manual (kalpa) concerning the fire, which accomplishes all purposes through mantras. || 14-207 ||

It is said that either a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) possessing the prescribed characteristics should be smeared with cow dung; having removed [impurities] from Tārā with a blade of grass, one should proceed.
Having leveled and smeared [the ground], one should then draw three lines toward the east— middle, southern, and northern— using a fragment of gold or other precious metal.
Then, having sprinkled [the ground] and reciting the Praṇava everywhere, one should draw lines toward the north from the middle, the west, and the east, and discard the scrapings.

Having observed fire brought from a fire-drill, a gem, or even from the house of a learned Vedic scholar, and having sprinkled it [with water] while reciting the Tāra mantra, [one should place it] in a shallow bowl or similar vessel. (14.211)
Having discarded the portion intended for the flesh-eaters, being pure and restrained in speech, facing the east,
he should then apply the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) and the lunar fire (*aindavāgni*) to this physical body.
The practitioner, having bathed, should worship both Śakti— who is in her menses— and Īśvara with the desire to create, using the Śakti-bīja mantra.
Having contemplated the seed-syllable of Īśa (H), one should cast it into the womb of Śakti;
then, having raised it up with two pieces of fuel, one should subsequently cover it with fuel.
Oṃ, O Citpiṅgala, slay, burn, cook! The Omniscient One commands: ṭhaṭha! Having kindled the sacrificial fire with this fan, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ, I revere the blazing fire, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations. (14.215)
Then, one should perform worship with this [mantra] to the fire, which is golden-colored, kindled, and facing in all directions, and one should cast a flower [into it]. || 14-216 ||
Having spread darbha grass individually starting from the east, the preceptor,
having sprinkled it with water silently, should worship the fire with the six limbs.
Having cast a drop of water, which has become the living soul, into the fire while reciting the Praṇava,
one should perform the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) in due order by means of the six limbs of one's own [mantra].
Having offered three counter-oblations and sprinkled water around the fire with the *Tāra* mantra,
one should place the vessels to the north of the fire upon *darbha* grass, as before.

Having strewn darbha grass around [the altar] in due order, according to the number required for the water-sprinkling and other rites, just as before, he should likewise prepare the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and the *vedhas*.
Having honored the *praṇītā* vessel and sprinkled water around the fire in due order from the beginning,
one should meditate [on the deity] seated upon a golden throne-lotus, white and radiant with filaments.
Then, there are eight forms of the fire-eaters situated upon the tips of the eight petals:
Agni shall be the first form, as well as Vaiśvānara and Hutāśana.
Jātavedas, Hutavaha, Hutavarmā, and thereafter Devamukha and Saptajihva—these are the eight forms (mūrtis). || 14-223 ||
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and likewise Havyavāha; Aśvodara, as well as Āja, and then the one named Vaiśvānara.
In the same way, Kaumāratejas and Viśvedevamukha, as well as the eight forms beginning with Agni-pada, are what others have proclaimed. (14.225)
He holds the Śakti, the Svastika, the Abhaya mudrā, and the Varada mudrā; he possesses the luster of saffron and is adorned with white unguents, garlands, and garments.
His circle of matted locks is radiant, his crown is set with jewels and pure, dangling pearl necklaces, and he shines brilliantly with golden chains.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god, who is gentle, the granter of desired objects, three-eyed, and of serene countenance.
Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, the one called Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā—these seven are proclaimed as the Sāttvika [Nāḍīs]. (14.227)
Padmarāgā, Suvarṇī, Bhadrā, Lohitā, Lohitā, Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālī—these are associated with the quality of rajas. (14.228)
Viśvamūrti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, Manojavā, Vilohitā, Karālī, and Kālī—these are endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas). || 14-229 ||

The tongues [of fire] are formed by the elements and seeds stated in reverse order, adorned with fire and wind; they are located in the directions starting from the east, and those of the Vasus, Dharā, and Īśa are situated in the corners.
Among the rites for the gods, those characterized by sattva are prescribed for daily and pacificatory ceremonies;
those characterized by rajas are recommended for rites with specific desires; and those characterized by tamas are for cruel deeds.
The deities, the ancestors, the gandharvas, the yakṣas, the nāgas, the piśācas, and likewise the brahmarākṣasas, are the lords of the tongues in their respective order. (14.232)
The earth is renowned as being composed of all the gods and serves as a sacrificial tongue;
upon it, desirable rites are prescribed, while the remaining ones are declared by the Vedas.
One should worship the forms and the tongues [of the fire] with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then follow the mantras: *sahasrārcis*, *svastipūrṇa*, and *uttiṣṭhapuruṣa*. (14.234)
Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and likewise the sixth, Dhanurdhara—
these six are the limb-mantras of Agni, each separately conjoined with its own seed-syllable.
The limbs and the forms themselves should be serene and four-armed,
adorned with ornaments of gold and decorated with spears, svastikas, and pairs of arms.
Likewise, one should worship Indra and the other world-protectors, as well as their weapons, on the outside;
and having meditated upon one's own form as being of the nature of fire, with the limbs [of the mantra] assigned to it.

Having worshipped the fire with perfumes and other offerings, having consecrated the clarified butter as before, and having likewise cleansed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles according to the path prescribed for the Vedic fire— || 14.238 ||

Then, having offered oblations with the *prājāpatya* and other mantras into the mouth of the fire of the altar, one should offer to the limbs, the forms, and the tongues, each with a single oblation of clarified butter in successive order.
Having performed the oblation with this mantra, one should again offer a single oblation:
first the syllable *tāra* (Oṃ), then the three *vyāhṛtis*, and after that the word *vaiśvānara*.
"O Jātavedas, bring that being here; accomplish all rites, ṭhaṭha.
The wise know this mantra, beginning with the Vyāhṛtis, to be the root-mantra of Agni.
Savitṛ is its seer (ṛṣi), and the meter (chandas) is known as the divine Gāyatrī. (14.241)
The deity Jātavedas Agni is employed at the beginning of rites for prosperity;
for he bestows great prosperity, and he should be recited ten thousand times or more.

Having first offered oblations in the directions starting from the east, in due order on the first lunar days and so forth, using rice, fuel-sticks of the Nyagrodha tree, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and milk-rice; 14-243.
And let him offer clarified butter into the fire one thousand and eight times, or one hundred times;
and on the eleventh day, having fed as many pure brahmins as his means allow.
By giving a red cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the mantra becomes successful for one seeking prosperity.

Having offered the aforementioned substances on the first lunar day (pratipad) either eight times each or a thousand times, or else having offered rice or old grain daily in the number of Rudras (eleven).
Prosperity will come through fuel that is either split or shaken apart for three fortnights, or through *pālāśa* wood mixed with sweet substances, or indeed through flowers.
One desiring prosperity should daily offer milk-rice with ghee from a cow, or milk, or the milk of a tawny cow (kapila), or cow-ghee;
or else, one desiring Lakṣmī should offer eight thousand flowers soaked in honey for a month.
One who subsists on milk and performs oblations with the milk of a red cow for a full month shall obtain inexhaustible prosperity.
One desiring intelligence, having consumed clarified butter from the *brāhma* vessel or that which has been touched [by it] on full moon days, shall obtain it. (14.247)
Having offered one hundred thousand oblations of dūrvā sprouts with clarified butter, one conquers death and attains long life;
and by offering even a single oblation, one establishes oneself at the beginning of all sacrificial rites through this mantra.

When one offers eight thousand oblations of milk-rice with clarified butter into the fire on the day of the Āhavanīya and other rites at dawn, that very offering becomes inexhaustible; indeed, the Āhavanīya itself brings forth wealth, gold, food, cattle, and prosperity.
Its meter is Atyanuṣṭubh, and its seer is said to be Kāśyapa;
Bhadrāgni is the deity, and the limbs and the means of accomplishment are as previously stated. (14.250)
By reciting a thousand *pañkti* verses dedicated to Prajāpati, and by performing oblations of boiled rice with clarified butter and curds, one attains *lakṣmī*.

Alternatively, there may be an oblation on the first lunar days (*pratipad*) using the aforementioned substances smeared with clarified butter, or an oblation performed with the *vyāhṛti* mantras. (14–251)
The *triṣṭubh* shall be its meter, the venerable Marīci the seer (*ṛṣi*), and Prajāpati the deity; the components of the practice are as before. (14.252)

Having extracted the word *uttiṣṭha* (stand up), [place] *puruṣa*, *hari*, *pada*, and *sārdhacandra*; then the two eyes, the side, the heart, the flesh, and the two bodies; then the middle of the left foot;
the long *atri*, the side at the end, and *marut*—this is said to end with *vahnijāyā* (the wife of fire, i.e., *svāhā*).
This mantra, ending with two *tāra*s (OM) and preceded by *vahni* (RAUM), is a wish-fulfilling tree for all the desires of the entire world. || 14-253 ||
Its metre is Gāyatrī, and its sage is Aṅgiras;
some say it is Bhṛgu.
The deity is Agni himself, in the form of a horse, the giver of gold. (14–254)
Whether daily, or on the first day of the lunar fortnight, or once under the asterism Kṛttikā, let one offer oblations of śāli rice mixed with ghee to Lakṣmī;
or, having offered curd-rice or ghee with fuel-sticks of śamī wood, one indeed attains the desired great prosperity. (14.255)

Having offered clarified butter, one shall obtain that which is desired; having offered half a hundred thousand lotuses, the city and other such things become easily attainable; with fuel-sticks from the *pippala* tree, one shall obtain a maiden; with sacrificial porridge mixed with ghee, one gains victory; with *jyotiṣka* oil, one acquires kingdoms; by recitation (*japa*), one destroys even diseases and waters; whatever indeed is accomplished through the perfection of recitation, let that be attained here in this world for the practitioner. [One sees] the form of a horse emerging from the hollows of the houses of the golden *aśvattha* and *kalpa* trees.

Meditating on the mass of clouds raining fire, with the sky turned tawny by the flames rising from the pores of his hair through the apertures of his body, one should offer a single oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) on the first day of the lunar fortnight; having placed it in a goblet filled with half-a-prastha of clarified butter, he shall before long become a lord of wealth.
Thus has been declared the procedure for the fire-sacrifice which bestows desired results; this ritual for the oblations is the same at every fixed time.
And let him cause the foremost of the twice-born to recite the mantra for the attainment of its fruit.
At the end, one should always feed them all here with flavorful food.
Feeding one-tenth as many Brahmins according to the sequence of oblations is the primary method;
likewise, feeding one-twentieth and a half is the middling method; and feeding one-hundredth is the lowest; one should apply these according to one's capacity.
The conclusion consists of giving gifts, providing a meal, and the worship of the deities. || 14-258 ||

In the same way, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the oblation is prescribed as one māna of gold; however, in rites pertaining to the gods, those for nourishment, and those for subjugation, it is two mānas. In rites of expulsion, driving away, and restraint, it is two mānas.
In cases of disease, delusion, and exhaustion, one should prescribe the three-measure dose.
In the same way, gold measured by a *kṛṣṇala* is used for the rite of killing;
for this has been shown in both the *Tattvasāgara* and the *Prapañca*.
[Such a person] would burn a man who performs a ritual practice devoid of the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Therefore, a wise person should not perform a sacrifice with inferior sacrificial fees.
This indeed is the supreme sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), while the middling is half of that;
the inferior shall be half of that again, as determined by one's capacity.
What is called "sacrificial fee" for this? It is the fruit of this ritual action.
It is demonstrated and experienced; therefore, that which is desired should be bestowed.
Now, regarding rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), one should abandon the preparation of the fire-pit (*vahnikuṇḍa*) and so forth in the city of Indra,
as well as in the ocean or rivers; instead,
one should perform there rites of pacification (*śāntika*) along with constant charity, dharma, and worship.
In such a way that the protection of one's own body, country, and lineage shall be accomplished. || 14-262 ||
In the same way, having completed the rites for pacification and so forth, ending with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), according to the procedure shown in the *Vaidikāgnikalpa*,
one should dissolve the deity and the fire into the lotus of the water-moon.
One should employ [the mantra] over that which rains down showers of nectar-water.

Thus, having examined and demonstrated here the procedure enjoined in the *Tattvasāgara* and other tantras, as well as that shown in the Vedic ritual manuals (*prayoga*), commentaries (*vṛtti*), and *gṛhya* texts, and that declared in the *Śivāgama*.
But let it be practiced sufficiently by practitioners for their own ease through application.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Fire Ritual," in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Thus the first chapter, the General Section, is completed.
May there be auspiciousness.
